IT will be difficult for the kindliest temper to give Prepossessions a friendly welcome to the medical philosophy of Saxon days. As man has an ever recurring proneness to make himself the standard of truth, to condemn, sneer at, and despise all that he does not choose or is unable to comprehend, so in a greater degree every generation of men admires its own wisdom, skill, science, art, and progress; it calls its own, whatever it has learnt from men of former days, and counts the few improvements which have had their birth in its own time, as triumphs and distinctions which elevate it above all the past.

If we consider the history of the ages gone by, these Our debt to high pretensions will soon abate somewhat of their past ages. confidence. The progress of those contrivances towards our comfort, which we sum up in the term civilization, has been very creeping and laborious. Our great capitals are smaller than Rome, the fortunes of our men of millions are trifles to the wealth of a Crassus or a Lucullus, our houses are less carefully warmed in winter than the Roman villas, our poetry has no Homeros, our sculpture no Praxiteles, our architecture no Parthenon, our philosophy has never seen a century such as that between Perikles and Alexandros, those hundred years of Attic wit and wisdom have given us an education in dead languages, and in the lore and manners of two thousand years since, and are driving our native words from off our tongues and making them strange to our ears.

PREFACE.

It will be difficult for even the kindliest disposition to give a friendly welcome to the medical philosophy of Saxon days. As man has an ever-recurring tendency to make himself the standard of truth, to condemn, sneer at, and despise all that he does not choose or is unable to understand, so in an even greater degree every generation of men admires its own wisdom, skill, science, art, and progress. It claims as its own whatever it has learned from men of earlier times, and counts the few improvements that have originated in its own era as triumphs and distinctions that raise it above all that came before.

If we consider the history of ages past, these lofty pretensions will soon lose some of their confidence. The progress of those contrivances that contribute to our comfort, which we sum up in the word civilization, has been very slow and laborious. Our great capitals are smaller than Rome; the fortunes of our wealthiest men are trivial compared to the wealth of a Crassus or a Lucullus; our houses are less carefully heated in winter than the Roman villas; our poetry has no Homer, our sculpture no Praxiteles, our architecture no Parthenon; our philosophy has never seen a century like that between Pericles and Alexander. Those hundred years of Attic wit and wisdom have given us an education in dead languages and in the customs and manners of two thousand years ago, and are driving our native words from our tongues and making them unfamiliar to our ears.

x PREFACE.

The Saxons
accept Greek
and Latin
learning.

The same victory over future ages which puts into
the hands of our children a Virgilius, a Demosthenes
an Horatius, produced a similar effect upon our fore-
fathers. When their driving, conquering, advancing
spirit brought them into the island of the Britons
and gave them the Keltic careless tribes for a prey,
they also found it worth their while to inquire what
was this system of Latin science, which raised fertile
crops of wheat for the food of every mouth, built
houses which gave warmth amid the tempest, and
fetched from foreign distant lands aids and helps
whether to health or to disease; and they, like our-
selves, became students of Latin and Greek. Something
of course they had learned of southern arts before,
but when they arrived in and became owners of ter-
ritories improved by the southron, they could only
enjoy their new acquisitions fully by understanding
the method of ordering them.

Indigenous
botany of the
Teutonic
races.

The Gothic nations had a knowledge of their own
in the kinds and powers of worts, that is they had
the more useful practical part of botany; this is
plainly proved by the great number of native names
of plants which are found in the works now printed,
in glossaries, and in the Gothic languages generally.
Their medicine must have consisted partly in the
application of the qualities of these worts to healing
purposes, for otherwise the study was of no real utility.
The uses of hemp and liquorice were first learnt by
the Hellenes, from the Skythians.¹ The Saxons evi-
dently were also willing to rely much upon amulets
and incantations, for while these resources are accepted
by the later Greek physicians, they occur much more
frequently as the northern nations obtained a wider
footing in the Roman empire.

This is page x of the Preface.

The Saxons accept Greek and Latin learning.

The same victory over future ages that puts into our children's hands a Virgil, a Demosthenes, a Horace, produced a similar effect upon our forefathers. When their driving, conquering, advancing spirit brought them into the island of the Britons and delivered the careless Celtic tribes to them as prey, they also found it worthwhile to inquire into this system of Latin knowledge, which raised fertile crops of wheat to feed every mouth, built houses that gave warmth against the storm, and brought from foreign distant lands remedies and aids for health and disease. Like us, they became students of Latin and Greek. They had of course already learned something of southern arts before, but when they arrived and became owners of territories that had been improved by the southerners, they could only fully enjoy their new acquisitions by understanding the methods by which they were managed.

Indigenous botany of the Teutonic races.

The Gothic nations had knowledge of their own regarding the kinds and properties of plants — that is, they possessed the more useful practical part of botany. This is clearly proved by the great number of native plant names found in the works now printed, in glossaries, and in the Gothic languages generally. Their medicine must have consisted partly in applying the properties of these plants to healing purposes, for otherwise the study would have had no real utility. The uses of hemp and liquorice were first learned by the Greeks from the Scythians. The Saxons evidently were also willing to rely heavily on amulets and incantations, for while these practices are accepted by the later Greek physicians, they appear much more frequently as the northern nations gained a wider foothold in the Roman empire.

¹ Herodotus, Book IV, Chapter 74. Theophrastus, Historia Plantarum, Book IX, Chapter 15.

translation:
PREFACE. xiii

reflected antennae, and make an amulet of him. For sleep, the gall of a sacrificed goat smeared on the eyes or placed under the pillow was considered effective.

Demokritos was a devoted follower of the teaching of the Magi, "the most devoted student of the magicians." He wrote of an herb whose root, made into pills and swallowed in wine, would make guilty men confess everything, tormented at night by strange visions of the spirit world. Another herb, the "food of Gods," kept the kings of Persia in health and mental vigor. The "gospel plant" was drunk by the Magi before divination. The "laughter plant" produced phantoms and laughter, which could only be stopped by eating pine nuts, pepper, and honey in date wine. They also had an herb for producing handsome and good children. A disciple of Demokritos, Apollodoros, possessed a plant that could revive old love, even love that had turned to hatred. All these had magical names. Pliny's view of the general standing of the Magi's doctrine was that it was, of all the sciences found across the globe, the most fraudulent — which, it should be noted, is saying quite a lot — and that it owed its acceptance to its incorporating within itself the three most influential sciences among men: medicine; and religion, in whose darkness, Pliny says, the human race is still entangled (to call it superstition would be too modern a term); and mathematics, that is to say, astronomy.

Pythagoras held that the entire air is full of spiritual beings, who send men dreams and the signs of disease and health; and not to men alone, but to sheep and other livestock as well; and that for these spirits, purification rituals, averting ceremonies, and invocations are naturally devised.

PREFACE. XV

"They report having discovered this: but by the judgment of Soranus, those who believed that the strength of passion could be excluded by rhythms and song seem to be boasting out of mental vanity."

Pliny records that the rule is to sow basil with curses and ugly words; that pills of elaterium, the powerful juice of a wild cucumber, hung about the waist in rams wool, help childbirth, if the patient knows nothing about the remedy; he knew a man of praetorian rank, a chief man in Spain, who was cured of intolerable disorders of the uvula by carrying hung around his neck on a thread a root of purslane; that Sappho fell in love with Phaon because he found a masculine root of eryngium; that an amulet made of the seed of tribulus cures varicose veins; that tradition holds that men afflicted with tertian fever are relieved of it if they tie onto themselves a root of autumnal nettle, provided that when the root is dug the sick man's and his parents' names are duly spoken aloud; that if a man carries a poplar wand in his hand he will not get his legs chafed; the herb selago, which resembled savine, was gathered without use of iron, with the right hand, in pickpocket fashion, poked through the left armhole of the tunic, wearing a white robe, with bare clean washed feet, after an offering of wine and bread. Since ordinary "clinical" medicine is of no use in quartan fevers, he will tell us how to cure it by amulets; by the dust in which a hawk has been rolling himself, tied up in a piece of cloth with a red thread; by the longest tooth of a black dog; by a solitary wasp caught in the left hand.

PREFACE. xvii

Xenokrates, who according to Galenos flourished two generations, or sixty years, before him, writes with an air of confidence about the good effects to be obtained by eating the human brain, flesh, or liver; by swallowing in drink the burnt or unburnt bones of the head, shin, or fingers of a man, or his blood. He also had a good list of nasty prescriptions, for which the veil of a dead language is required.

Galenos is cited by Alexander of Tralles as paying reluctant homage to incantations. His words perhaps do not go further than the conclusions of an unprejudiced physician of our own day might reach, were he willing to brave the quickly rising charge of superstition. "Some think that incantations are like old wives' tales, as I too did for a long while. But at last I was convinced that there is virtue in them by plain proofs before my eyes. For I had trial of their beneficial operation in the case of those stung by scorpions, and no less in the case of bones stuck fast in the throat, immediately thrown up by an incantation. And many of them are excellent, severally, and they reach their mark."

Pamphilos makes Galenos angry with his gypsy trickeries: "his old wives' tales, his Egyptian quackeries, his babbling incantations used by the folk employed to collect plants, his charms, and his humbugs — not merely useless, not merely unprofessional, but all false; no good even to little boys, not to say

PREFACE. xxi

The practical wisdom of such men as Hippokrates, and the Epicurean skepticism of the age of Horace, had reduced the influence of magicians among educated minds to some reasonable limits. The revival of their power has been attributed to the depressing effect of imperial tyranny; but a larger share is probably due to the inroad of barbaric minds which the calm light of knowledge had not reached.

Saxons, Angles, and all the Gothic races were wholly unable to accept, to use, to learn the medical skill of Greece and of its pupil Italy. The point to which surgery had been brought was high; and if we don't say the same of medicine, perhaps we are not very good judges, having discovered very few remedies of our own. Our measure of their proficiency will be much safer in surgery than in pharmacy.

It seems pretty well agreed by competent and careful critics that the book on Wounds of the Head is by the great Hippokrates, who flourished at Kos during the Peloponnesian war (active 436, died 377?). He used a small drill, called a small trepan, which implies also some greater saw, which had a circular motion, and which is judged by medical men to be the trephine, and a jagged saw, which is held to be the trepan, and he gives careful directions to the operator to withdraw the instrument frequently and cool both it and the bone with cold water, and to take all care not to wound the lining membrane. The employment of splints on broken limbs is not of much note here, as we find our Saxons could adopt that resource. In the opinion of Dr. Greenhill, the Oath in the works of Hippokrates may be his; according to the last editor of his works, it is his, or of the Koan school.

Not only the Engle and Seaxe, the warrior inhabitants of our own island, but also all the races of Gothic invaders, were too rude to learn much of Galenos, or of Alexander of Tralles, though they would fain do so. The writings of Marcellus, called Empiricus, the Herbarium of Apuleius, the stuff current under the name of Sextus Placitus, the copious volumes of Constantinus Africanus, the writings of St. Hildegard of Bingen, the collections out of Dioskorides, the smaller Saxon pieces, are all of one character, substituting for the case of instruments and Indian drugs, indigenous herbs, the worts of fatherland, smearings, and wizard chants. Over the whole face of Europe, while the old Hellenic school survived in Arabia, the next to hand resource became the established remedy, and the searching incision of the practised anatomist was replaced by a droning song.

The triumphant barbarians had no Pæan, no Æsculapius, no Chiron, far less an Hippokrates. That they must have employed herbs before their pouring down over the south seems indisputable, and leeches are not only Teutonic in the form of their name, but are mentioned as driving a profession in the rudest ages.

Marcellus, an author of little other worth, is useful in showing both how the skilled use of surgical instruments had been lost, and how much more vigorously this weed of faith in spiritual influences had grown. The following story is from the Heimskringla: "Vanlandi was the name of a son of Svegð, who succeeded him to the kingship and managed the wealth of the people of Uppsala. He was a great man of war, and he traveled far and wide across lands. He spent the winter in Finland with Snio the Old, and took his daughter Drifa as his wife. In spring he went away, and Drifa was left behind; and he gave his word to return within three winters' time, but he did not come back for ten winters. Then Drifa sent for a cunning woman, Huld, and sent Visbur, her son by Vanlandi, to Svithia, the Uppsala country. Drifa bargained with Huld, the cunning woman, that she should bewitch Vanlandi back into Finland, or failing that, should put him to death. When the witchery was worked, Vanlandi was at Uppsala; then he made himself ready to travel to Finland, but his friends and his counselors urged him not to, and said that the hand of a Finnish witch was behind his eagerness to go. Then a heavy drowsiness came over him, and he lay himself down to sleep. When he had slept a little, he called out and said that a mare was trampling him. His men came to him and tried to help him, but when they lifted his head, she trod upon his legs so that they nearly broke. When they lifted his feet, she danced upon his head, so that he died."

The Exorcist, called upon at times to drive out devils other than Chemosh, was a recognized officer in the Church, and was given his proper position and dignity. It is far less common to find a woman made pregnant by such devilry, and of a pregnant she-devil I have never read. Hence in the passage from the Leechbook, I. lxiii., where the only known meanings of the word ƿeban are — 1. to procreate, beget, bring forth; 2. to nourish — and since the second meaning is inappropriate, we may understand the former as applying to the father. Geƿebeð, meaning born, in Beda, p. 565, 29, implies an active verb ƺeƿeban, meaning to beget. We find then in the Leechbook not only the assertion that a devil has sexual intercourse — that is, that a she-devil couples, or that a he-devil does so — with mankind, but even that offspring may result from this vile union. This goes beyond the ordinary range of opinion. translation:
PREFACE. xlv

"...mischievous stuff, that they may have them for wives." In the Shrift book of Ecgbert, archbishop of York, one of their methods is censured, and it is so filthy, that I must leave it in the obscurity of the original old English. [Old English passage too corrupt to translate fully] It is necessary to quote another record of their nasty ways, in a language more generally known. "Certain women have been heard boasting of offering their own excrement to others to consume, especially their menstrual blood, to compel men to love them." St. Hildegard speaks of bewitched love as familiar; "But if any man has been deceived by a woman, or any woman by a man, through any magic art, or has been touched by any illusion of that matter, or has been bound by any fantastical and diabolical incantations, so that a man goes mad with love for a woman or a woman for a man in such a way, then let him seek out betony." The herb will be a cure, "if no love-inducing food or drink has been tasted either by eating or drinking." It is also a good remedy for love caused by magic words.

A man's death was sometimes brought about by the arts of the sorcerer, who was undoubtedly a true poisoner, compounding poisons when occasion required, but who was also supposed to work by incantation and fascination.

The prevalence of superstition is well seen in a Doom of King Knut: "And we earnestly forbid every heathen practice; a heathen practice is when a man reverences idols — that is, when a man reverences heathen gods."

translation: This page is already written in modern English and requires no translation. It is a preface passage discussing historical accounts of weather magic and sorcery. A child learned from her mother how to summon rain and hail by stirring water with her finger in the devil's name; her father, after witnessing this, reported her mother to the authorities, who burned the mother alive, while the child was reconciled to the church and made a nun. The text then cites the Saga of Saint Olaf, noting that the Finns used cunning sorcery to raise storms at sea, and recounts how King Hakon Hakonarson, while in the Southern Isles (the Hebrides), was struck by a great storm on the night before Monday following St. Michael's Mass on a Saturday. The storm drove ships onto the Scottish coast with such violence that some crews cut away their masts. The king's ship was driven into a sound where seven anchors were deployed, and even the eighth and largest anchor barely held, though eventually it did hold fast.

So great was this storm that men said it was the work of enchantment, and someone composed these skaldic verses about it:

"There met the far-seeking sustainer of war, the sorcerer's arts of Scotland's warlocks. The roaring, raging sea drove with its fair sails many a proud ship of the ring-giver broken onto land. It blew with its loud blasts upon the sea-going vessels, fully laden with warriors — the sea storm fiercely stirred by the wizards. Up onto Scotland, scattered and tossed, the wide crashing waves threw brave men of battle with their shields and war gear, shattered and torn."

He relates how Germanus and Lupus, bishops of Auxerre and Troyes, when sent by a church synod to Britain, were encountered by a "hostile force of demons," a hostile lot of demons, who raise storms and turn day into night, driving the bishops' vessel from its course, and flinging the waves over it. Theodorus, archbishop of Canterbury, mentions this power of the witches: "If anyone is a sender of storms, that is, a sorcerer, let him do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water."

translation: This text is already in English and requires no translation. It is a preface discussing errors made by Pliny and medieval translators when rendering Latin plant names into English. The author notes that Pliny made many mistakes, including incorrectly identifying cyprus as privet rather than Ligustrum. Translators of Latin botanical works faced great difficulty, as they did not always know which plant a Latin name referred to. For example, in the Herbarium, article xxix, the word Ostriago was rendered as "water elder," which is incorrect; the author believes it actually refers to the Ostrya tree known to Theophrastus and to modern botany. In article xxv, the word chamaelaia, meaning the Daphne mezereon, was confused with chamaeleon, a stalkless thistle, and translated as "wolf's comb," which is a thistle but a stalked one. Other mistranslations are noted: hedera nigra is far from earth ivy, Tribulus is not gorse, Strychnus is not foxglove, Sampsuchos is not elder, Capparis is not woodbind, and Iuniperus is not gorse. The most striking confusion, however, was the identification of Dymele, which by all its Teutonic connections should be the hop plant, with the poisonous Bryony. Any doubt about the correct lexicographical identification has been settled by the Saxon author himself, who, speaking on his own authority and not merely translating, says that this plant is so excellent that it is mixed into ordinary drinks, that is, into beer.

It is a preface (page lvi) discussing the reliability of an Anglo-Saxon herbal writer and translator, noting that the writer confused two plants — likely bryony and hop — an error shared as late as 1659 by Lovell in his Herball, and possibly originating with Pliny, who was unclear at the start of his 23rd book. And in some sense our ordinary scholars may be said never to have seen a Greek book, since our Hellenic authors are scarcely ever printed in the true alphabet, but in an imitation of an Alexandrine or Byzantine cursive character, which neither Plato nor Aristophanes could have read to save his neck. These considerations forbid our lashing out in hasty declarations that unless proof can be produced that the Saxons read Greek in the Greek character, they cannot well be said to have read it all. translation:
lviii PREFACE

The Tonian copy, which is glossed, serves as a tutor's key, and is, for all I know, the earliest example of those wooden legs provided for halting teachers. The "more difficult" piece by the scholar of the almost famous Ælfric has a few scattered glosses, mostly occurring at the names of trees and herbs. This also was a scholastic exercise.

At the end of the manuscript, added after its completion, is found a third exercise, glossed, and it bears somewhat upon the question of education and proficiency in languages among the Saxons. We should remember that what we call classics, and authors of the golden age, and Attic dramatists, are not the whole nor the most practical part of foreign literature. The writers who treated of matters ecclesiastical and scientific were in early days much more valuable than what we have chosen. For the improvement of our acquaintance with what our forefathers were doing, I shall print the third piece, with its glosses, as far as I was able, in the bright days of summer, to read its blurred and worn record; and it will be seen that Greek words were taught to the students. "Ah!" the self-satisfied may cry, "taught in a way!" But our academic teaching has perhaps some weak points also.

O cleric, an educational exercise: O cleric, you never learned from the diptychs [a kind of tablet], from play, from reasoning, from the corcula [prudence], from the failing pleasures, nor from the heights of hell, nor from the heraldic office, nor from the local ruler, nor from battle, nor from the hierarchy, nor even from the sewer — none of these things were yours.

Footnotes: 1. diptychs. 2. Read "fugias" [flee]. 3. Read corculum = prudent (Cicero, Tusculan Disputations). 4. Perhaps fetialis, heraldic. 5. toparches [local ruler]. 6. battle. 7. hierarchy.

translation:
(Preface, page lix — a mixed Latin and Old English passage, partly glossing rhetorical and grammatical terms)

Indeed, consider the treasure of the spirit; thus — not irrational speech, but let it truly move in common. Let not the mind be sharpened against you; since it does not bite, and let not the inward parts be consumed by strife; your mind, your own agonothete [contest-director], your own belly, shall not choose elegantly. But only in accordance with the heavenly order, because the man is accustomed — beyond the greatest fault, the man errs. To be greatly skilled in seeking a twin remedy is indeed to be a great physician — free from discord. Let it bring together and heal; may it not be absent, let strength remain.

Let it be known frequently, that writings and vessels are often gathered and seen; let them be sought out repeatedly; let them restrain from error, truly. Let the golden resplendence [platung] depart from pride; let glaucoma [a disease of the eyes], and the weal in the flesh from punishment, be far off; and thereafter let the humble maiden neither contend nor strive. Let the enclitic forms, the prosodic elements, not be absent from the service of the unattached military force.

Through the shoulder, leprosy, also epilepsy — per, through ... amphitapa [a double-fringed carpet], from the common people, traveling litter, likewise, bath-woman, horse-cloth, frankincense, scragulum [a coarse garment], worn through, a drink and a potion for the face, hair-bringing, turbacamque, a fore-drink, scragula, a court-garment, a regimen, one uses the pipe, heals, nourishes, and relieves shameful [conditions], takes care, the woman suffers, anabola [a head-garment], but abuses it — broth, she grows angry, broth, also epilepsy, unhealthy — the apozema [decoction] itself is fitting, as is the placenta [afterbirth], alas, you cleric, believe that one would not be an heir — you would become heated, a horse, and cobbe [a spider] — not luxurious, with horses [testicles], therefore you will forget your name, that you [would be] golden-mouthed, you will keep the household's mouth, speaking, you will be a secretary, serving the aphorisms which will stand by you — you king, among the notaries, be among the messengers, the basileus [king], the secretary, and the antigraphus [counter-writer], and so the cosmographer, and the emplacer, and the scout — that you not be naked of these things.

translation:
PREFACE. lxi

[The text is a mixed Latin and Old English passage from a preface, with scholarly footnotes. The Old English portions interweave with Latin, making a full coherent translation difficult, but the general sense runs as follows:]

Be not one who contradicts, be not contentious, nor a braggart, nor a boaster; let not your horizons be narrow nor your learning shallow. Let not your bread be leavened improperly, nor should you be found in a chorus of impropriety. Henceforth be humble in spirit and refrain from pride; be forbearing. Do not gossip nor speak idly of others; let not pride lead you astray. Keep to yourself; do not speak of what ought not be spoken of. Let not your mouth utter things shameful, nor let your bath become an occasion for sin. Keep your eyes lowered with modesty; let not your conduct be crooked or wasteful toward the drain. Seek not the company of flatterers; hell awaits the deceivers and mockers. Let not your steps lead you to gather with idle babblers; keep far from the amphitheatre. And these same things breed yet further troubles and scruples of conscience.

[Footnotes indicate Greek sources and glosses for the Latin terms, with references to Isidore, Du Cange, and the Regularis Concordia.]

translation:
[Preface, page lxii]

Warm water: rinse, heal the mouth, refresh with drink — gold.
Let it illuminate the pupils of the eyes as a reading-stand (analogium), scrub thoroughly.

Mouth: the lip-opener, wash with a two-wheeled vessel, rinse. Teaching: decline bitterness, receive the prize of chariot racing.

Good scold: take a preparation of pitch, take a measure of healing. The key-bone: have this leather bag, the sciatica: the diameter.

Do not use the remedies unless you apply healing to the side — then: the ergastula. Apply the half-verse with it.

When you write two verses, drink from the wine-vat, let it purge the sculpes: two-verse stanzas, the wine-jar, fresh, laxative.

Rub the stomach, take the veins of water, heat it until it boils: wash away with the guest-house, on the opposite side, jealousy — rub vigorously. Then: vinegar, until it measures the wine, with a cup. Let this be the roof.

Buy: take the wild apple. Let the orchards go to their apples. Let the apples of the orchard be fitting.

Rinse: let the poppy seeds moisten the church — let the oil stand long, be established.

Pound: crush the pine-berry drink, the mulberry-drink flees. Let the breezes that trouble you drive away the mulberry drink, that it might flee.

Breathe in: buy yourself all the vapor from there. Drive away, far off: Gorgon. Despise the whole platen, so that it...

translation:
[Old English passage, partially reconstructed:] You who lighten the burden of the dear community, hasten forward — health, shield, spirit, and way — attend to this work; do not fail, do not depart from the proper path of speech; do not be absent from the light, that it may not grow dim — be mindful of your foundation. Let the table be set before you; be mindful of your servant.

While this sheet was in proof, most happily arrived a communication from Mr. Henry Bradshaw, of Kings College, Cambridge, forwarding a copy of the same piece, tending much to the better understanding of the words and sentences, from a manuscript in the University Library, formerly belonging to St. Augustine's, Canterbury, where it was distinguished as "Collectiones cum A."

Cleric, never put aside your writing-tablets; flee the pleasures of those who slide toward ruin — lest a base wretch rejoice over your bier, and the local ruler Machia sit in place of sacred hierarchy over the pit of hell. Let no money or gluttony, but rather brightness dwell with you — let not sharpness of spirit consume the mind, for the champion's role should be the belly of your purpose. Let no one read only the heavenly beyond mere color — for to many [the text continues].

translation:
lxiv PREFACE.

He is accustomed to be a god; pursue medicine as a twin companion,
Stand firm, slanderer, stand in awe: yet be present as a vigorous supporter.
Let scripture touch you, and pastoral vessels, and poetic garb frequently;
Let learning and its composition stand far from you if too frequent;
And truly let dimness of eyes keep away: let the lump of sin depart,
Gold leaf and purple, and thereafter the inclining one, and the humble and noble,
Let the soldiers of Christ by no means be absent through you,
The shaggy carpet on all sides exists, and the traveling bed besides,
The fitting ornament they greatly love, the painted garment, and equally the bright drink,
The procurer drives away the cleric; nor shall I wash away the chaff;
The boys' garment and the court's embroidered covering is a palatine concern,
The woman uses female ornament, but she misuses it, led astray by a bad man,
Broth cooked with various spices is suitable for the sick, as is porridge,
O cleric, noble poet, may you remain, and be skilled and eloquent as one,
Do not keep horses in a purse, be a guardian of your wife,
Be free from the name of the mad, so that you may be one of the golden-mouthed,
Let the minister of secrets be present, let brief maxims guard your mouth,
Be established as a king, sober, and a registry scribe,
And be a describer of the world, and let the explorer of your own self alone be so.

1. Medicine. 2. Slanderer. 3. Vigorous and robust. 4. Scripture. 5. Pastoral vessels. 6. Poetic garment. 7. Of letters. 8. That is, composition. 9. Dimness of the eyes. 10. A mass. 11. A sheet of gold. 12. Purple. 13. Inclining. 14. Humble, noble. 15. A carpet shaggy on all sides. 16. Of laymen or peoples. 17. A traveling bed. 18. A fitting ornament. 19. They greatly love. 20. A painted garment. 21. A bright drink. 22. A procurer or pimp. 23. Drives away. 24. Chaff. 25. A kind of boys' garment. 26. Palatine. 27. Female ornament. 28. That is, king. 44. That you may be. 45. Sober. 46. That is, a registry scribe. 47. Describer of the world. 48. Explorer.

translation:
PREFACE. lxv

Be naked — that is, keep away from unlawful things — and do not be a worldly, secular actor,
Do not be Acrizimum — leavened bread lightly fermented — celebrated, an inspector of hours, nor a protomagister,
And in the bed do not have an amphiballum — a garment shaggy all over — nor a beardless youth, far from it,
Nor a Canterius — that is, a horse — in abundance for you, nor one loved for his baseness, far from it,
Beware of being Cerritus — furious and wrathful — and likewise a circumlocutious perifrasticus,
Let Abbachus — a painted tablet — shine in your hand, and theologus — divine speech — in your mouth,
May you happily see yourself carrying a Baccaulum — a bier — to the sewer,
Do not be a Prodigus — a squanderer — nor crooked, nor a one-eyed Monotalmus, nor fraudulent — indeed, be none of these,
Avoid Ludibrium and the abyss — that is, hell — seek to follow the path of victory,
Let the Amphitheatres — places where gladiators fight — be far from you, and eye-wounds likewise,
For they generate anguish — that is, anxiety of the soul — and vex the pupils of the eyes.
Climb up by analogy; gold shines in the mouth of the teacher;
Avoid the two-wheeled cart, the crown, and the pliant seat;
Possess a vessel smeared with pitch, know the half-sphere of the sundial, and be ignorant of the places of exile for bad slaves and convicts,
Place a half-verse alongside distichs — two verses — and you will write,
Pour a libation to Enoforus — a wine vessel — and accustom yourself to relieving yourself of urine,
Love the xenodochium — the house where the poor are gathered — and hate jealousy.

From here may small cups bind your house like a full measure, may the orchard enclosure? and the fruit gardens fittingly attend to apples, may purple gleam in the churches, far away be the stench, may the estates appointed for you be stirred by breezes and rods, may the serpent flee far off, drink to the full measure, spurn the mud entirely, and the banquets insofar as the road, may a half-measure purify you, may you be strong if you cannot be innocent? PREFACE. lxvii

Irish MS. by Mr. Whitley Stokes, who has had the assistance of Dr. Wright in making out, to a good extent, the Syriac or Hebrew words disguised in it. The mere presence of two glossed copies now first printed will clear up some difficulties, and one or two words I may perhaps myself have rightly guessed. The Irish MS. of the Latin text declares the composition to be written in hendekasyllabic verse; but lest a purer classical taste should suppose that by this term the " hendecasyllabi," or Phalaekians of Catullus have been emulated, the opening lines arranged with due regularity may be taken as a specimen of the rest. It will be seen that they are scanned by the accents.

Suffragare, quaeso, michi possito
Magni maris uelut in periculo,
Ut non secum trahat me mortalitas
Huius anni neque mundi uanitas.
etc.

The Irish MS., " in the opinion of Dr. Todd pro- " duced in the latter part of the fourteenth century," tells us also, that " Gillas hanc loricam fecit," and " Laidcend mac Buith Bannaig uenit ab eo in insolam " Hiberniam: transtulit et portauit super altare sancti " Patricii episcopi sanos nos facere, amen." The Latin text of the Cambridge MS. is of the eighth century; it was not intended to be glossed; the glosses were introduced afterwards in a small hand;¹ the earlier ones marked with an asterisk belong to the end of the tenth century, the others to the eleventh. Its readings agree closely with those printed by Mone; errors and all. By one or two mistakes in the glosses of MS. C. it seems probable that they were a transcript, and as the newer are sometimes written above the wrong words, the same may be concluded of them also.

¹ Mr. Bradshaw thinks the glosses cotemporary.

PREFACE. lxvii

An Irish manuscript prepared by Mr. Whitley Stokes, who had the assistance of Dr. Wright in deciphering, to a considerable degree, the Syriac or Hebrew words disguised within it. The mere existence of two glossed copies now printed for the first time will resolve some difficulties, and one or two words I may perhaps have correctly guessed myself. The Irish manuscript of the Latin text states that the composition is written in hendecasyllabic verse; but lest those of a more purely classical taste should suppose that by this term the hendecasyllabi, or Phalaecians of Catullus, have been imitated, the opening lines arranged with proper regularity may be taken as a sample of the rest. It will be seen that they are scanned by the accents.

Help me, I pray, placed as I am
In danger like that of the great sea,
Lest mortality drag me down with it,
And the vanity of this year and world.
etc.

The Irish manuscript, "in the opinion of Dr. Todd produced in the latter part of the fourteenth century," also tells us that "Gillas made this lorica," and that "Laidcend son of Buith Bannaig came from him to the island of Ireland: he transferred and carried it above the altar of holy Bishop Patrick so that it might make us whole, amen." The Latin text of the Cambridge manuscript dates to the eighth century; it was not originally intended to be glossed; the glosses were added afterwards in a smaller hand. The earlier ones marked with an asterisk belong to the end of the tenth century, the others to the eleventh. Its readings agree closely with those printed by Mone, errors and all. From one or two mistakes in the glosses of manuscript C., it seems likely that they were a transcript, and since the newer glosses are sometimes written above the wrong words, the same conclusion may be drawn about them as well.

¹ Mr. Bradshaw believes the glosses to be contemporary.

translation:
MS. Bibl. Publ. Cantab. Ll. 1. 10. fol. 43.

He sang a lorica, a hymn of protection, going into every danger.

Grant me remission, assist me O Trinity, Unity, unity, have mercy.

I pray that I may be aided, for very great are my needs as the Trinity itself — assist me, I pray, inquire for me, that the greater powers may help. So that they do not lead me into peril, that mortal sin may not drag me down, and that worldly vanity of this year shall not claim me — and this same thing I pray, from the highest and most ancient powers of heaven, of the militia of the celestial court — that great hosts may not overthrow me in battle against enemies, and that those enemies may not strip me, nor foes surround me. But let me be shielded by the strong spiritual armor so that they cannot overcome me, for those arrayed against me in battle — the ranks of the forces of the piercing ones — let the fire of God burn them, the Seraphim and Raphael with Michael and Gabriel. Among them I choose to drive away those burning ones, the ranks of the heavenly host. I pray to the Thrones, living Archangels, patriarchs and leaders of the angels, that they may protect me and defend me from enemies, so that I may repel them; then after the champions who will heal me, and after the rest of the patriarchs — the four.

translation:
PREFACE. lxix

[I invoke] a guardian, a protector, an apostle, sailing across, a protector, and I ask for a champion, that through him I may be preserved from the worst, that every evil may depart from me, away from me — the pepper, the rheum, the fever — and that the powerful pact of the demon-host, row upon row, may be broken by the all-penetrating protection. O God, impenetrable shield, protection on all sides — protect me from the strength of my body's foe. Give me the limbs of all, the living flesh, the shield entire, protecting the joints, every one of the ribs, that the powerful [forces] may not shake my sides in any joint, nor may the demons on my left jostle against one another — [protect] skull and top of the forehead, the temples, with the locks, and the eyes, the face, the tongue, the throat — together with the jaw and the chin, the face, the chin-bone. Senna.

translation:
lxxii PREFACE.

Nails, spine, fire — the stomach-warmers, the breast. Throat, sinew, quinsy — thus the chest; the gullet, the chest-bone, the stomach, the navel-cord, the womb. Thus the belly. And the natural members, and the hips, and the throat. The loins, the genitals, and the white matter, and the ribs. The flanks, the kidneys, the lungs. The vital parts — thus the diaphragm, the liver, and the intestines, the loin-sinews, the tonsils, the navel, the bladder, thus the bowels, thus the whole — with the palate. With the cheeks. Thus the flesh, the groin, with the spleen, the spleen, the bowels — with the intestines. Thus the bladder and all, those joints, those unattached members of the belly, the womb, the fat, and the compartments — the innumerable inner parts. The sinews and the other limbs lie weakened, those inner parts. Thus the hairs and whatever remaining members of the body are to be described here. I name these terms: thus the whole of me with five senses — a very sharp and vigorous body, fore and aft, from the limbs up to the top of the head, to the crown — to no member is there any slime or dirt at all — the plant from vertex to crown. In no member at all does anything impede life.

translation:
PREFACE. lxxiii

[Opening Latin-derived text with Old English glosses, running continuously:]

Rather than print at every word a variation, it is better to give the glosses of the Harleian MS. continuously. (Harl. 585, fol. 152.)

May this affliction and these yearly, annual pains be gentle to me; may this yearly affliction allow me to settle my great debts — so that, among the vigorous, with her I may no longer suffer from the deadly nature of these diseases, nor from the emptiness of such things — that same thing I pray, away from the highest of heavenly hosts, that they not let me loose to engage in strife; but rather, having shielded me in truth with strong weapons, so that they not overcome me again in the darkness before the heavenly peoples' protectors, of the army's guardians, and with good graces among the troops. Just as God and God's strength, like a fish in the depths, the high angels and a host of powers, so that they may thickly shield me — may I be able to shield myself thereafter when the other warriors, the high counselors, all the apostles, all the leaders, I pray to God's warriors, that through them and her the eternal salvation may encircle me, and every evil depart from me — may Christ be with me, a lasting, firm protection; may a vigorous firmament, a terror to the dark ones, drive away the host of evil from me, an unceasing protection; shield, O Lord, with your might my body from all these afflictions; may your protection from each one keep the dark forces from my members in my afflictions, just as they are accustomed to run, gliding along...

widening all the flaws; stout pieces of cardboard were then prepared as a frame to carry the leaves, which were fixed into these paper frames by ligaments of goldbeaters skin. Thus once more the burnt leaves became a volume. The binder had probably some superintendence in his task, for as long as the Latin text of Apuleius afforded its guidance the folios were rightly numbered, but beyond that they have been frequently misplaced. It is possible that on the publication of this work, the binder may be directed to rearrange the folios, in which case the references to the drawings printed in the text will no longer correspond with the numbers in the manuscript. Besides the serious mischief from the fire, the pages had also suffered from the paintings placed upon them. The green pigment used, probably sulphate of copper, has eaten away the vellum upon which it was laid, so that not only the drawings so far have perished, but also the writing at the back has gone. Thus this manuscript, taken by itself, had become in many places illegible; yet, when a parallel text was laid by the side of it, the broken lines and half surviving words were again significant, and it was possible to print nearly all the letters of the book from the richest and most beautiful copy.

Foundation of our text. In editing an ancient work, the rule is now recognized, which due consideration has suggested; to print from the best manuscript and supply its defects, if any, from the next best. The three best manuscripts conspire in making the extravagant slip in Herbarium, article lxxi., and the fourth is not taken into account. But in the orthography of old English words, a certain method has prevailed, and the mode of Ælfric, it may be, has been followed in modern grammars and by modern editors, no objection to such a course, as of a choice, being now taken; yet this customary spelling has also been called "pure Saxon," and other methods

text:
PREFACE. lxxvii

have been damned as dialects, to both of which judgments I take leave to lodge an appeal, which shall be pleaded to on some future occasion. It so happens, however, that the spelling of MS. V. is nearer to the customary manner than that of MS. B., so that no discussion need arise out of the choice of a base for printing. The fainter strokes of the reed in this wasted MS. are scarcely visible: the accents often are vanishing; and only the visit of a sunbeam revealed to me, that what has been printed on page 216,¹ as fræniIcum, was really written frænihtum. The letters a and u are scarcely distinguishable in the handwriting of this MS.

MS. V. in its pristine beauty had two large paintings each filling a page. The first contains a tall figure standing on a lion, habited in loose tunic or amice, chasuble and stole;² to all appearance an ecclesiastic of rank, holding in the right hand a crozier, the small cross bar of which is, though not easily, discerned; it rests on the ground, and the lion has seized it in his jaws. In the left this tall personage holds a heavy book. The draperies according to Saxon custom seem caught by a gust of wind. Over him waves a baldachin or canopied curtains. On his left approaches reverentially a tonsured priest presenting a volume. On his right a soldier, with a full sized shield, looks up for orders. The purport of this painting is scarcely conveyed by the design itself: it seems, however, to represent the church dignitary for whom the work was copied; the stole marking a churchman: though some hesitation is produced by the presence of a soldier with a Roman air. This painting was meant for this book, since the border matches that which backs the title.

lxxviii PREFACE.

The second large painting is explained by the inscription at the foot, as exhibiting Æsculapius, the Centaur Chiron, and Plato. Æsculapius is a tall beardless figure, the Centaur is a Hippocentaur with bald head, and Plato has right shoulder bare. All three grasp a large volume in plain binding, with a broad tie round the middle, as if the two, the Centaur and Plato, were each at once receiving it from Æsculapius. The foreground is infested with snakes; the background is full of animals, of which the boar, wolf, hare, roebuck, bear, and dog are still distinguishable. On the other side of the leaf a broad ornamental fillet surrounds the title of the book, "Herbarium, etc."

Whence came MS. V.
The owners of MS. V. I have been unable to trace to any good purpose. No information is derivable from Sir Robert Cottons private catalogue in manuscript, which I have inspected. On the middle of fol. 74 a, between lines is written "Richerd Hollond this boke," for "his boke," in a hand of the fifteenth century. There was a Richard Holland, brother of John, restored Earl of Huntingdon 1417, created Duke of Exeter 1442, died 1447, which Richard was Admiral of England, and died 1404. Whether he were owner of the MS. I shall not pretend to decide: but I know of no other so likely. On the face of an early folio is written "elizabeth colmore," in a text hand, perhaps of the age of Sir Robert Cotton. Among the books in the old library of (the Cathedral) Christ Church, Canterbury, mentioned by Wanley in his preface, occurs "Herbarius Anglice, depictus," and as this answers to the description of MS. V., Wanley has concluded it is perhaps the same copy. translation:
PREFACE. lxxix

The Holland family would have had access to a few books from Canterbury. Those who enjoy fitting pieces together may choose to combine the probable date of the manuscript (1040–1050), its Canterbury origin, and the archbishopric of Eadsige (1038–1050); but such calculations carry considerable uncertainty.

The drawings may once have been accurate likenesses of the plants; in some cases we can see that the artists were capable of the work — betony, arum dracunculus, an orchid or satyrion, goosegrass, centaury, yarrow, lily, mandrake, and castor plant all suggest to the eye the plant the artist intended. With the exception of goosegrass, these are also mentioned in the authors' text. But it often happened that when a pattern was handed to an illustrator to be faithfully copied, he viewed it with too artistic an eye and considered how he might improve it. The facsimile shows us the drawing in MS. V. that represents saxifraga granulata. This plant produces, clinging to its roots, many small bulbs shaped and coloured like onions, but no bigger than the heads of large pins. Remove all colour from the picture and you will see that the outline captured these features of the plant: an oval piece of turf indicated that the underground portion was shown, with roots and granules visible below it. The artist, knowing nothing of this, did what clever people always do — he improved upon his original. He deepened the colour of the underside of the turf, and, seeing no leaves, rounded the granules and coloured them green so that they would serve as leaves. In many other cases similar improvements were introduced; thus the flowers of chamomile have had their white rays and yellow discs coloured alike blue. In other cases the botanical framework in use during the earlier centuries of the Christian era was the source of our dissatisfaction; for in those days, the practice of relying chiefly

translation: This passage is already in English and requires no translation. It is a preface discussing the difficulties of plant identification in ancient illustrated manuscripts, noting that illustrators often failed to capture the distinctive features needed to identify plants. It mentions the Vienna manuscript of Dioskorides, copies of whose woodcut plates were sent to Sibthorp (now at the Botanic Garden, Oxford) and to Linnaeus (now held by the Linnean Society). The copy held by the Linnean Society, though smaller, is considered more valuable for containing ink annotations by Jacquin describing colors, and pencil notes by Sir J. E. Smith attempting to identify the plants. The botanical world had long been in dispute over the names in Dioskorides, and these drawings were expected to resolve the matter.

PREFACE. lxxxi

of great assistance: controversies raged, and folios were published, till at length the struggles of the learned "terminated only by despair of success."¹ It was by no means in hope that I should add to botanical knowledge that I paid a visit to Oxford specially to see these plates, but from a desire to elicit, if I could, from a comparison of the Saxon drawings in the Herbarium, from art. cxxxiv. to the end, with those from the Vienna manuscript, some solution of the difficulties of the subject. If the Saxon artist had altered a little here and a little there, some light would be thrown on the matter. The Vienna Greek copy might be even the original, or if not so, very near to the original of the English. But though in many cases the Vienna copy gives faithful drawings of the plants, as in sedum arboreum, which is spoiled in the English figure (art. cxlvii.), yet there was no such similarity between the drawings as to lead to any useful result. Dr. Daubeny gave me a small book of his own publishing, running to seventeen pages, in which he has assigned modern scientific equivalents to the old Hellenic appellations of Dioskorides. On the face of it this book treats rather of the figures than of the written text; yet, of course, the words of the author were always kept in view. The Professor, then, "characterizes the drawings "of the plants in the Vienna MS." often as "fictitious," often as having "slight resemblance," as "doubtful," "bad," "very rude," "indifferent," and all this in a treatise where the conclusions were drawn in a good measure from the drawings. Anxious to learn more about Brittanike, the Vienna MS. gave me a drawing, showing the flowering stems of Lythrum salicaria, with leaves which must belong to a monocotyledonous plant. On type forms and their value: The text has been printed in a form that preserves the shape of the characters as they appear in the original manuscripts. Beyond the objection to printing in the letterforms of our own day — an objection that arises naturally in anyone who dislikes dressing up antiquity in modern clothing — there is another objection that is not sentimental at all: by making everything uniform we lose all the chronological characteristics of a manuscript that arise from the shape of its letters. The age of an English manuscript can generally be determined to within half a century by the shape of certain letters. Print all these forms alike, and you, as far as it lies within your power, shut out from your readers the information contained in those forms. The letter ꝼ is a hallmark of an early English manuscript, one belonging probably to the ninth or tenth century. It may be seen in the facsimiles of the Lauderdale Orosius, of the Codex Exoniensis, and of the C.C.C. copy of the Chronicle. It occurs frequently in the Leechbook, but not in the copy of a lost chapter which we shall restore to its proper place — not because of the text itself, but because of the

Vocalisation. The vocalisation of the oldest English MSS. differs from that which may be called the received standard, from the printed homilies of Ælfric, for instance, and from the grammars which are all based on Ælfrics Latin grammar. One editor of Orosius has furnished us, at the expense of Mr. Tollemache, with fac-similes of three pages of the Lauderdale MS. Of the antiquity and superior value of this MS. there can be no doubt. We there see ie river, as well as ea, hætt calls, æpielme source, pinperc, ziet, ponun, pnom for pnam, hiepa and hiopa, hoppc for hopp. Just as was to be expected from current notions, the editor who had access to this good MS. did not use it; it has, says he, "a " northerly aspect." This expression were true, had it been used of a manuscript of the eleventh century; but the Lauderdale MS. is older, and agrees in spelling with others of nearly the same age. If the book called Cædmon, be his, which I neither assert nor deny, the copy we have is much later than his times; but it exhibits proofs of having been transcribed from an earlier book in which the same method of vocalising prevailed. The penman altered, as was customary, the spelling as he went; but at page 55 of the MS., line 3,¹ he came to a slip of the earlier pen, which he was unable to understand: it had been meant for

The syllable un–, with the privative sense is frequently accented, as marking a change of meaning. Indifference of vowels. Final syllables with short vowels are written with e, i, o, or u. Hence a verb ending in -obon became, on dropping the N, -obe in its termination; and pærtmar, dropping the s, might become pærtme.

Final vowels dropped. The general analogies of the oldest English with Latin and Greek would lead us to expect the neuter plural to end in a short vowel such as a; so that ponba should represent verba; and this is so. But English also loses the vowel, and the plural becomes ponb. This is the case with most of our neuters. And not only that. Other terminations lose the vowels we expect to find. The adverbs ending in -on, and like -ther, meaning "from," are often found to have, and doubtless originally did, end in -one, as heonon, heonone, hence.

The omission of a final short vowel affects the orthography of nominatives: thus Kemble says, on ærende, "In later times the final e was sometimes omitted, but should not have been so." The word for pain (a masculine, not to be confused with the neuter word for work) is written in the nominative form twice in the manuscript of Cædmon. The forms meaning "goddess" lead us to suppose that the language had a feminine -ne ending for names of women's offices, as Dirne, Old German Diorna, famula, puella. The St. Johns Oxford manuscript gloss for monacha or monialis has mynecenu, which, and not mynecen, is the true form of the nominative. So that piln was perhaps once pilne, and þeznen, þinen, has lost a vowel. See fpnæc for fpnæce, Codex Exoniensis, p. 421, line 3.

translation:
The inflectional endings set out in grammars are, or ought to be, the forms normally observed in the language. In all less well-known languages, Greek included, the standard grammars are often substantially in error. In the oldest written English, misleadingly called Anglo-Saxon, these inflectional endings are less certain, since the writings have had few scholars; and we cannot be expected to take our rules from the grammars. Yet it would not be reasonable to favour a reading merely because it is exceptional: we dare go only so far as to accept more readily those less usual, less established forms which accord with the tendency of the period, which was to drop endings, as is seen in the English of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, the "Semi Saxon" and the "Early English" of conventional literary terminology. The infinitive meaning "to give thanks" is found in the Exeter book written without the N. These two passages carry more evidential weight than two agreeing manuscripts, and it follows that in the tenth century infinitives had already begun to drop the N. The Hatton Gospels read "the spiritual poor," "the peaceable," "the uttermost farthing," and so on; and it is asking too much of any reasonable partisan to fix closely in time the beginning of such a dropping off of "the marching soldiers."

The s of the nominative and accusative plural in -aȝ is sometimes absent, at least in the manuscripts; as in Cædmon, if it is indeed Cædmon, MS. p. 42, line 17, ðbame.

Even such phrases as "king almighty" are better sense, if treated as "eall" for "ealþa," than if considered as compounds.

I have before observed that the case ending –um becomes, by loss of the final consonant, –e. Rask had remarked this of adjectives, but the translator struck out his words. The change however is seen in substantives, and in short, it is a mere decay of termination.

Plural verbs in –e. In former treatises I have observed that by the loss of N, verbs plural in –on come to end in –e. By this simple explanation, harmonizing with other changes in our early language, we fully understand what has been called "a verb with a singular termination joined to a plural nominative," "a singular for plural."

Substantives out of adjectives. Adjectives become substantives, and are sometimes masculine, sometimes feminine, sometimes neuter.

PREFACE. cv

Just as the Greek genitive "hudatos" means "some water" used partitively, so in Saxon English the genitive denotes "some of." An example of the partitive genitive occurs in Med. de Quad., viii. 6. In that passage, observe also that "swete" agrees either with "apulbne," which is feminine,¹ or with "wunde," whereas it is the apple that is sweet, and "appel" is masculine.

The Leechbook takes considerable licence with careless grammatical construction. In a list of the ingredients of a recipe it commonly uses nominatives, even though a verb requiring accusatives had preceded. It often constructs sentences as if we should say in Latin: "Given to the sick patient this medicine, fasting"; either because it is equivalent to "Let the sick patient drink this medicine while fasting," or from simple carelessness, or on the principle remarked above, that a grammatical ending was superfluous.

"Gelacniad" for "gelacnad," p. 322, line 7, and "arandан" for "arandab," p. 374, line 19, are errors of the manuscript, not of the typesetting.

There are some other points to be noticed, but for the present my scope does not allow me to speak of them.

I must gratefully acknowledge the privilege of access to the library of Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, and the especial kindness of two gentlemen, who gave me the means of complying with the rules, at the sacrifice of their own convenience.

translation:
[A FIGURE OF BETONICA OFFICINALIS.]

I. This plant that one calls betonica grows in meadows and in open sunny places, and in shaded spots and thickets. It is very beneficial both for a man's spirit and for his body. It protects him against dreadful nightly terrors, and against fearful visions and dreams. And this plant is very holy, and you must gather it in the month of August, without using iron. And when you have gathered it, shake off the soil from it so that nothing of it clings on, and then dry it in the shade very thoroughly, and with all its roots reduce it to dust; make use of it then, and keep it by you.

If a man's head is badly afflicted, take the same plant betonica, clean it, and then grind it very fine into dust, then take two spoonfuls of it and let him drink it in hot water; then the head will heal very quickly after that drink.

The only Saxon MS. which contains the figure, MS. V., has lost a portion of it by decay, but there has been a sufficient representation of the plant.

BETONY. I. Betonica officinalis. Bot.

1.a This wort, which is named betony, is produced in meadows, and on clean downlands, and in shady places; it is good whether for the mans soul or for his body: it shields him against monstrous nocturnal visitors and against frightful visions and dreams; and the wort is very wholesome, and thus thou shalt gather it, in the month of August without (use of) iron: and when thou have gathered it, shake the mold, tillb nought of it cleave thereon, and then dry it in the shade very thoroughly, and with its roots altogether reduce it to dust; then use it, and taste of it when thou needest.

2. If a mans head be broken, take the same wort betony, scrape it then and rub it very small to dust, then take by two drachms weight, and swallow itc in hot beer, then the head healeth very quickly after the drink.

a The figures in MSS. V. and A. are intended for the plant.
b þær, in the sense of oþ þær, is very common; but perhaps it had been intended to give or- oþ þær.
c burt is neuter.

APULEIUS. 71

The only Saxon manuscript which contains the figure, MS. V., has lost a portion of it through decay, but there has been a sufficient representation of the plant.

BETONY. I. Betonica officinalis. Botany.

1. This plant, which is called betony, grows in meadows, on open downlands, and in shady places. It is beneficial both for a man's soul and for his body: it protects him against monstrous nocturnal visitors and against frightful visions and dreams. The plant is very wholesome, and so you shall gather it in the month of August without the use of iron. When you have gathered it, shake the soil from it until none clings to it, then dry it thoroughly in the shade, and grind it together with its roots entirely to dust. Then use it and take it when you have need of it.

2. If a man's head is injured, take this same plant betony, scrape it and rub it very finely to dust, then take a measure of two drachms by weight and swallow it in hot beer; the head will then heal very quickly after the drink.

Thyme: pound it, put it in pure wine, drink it; then for a night thirty times, then his body will be lightened.

If a man is in great distress or great suffering, take betony, one thyme-measure full, boil it in spiced wine, drink it then at night thirty times, and then he will soon be free of pain.

If a man is inwardly unwell or inflamed, then take betony, two measures of thyme, four of honey, one measure of vinegar, boil it then in good strong beer, drink it thirty full measures at night, then his inward parts will soon be healed.

If you wish that your food be easily digested, take then betony, a measure of thyme, four of honey, one of vinegar, boil it then until it is thick, drink it then in water, two full measures.

For one who cannot keep his food down after he has eaten it, take then betony, four measures of thyme, pressed honey, season then a little with sea-salt; eat then one by one in hot water and add wine together, reduce it then until it is better, drink it full measure.

For internal soreness, or if he is swollen, take betony the plant, grind it in wine very small

...teach not on the hip; then the pains of the loins are healed, and the pain of the thighs is soothed.

For a rotable [swelling]: take the same plant, boil it in a vessel until the liquid is reduced by half, pound it; then take the plant and lay it on the place, and smear it on; and drink of it so that it works from within, and you will find healing thereupon.

Plantain. II.

If a man has headache, let him take plantain root and bind it on the back of his neck; then the pain will pass away from him.

If a man has stomach trouble, let him take plantain juice, take the plant and squeeze it so that it is dark, then take a great plateful, apply it on the way, so that the stomach, if it be swollen, is thereby eased; then lay the plant on the stomach and it will soon be well.

For internal soreness: take plantain juice, put it in summer's [warm] drink, and drink it hot; then it will cleanse within and purge the stomach and the bowels very thoroughly indeed.

Also for a man who has growths in the stomach...

1. If a man's head aches or is sore, let him take the roots of waybread and bind them on his neck; then the soreness will depart from the head.

translation:
Then boil the herb-of-grace shoots, and eat them, and then the belly-ache will soon pass.

Again, if a man bleeds internally through his bowels, take the juice of herb-of-grace and give it him to drink, and it will soon stop.

If a man has a swelling, take herb-of-grace, scrape it down to a pulp and apply it to the wound, and it will soon be healed. If the body is inflamed with severe internal heat, pound the same plant and lay it on; when the body cools it will heal.

If you wish to purge a man's bowels, take the plant, boil it in vinegar, add pepper to it and let the patient drink it in the night before dawn; a full cup each time for purging.

Against a snake bite. Against the bite of a snake, take herb-of-grace, cut it up small and eat it.

Scorpion. Against the sting of a scorpion, take herb-of-grace and the plant called navel-wort, bind them onto the man so that the good may come to him at once.

If a man has worms inside him, take the juice of herb-of-grace, pound and press it out, and give it him to drink; take the same plant, pound it, lay it on the navel and rub it in very firmly.

APULEIUS 83

WAYBREAD, Article ii.

Boil the waybread generously in water, and let the patient eat a good amount of it; then the swollen belly will soon shrink.

5. Again, in the case that a man passes blood from his anus (has a hemorrhage): take the juice of waybread, give it to him to drink; then the hemorrhage will soon be stopped.

6. If a man is wounded, take seed of waybread, grind it to powder, and sprinkle it on the wound; it will soon be whole. If the body is troubled anywhere by intense heat (inflammation), pound the same plant and lay it on the affected area; then the body will cool and heal.

7. If you wish to reduce the size of a man's belly, take the plant; boil it in vinegar; then put the juice and the boiled plant into wine; let him drink this at night while fasting, always one cup to produce a discharge.

For a snake bite.
8. Against an adder's bite, take the waybread plant, rub it into wine, and let the patient eat it.

For a scorpion sting.
9. For a scorpion's wound, take roots of waybread and bind them on the man; it is believed that this will be of good service to him.

10. If internal worms afflict a man, take the juice of waybread, pound and squeeze the plant, and give it to him to drink; and take the same plant, pound it, lay it on the navel, and bind it there very tightly.

Footnote a: Latin: "For those who pass matter mixed with blood." The English translator appears to have confused the Latin exscreare with excrementum and excernere.
Footnote b: Latin: "To tighten the belly." The Saxon-English means "to make shrink."

translation:
For whatever condition of the body causes swelling, take then the herb wall-pellitory, and pound it with grease, without salt, and apply it like a poultice, then lay it on the swelling — it will soften the soreness and heal it.

For whatever man has a daily recurring fever, take then the juice of that same herb, pound it, strain it; give him to drink at the times before the fever comes upon him greatly, so that the fever comes to him no more in his sleep.

For gout, and for pain of the sinews, take then the leaves of wall-pellitory, pound them with salt, put them on the feet, and on the sinews — that is a sure remedy.

For the illness that comes upon a man on the third day, take wall-pellitory, three berries, pound them in warm liquid — or give it to him to drink before the fever comes upon him — at night, fasting.

For the illness that comes on the fourth day, pound the same herb, small, give him to drink in ale so that it seems to him he may heal, so that it passes.

For hot wounds, take then wall-pellitory, pound it in fresh butter without salt, lay it on the wound — he will soon be whole.

For a man's feet that are painfully sore, take then wall-pellitory, pound the herb in vinegar, bathe the feet therewith and rub them — they will soon shrink back.

translation:
APULEIUS 85

11. If any man's body is hardened, take waybread the plant, and pound it with lard without salt, and work it into a poultice; lay it then on where it is hard; it will soon make it soft, and heal it.

12. If any man has a quartan fever, take then the plant's juice, mix in water, give it to him to drink two hours before he expects the fever; there is hope that it may bring much benefit.

13. For gout, and for sore sinews, take leaves of waybread, crush with salt; apply it then to the feet and to the sinews; this is a reliable remedy.

14. For the fever which comes upon a man on the third day (tertian fever), take three sprouts of waybread, crush them in water or in wine; give it to the patient to drink before the fever comes upon him, at night, fasting.

15. For the fever that comes every second day, pound this same plant very small; give it to him in ale to drink. It is to be believed that it may help.

16. For inflamed wounds, take waybread the plant, pound it with lard without salt, lay it on the wound; the patient will soon be healed.

17. If a man's feet swell during a journey, take waybread the plant, pound it in vinegar, bathe the feet with it, and smear them; the swelling will then soon diminish.

a Poultice, Latin 1528.
b For secondary pain. Latin 1528.
c "tumuerint," Latin 1528. Lye prefers "tenescere" (tenerescere), but it is better not to hold to opinions against evidence.

Against swellings or growths on the nose or cheek: take then the juice of greater plantain, wring it through soft wool, lay it thereon; let it hang nine nights, then it heals itself afterwards.

For any unknown pustules that appear on a person's face: take greater plantain, rub it, grind it fine, mix with water, add a little salt to the paste, smear the face therewith; then the face will be soothed and it heals.

For a sore of the mouth: take the juice of greater plantain and the juice of ivy, grind them together, hold it long in your mouth, and eat the root.

For a dog bite on a person: take the same plant and grind it, and lay it on; then it will soon be whole.

For any man's internal weakness: take greater plantain, put it in wine and let it soak, and eat the plantain; then it avails against all internal ailment.

For a man whose limbs ache or are swollen: take feverfew, the plant, pound it smooth, very fine; lay it thereon without salt, and then it heals itself soon.

For stomach trouble: take the juice of feverfew, bathe with it, take two spoonfuls of wool-water; give it him to drink; then it will cleanse all through.

translation:
Agrimony. IV.

The plant that men call "uepmenacam" and by another name "agrimony" grows here and there in rough lands and in meadows.

For wounds and for deadening pain and for swellings, take this same plant's root, and mix with it wormwood, and apply it around — then it heals remarkably.

For swellings, take the juice of the plant called "uepmenacam," pound it and lay it thereon — it heals completely.

For those who have hardened internal growths, so that the blood cannot follow its natural course and the passages cannot be kept open — take the juice of this same plant, and boil it and mix with it wine, and honey, and pepper together, and it will soon heal those who cannot urinate.

For pain in the side, take some of this same plant, grind it to dust, then take three cups of good wine mixed together, let the patient drink it — it will relieve greatly, and likewise many other ailments of a similar kind.

For those who have stones growing in the bladder, take this same plant's root, pound it well then boil in hot wine, give it to drink — it heals the bladder ailment completely, and not only that, but also whatever prevents urination — it gently cleanses and purges.

For headache, take the same plant and bind it to the temples, and it will draw out the pain from the temples.

APVLEIL 91

ASHTHROAT, that is, Vervain. IV. ASHTHROAT.
Art. iv.

1. This wort, which one nameth verbenaca, and by another name ashthroat, is produced everywhere in smooth lands and on wet ones.

2. For wounds, and for dead springs (ulcers), and for kernels (strumous swellings), take roots of the same wort, and wreathe about the swere (neck); then it will benefit highly.

3. Again for kernels (strumous swellings), take the same wort verbenaca; knock (pound) it, and lay it thereto; it will heal wonderfully.

4. For those that have stopped veins, so that the blood may not have its kindly (natural) run (course), and are not able to retain their food, take juice of the same wort, and give to drink, and afterward take wine and honey and water, mix them together, and it (the remedy) will soon heal the infirmity.

5. For sore of liver, take on Midsummers day the same wort, and rub it to dust; take then five spoons full of the dust, and three draughts of good wine; mix them together; give (this to the sick man) to drink; it will benefit much; also in like manner for many other infirmities.

6. For the infirmity by which stones wax in the bladder, take roots of the same wort, and pound them; boil them then in hot wine; give to drink; it will heal the infirmities in a wonderful manner, and not that only; also whatsoever lets (hinders) the urine, it soon makes away with, and leads forth.

7. For a head sore, take the same wort, and bind to the head, and it will make to wane the sore of the head.

translation:
APVLEIL 91

ASHTHROAT, that is, Vervain. Article IV.

1. This plant, which some call verbenaca and others ashthroat, grows everywhere in open fields and in wet places.

2. For wounds, festering sores (ulcers), and swollen glands (strumous swellings), take the roots of this same plant and wrap them around the neck; it will be greatly beneficial.

3. Again for swollen glands, take the same plant verbenaca, pound it, and apply it to the swelling; it will heal wonderfully.

4. For those who have blocked veins, so that the blood cannot flow naturally, and who are unable to keep down their food, take the juice of this same plant and give it to drink; afterward take wine, honey, and water, mix them together, and this remedy will soon cure the ailment.

5. For a sore liver, take this same plant on Midsummer's Day and grind it to a powder; then take five spoonfuls of the powder and three drafts of good wine, mix them together, and give this to the sick person to drink; it will help greatly, and similarly for many other ailments.

6. For the condition in which stones grow in the bladder, take the roots of this same plant, pound them, then boil them in hot wine and give to drink; it will heal these ailments in a wonderful way, and not only that — whatever else hinders urination, this remedy soon clears it and brings relief.

7. For a sore on the head, take this same plant and bind it to the head, and it will cause the sore of the head to diminish.

92 HERBARIUM

Against adders.

Against the bite of a serpent, when a man is in such a way harmed by a poisonous creature, this plant with its roots applied to him will guard against all serpents and he will be whole.

Against spiders.

Against the bite of a spider, take the leaves of this same plant, boil them in pure water crushed, when it is hot apply it with a poultice so that the wound shall soon be opened, and when it is opened, then chew the plant with honey, and lay it to the wound until it is healed, and it will recover very quickly.

Against the bite of a mad dog, take the same plant and wheaten bread together and lay it to the wound, and let the bread soak through the wound's moisture so that it becomes softened, and then take the bread and rub it into a fine powder. If he will not eat it, then take one piece of bread and mix it with the measure of the plant as you did before, and lay it on the wound until you perceive that the stench is drawn out of it.

For new wounds, take the same plant and pound it with butter and lay it to the wound.

Against adders.

Against the bite of a serpent, take the same plant three times and boil it in pure water, and pound it, then if the wound is inflamed and swollen, lay it on without being soaked, and then the wound shall soon open; and when it is opened, then take the same plant uncooked and pound it with honey and lay it on the wound.
