8. For the bite of an adder: whatever man has this plant, verbenaca, with its leaves and roots, upon him, he will be protected against all snakes.

[Two drawings of spider-creatures, resembling two horned locusts. MS. V., folio 19 c.]

9. For the bite of poisonous spiders: take leaves of the same plant and boil them, pounded, in wine. If the venom is retained in the body with swelling, apply it to the wound; the wound will soon open, and when it opens, pound the plant with honey and apply it until the wound is whole — and this will happen very quickly.

10. For the bite of a rabid dog: take the same plant, verbenaca, and whole wheaten grains, and apply them to the wound until the grains have softened through the moisture and have swollen up. Then take the grains and offer them to a cock or hen; if the bird will not eat them, take other grains and mix them with the plant as before, and apply to the wound until you are certain the harm has been drawn out.

Henbane.

The plant which one calls symphoniac — that is, henbane — is also called by other names: some men call it henbane, it grows in cultivated lands and on borders of lands and in enclosures. When one crushes the same plant, it gives forth a smell at the hip, and has stiff leaves and also joints. Then it has one white flower and it bears seed.

For sore eyes: take juice of this same dry plant, and rub it on the eye so that it reaches into the wound of the eye; smear the eyes with the juice thereof, and also in the same way, though the eye may be inflamed, it will kill it.

For swelling of the knees or of the shins, or wherever on the body there is a swelling, take the same plant, henbane, and pound it, and lay it on the swelling, and it will reduce the swelling.

For toothache: take the root of this same plant, boil it in strong wine, hold it in the mouth as a steam bath, and it will at once heal the pain of the teeth.

For pale swellings or swelling wherever it may be: take this same plant, henbane, and crush it until both the root and the swelling of those old ones he reduces.

Lay it to the wound until it is completely healed; it will heal very quickly if a man applies it in this manner.

HENBANE. Chapter V. Botanical name: Hyoscyamus niger.

1. This plant, which is called symphoniaca, or hog's-bean, and by another name belene, and which some men call henbell (now henbane), grows in cultivated places, in sandy lands, and in gardens. There is another variety of this same plant, dark in color, with stiffer leaves, and also poisonous. The first kind is white, and it has these medicinal properties.

2. For earache, take juice of this same plant and warm it; drop it into the ear. It wonderfully drives away the earache; and likewise, even if there are worms in the ear, it kills them.

3. For swelling of the knees and of the legs, or wherever on the body a swelling may be, take the same plant symphoniaca and pound it; apply it to the swelling; it will take away the swelling.

4. For toothache, take roots of the same plant; boil them in strong wine; let the sufferer sip it while warm and hold it in his mouth; it will soon heal the toothache.

5. For pain or swelling of the groin, take roots of the same plant and bind them to the thigh; it will take away the pain or the swelling of the groin.

This plant, which one calls in Latin venerium, and in another tongue bee-wort, grows in enclosed places and in plant beds and in meadows. And you shall gather this plant in the month that one calls August.

Those who called it venetian and thought it hostile to themselves — it then stings them and does not bite, but pleases them. This plant is seldom found, and one cannot recognize it by touch, only when it breathes out and blooms.

If someone cannot urinate and the urine has stopped flowing, let him take the dried leaves of this same plant, called lion's root, and boil them down to a third part in liquid, and let him drink it. Then within three days he can pass the urine outward; it excellently heals that infirmity.

Leon Root. VIII.

This plant, which men call by the Latin name leonir and by another name leonrot, grows in fields, and in ditches, and in shaded places.
If a person is in the suffering of infirmity, so that he cannot make water, you can relieve him: take the dried root of this plant which men call lion's root — its leaf only, without the rootstock — boil it in liquid during the waning moon, and bathe him with it, and lead him out of the house on a clear night, and sprinkle him with the liquid of the plant which men call aristolochia, and when he goes out, let him not look back. In this way you can free him from his infirmity.

Clurthunge. IX.

This plant, which men call by the Latin name scelenarum and by another name clurthunge, grows in open ground and in watery places. Whatever person eats the plant growing there, he lets out what is in him while laughing.

translation:
For swellings and for death-stiffness, take the same plant and pound it, mix it with grease without salt, and lay it on the wound. When it draws out whatever corruption is in it, do not keep it on too long, lest it consume more of the healthy body. Then with care pound the plant again and bind it on the man's sound limb, and so it draws out the matter.

For swellings and for abscesses, take the same plant and pound it, mix it with brine, and lay it on the swellings and abscesses. Within a few hours it will draw out the evil matter.

Clover plant. x.

This plant that men call by the open name clover is found on hilly lands and in lowland places; it has rough leaves and thin ones.

For monthly sickness, take the plant and wrap it in a red cloth around the person's loins during the waning of the moon, in the month that men call October, and soon he will be healed.

For festering wounds, take the same plant along with its root and pound it, mix it with vinegar, lay it on the wounds, and soon it will cleanse them, and do the same for the other wounds likewise.

Mugwort. XI.

This plant that one calls artemisia and by another name mugwort is born on rocky slopes and on borders. When someone wishes to begin a journey, let him take in his hand this plant artemisia and have it with him; then he need not greatly fear weariness on the road, for it also drives away evil vapors and noxious spirits, and in the house where it is kept it drives away evil remedies, and also it opens the eyes of wicked men.

For pain of the bowels, take the same plant and pound it to dust and mix it with new beer; give it to drink, and soon it will relieve that bowel pain.

For pain of the back, take the same plant and pound it, and lay it with the back-pain remedy upon the wounds, and the back pain will be cured.

XII. Tansy, which is artemisia tanacetum, is mugwort.

For pain of the bladder, and when a man cannot urinate, take the juice of this plant which is also called mugwort; though it be of another kind and variety, boil it in water or in wine and give it to drink.

MUGWORT.a XI. (Midgewort.) Artemisia

1. This wort, which is called artemisia, and by another name mugwort, is produced in stony places and in sandy ones. APULEIUS 103

MUGWORT XI. (Mugwort.) Artemisia vulgaris. Botany.

1. This plant, which is called artemisia, and by another name mugwort, grows in stony places and in sandy ones. Then if anyone plans a journey, let him take this plant artemisia in hand, and let him carry it with him; he will not feel much weariness on his journey. It also puts to flight demonic possession; and in the house where the man of the house keeps it within, it forbids evil medical practices, and also it turns away the evil eyes of evil men.

2. For soreness of the internal organs, take the same plant, and pound it to dust, and mix it with fresh beer; give it to drink, and it will soon relieve the soreness of the internal organs.

3. For soreness of the feet, take the same plant, and pound it with lard, apply it to the feet; it removes the soreness of the feet.

MUGWORT XII. Artemisia dracunculus. Botany.

1. For soreness of the bladder, and in the case that a man cannot pass water, take juice of this plant, which is also called mugwort; it is, however, of another variety, and boil it in hot water, or in wine, and give it to drink.

104 HERBARIUM

For pain of sinews: take the same plant and pound it, and squeeze it, and smear it with vinegar, bind it then to the sinew on that same day — it will be of benefit to him.

For raw wounds and for suppurating sores: take the same plant, Artemisia, pound it with oil, smear it over the sores, lay it as a poultice — it heals wounds wonderfully.

If a person has become greatly and sorely wasted inside, then take of this same plant the root, let him eat it in honey, and eat likewise — then he will be healed and cleansed so that you would not think it possible that it could have such great power.

If a person is injured with wounds, let him take this same plant's juice with oil and anoint himself therewith — then it will draw out the pain from him.

XIII. Mugwort.

This plant, which is called Artemisia in the language of the learned, and by another name mugwort, is born about ditches and in old dwelling-places. If you taste its blossom, it has a flavor somewhat like elder.

For pain of the stomach: take the plant and pound it, and squeeze it with almond oil, onto the food that you wish to apply as a poultice; then lay it within a clean cloth as a poultice for five days — he will be healed. And if the seeds of this plant are hung over some one, then no man can harm that person thereafter.

106 HERBARIUM

[One] rubs it mixed with oil of fenugreek, then smears it on; it removes all the rash entirely.

It is fitting that the herbs which we call Artemisia — we read that Diana gathered them and made use of them, and their virtues and remedies Chiron the Centaur first compiled from powerful plants — and he named these plants after Diana's name, that is, Artemisia.

XIV. Dock.

This plant, which men call lapatium and by another name dock, grows in sandy places and in old dunghills.

For knots that grow under the skin: take the plant lapatium and pound it with old ale without salt, so that the presser's juice is twice as much as the plant when well mixed; put it then in a linen cloth and bind it on a cabbage leaf and beets, on hot embers; and when it is hot lay it over the knots, and bind it on — this is the remedy for knots.

Dracontea. XV.

This plant, which men call dracontea and by another name dracontea, we read that it should have sprung from a dragon's blood. It grows on the upper mountains where waterfalls are most powerful, in holy places, and in the land which men call Apulia. It...

108
HERBARIUM

On stony ground it grows, its smell is like pennyroyal, and like the smell of green circle-plant, and its roots downward are like a dragon's head.

Adder.

For the biting of adders: take the dry root of dragonwort, pound it with wine, and give it to drink — it will purge out all the poison.

For broken bones: take the same dry root of dragonwort and pound it with smooth fat as you would a poultice, and it will draw out from the body the broken bone fragments; but this root you must gather in the month that men call July.

Hawthorn-leaf. XVI.

This plant that men call scordion, and by another name serpent-leek, grows on high hills and on hard hillsides and in flat meadows and in rough pastures and on rough banks.

For severe wounds: take the dry root of this plant — the one we called scordion, which some men also call piacri — and pound it together; it cleanses the wounds and heals the gashes.

For soreness of the eyes, if a man wishes to cure it: take the juice of this same dry plant and the fluid of rue, and bathe the eyes therewith on the outside; it will take away the soreness.

RAVENS LEEK. XVI. Orchis. Botany.

1. This plant, which is called satyrion, and by another name ravens leek, grows on high downs and in hard places, and also in meadows, and in cultivated lands, and in sandy ones.

2. For difficult wounds, take roots of this plant which we call satyrion, and which some men also call priapiscus, and pound them together; it cleanses wounds and cures scars.

3. For sore eyes, that is, when the eye is watering, take juice of this same plant and smear the eyes with it; without delay it removes the soreness.

HERBARIUM

Felwort. XVII.

This plant which one calls gentiana and by another name felwort is found on hills, and it is named to all peoples; it is bitter in taste and bitter in flavor.

For nausea.

For nausea take a little of the same plant, gentian root, and squeeze it; pound it then into a paste, mix it; give to drink in pure wine three cups full; it helps greatly.

Slit-wort. XVIII.

This plant which one calls orbicularis and by another name slit-wort is found on stony ground and on sandy soils.

For a man who has flux: take the same plant and apply it to the bowels.

For inner pain: take the same plant and cook it in salt; lay it upon the inner part; it also helps well against heartache.

For pain of the spleen: take a decoction of the same plant, one cup, and let the man drink it fully nine days; take also the same plant's root and hang it above the man's spleen so that it hangs over the spleen; he will be healed. And if any [person...]

112 HERBARIVM

one may take the juice of this plant for a dry cough; it relieves the chest congestion, and one may take the plant at any time.

Periwinkle. XIX.

The plant that men call periwinkle, and by another name call unrontnebbe, grows and is found on slopes and in thickets. You must gather the juice of that plant in the morning.

For a man who spits blood: take the juice of this plant without fat, boil it well in strong pine drink, and then fast nine days; within that time you will perceive improvement in that condition.

For old wounds: take the juice of this same plant with oil and frequently apply it to the wound — it will heal it.

For sore nipples that are swollen and broken: take the same plant and pound it and mix it with butter. Apply it then as a poultice; it will dissolve the swelling thoroughly, the broken sores, and will heal them.

For sore eyes, before sunrise or shortly after it fully rises, go to the same plant periwinkle and bind it around with a green twig and say that you take it for the healing of eyes; and after three days go again before sunrise and take it and hang it inside the house where it may drip — it will heal them well.

For indigestion: take of the same plant — nasturtium and pennyroyal — boil in water, let the body drink it when the preparation is made; and take the juice, apply it.

For lice: take of the same plant, crush it with oil; lay it on the lice, then take of the same plant again, lay it on.

For warts: take of the same plant, knead with yeast, apply; they will soon be consumed.

Plant Chapter XXII.

This plant which men call by the Greek and another name — the plant called "ineate" — grows around hedges and in foul places.

For pains of the limbs: take of the dry same plant which we named above; take six draughts and a strainer; put through with oil of cypress the inner kernel of the nut, of elder, and of terebinth; grind together — it will take away from the bowels and from the limbs their pains.

For pimples on the face: take of the dry plant, mix with oil; wash the face with it — it will cleanse all the pimples from the face.

APULEIUS. 119

Pound together; it draws the whiteness of scurf from off the head.

4. For soreness of body (indigestion), take this same plant nasturtium, and pennyroyal; boil them in water; give to drink; then you will relieve the soreness of the body, and the ailment departs.

5. Against swellings, take this same plant, and pound it with oil; lay it over the swellings; then take leaves of the same plant and lay them on as well.

6. Against warts (boils), take this same plant and yeast; pound together, lay thereto; they will soon be taken away.

GREAT WORT. XXII. Colchicum autumnale?

1. This plant, which people call hierobulbus in Greek, and by another name great wort, grows around hedges and in foul places.

2. For sore joints, take six ounces of this same plant, which we named hierobulbus, and the same measure of goats grease, and oil of cypress (oil of privet, one pound two ounces) by weight; pound together; when well mixed, it will take away the disease, whether of the internal organs or of the limbs.

3. If pimples grow on a woman's face, take roots of this same plant and mix with oil; then wash the face with it afterwards; it will purge away all the pimples from the face.

a Latin, Ad cruditatem, meaning indigestion.
b Latin, Ad furunculos, meaning boils.
c Latin, Cyprinum oleum, at one pound and two ounces; oil of privet, one pound two ounces. The translator had difficulties with this passage.

translation:
THE HERBAL

This plant, chapter XXIII.

This plant, which people call apollinaris, and by another name glorwort, they say that Apollo found it and gave it to Aesculapius the physician, from whom it received its name.

For wounds, take the juice of this same plant apollinaris, pound it with old wine, add salt, boil it, add vinegar, and let it cool a little; then pour it under the wound and let it be bound, so that it may smear the swelling — pour it on the wound to enclose the swelling that you wish to compress; then apply the plant and lay it upon the wound.

Chamomile, chapter XXIV.

For eye complaints, take the juice of the plant that people call camomile, and by another name chamomile; and when a man wishes to take it, it is said that he should take it both to cleanse the eyes and to relieve the pain; take then the juice of this plant and with it wash the eyes of the patient.

Heartsease, chapter XXV.

This plant, which people call chamedris, and by another name heartsease, it is found growing on hills and in open lands.

APVLEII. 121

GLOVEWORT, Lily of the valley. XXIII. Convallaria maialis.

1. Of this wort, which is named Apollinaris, and by another name glovewort, it is said that Apollo should first find it, and give it to Æsculapius, the leech, whence he set on it the name.

2. For sore of hands,a take this same wort Apollinaris, pound it with old lard without salt, add thereto a cup of old wine, and let that be heated without smoke,b and of the lard let there be by weight of one pound; knock (pound) together in the manner in which thou mightest work a plaister, and lay to the hand.

MAYTHE. XXIV. Anthemis nobilis.

1. For sore of eyes, let a man take ere the upgoing of the sun, the wort which is called χαμαίμηλον, and by another name maythe, and when a man taketh it, let him say that he will take it against white specks, and against sore of eyes; let him next take the ooze, and smear the eyes therewith.

HART CLOVER. XXV. Medicago. Bot.

1. This wort, which is named χαμαίδρυς, Germander,c and by another name hart clover, is produced on downs and on solid d lands.

a Ad vulnera cyronia. By Celsus (v. xxviii. 5.) vlcus chironium is defined as "quod et magnum est, et habit oras "duras, callosas, tumentes." But the interpreter knew some Greek, and in that language χείρ is hand.
b Latin, Vinum vetus sine fumo. The interpreter did not know that the Romans evaporated some watery particles of the must before fermentation. The words "be heated," are his interpolation.
c Teucrium chamaedrys, Bot.
d Latin, Sabulosis, sandy.

translation:
APULEIUS. 121

GLOVEWORT, Lily of the Valley. XXIII. Convallaria majalis.

1. Of this plant, which is called Apollinaris, and by another name glovewort, it is said that Apollo first discovered it and gave it to Aesculapius, the physician, who then gave it its name.

2. For sore hands, take this same plant Apollinaris, pound it with old lard without salt, add a cup of old wine, and heat it without smoke, using one pound of lard by weight. Pound it all together as you would work a plaster, and apply it to the hand.

MAYTHE. XXIV. Anthemis nobilis.

1. For sore eyes, let a man gather, before the rising of the sun, the plant called chamomile, and by another name maythe. When he takes it, let him declare that he will use it against white specks and soreness of the eyes. Then let him extract the juice and smear the eyes with it.

HART CLOVER. XXV. Medicago. Bot.

1. This plant, which is called chamaedrys, or Germander, and by another name hart clover, grows on open downs and on firm sandy ground.

a Regarding hand wounds: Celsus (v. xxviii. 5.) defines a chironium ulcer as "one that is large and has hard, callous, swollen edges." The translator knew some Greek, and in that language cheir means hand.
b Latin: old wine without smoke. The translator did not know that the Romans evaporated some watery particles from the must before fermentation. The words "be heated" are his own addition.
c Teucrium chamaedrys, Bot.
d Latin: Sabulosis, meaning sandy.

translation:
If anyone breaks a rib, take the same plant, pound it very fine, let him drink it in pure wine; and also apply it likewise so that it heals him.

Against nettle-rash: take the same plant, pound it very fine in butter, let him drink it in white wine; this will cause the tooth-pain to cease.

Against intestinal disorder: take the same plant, let him drink it in his drinks; what the frogs, called "punþoplice," say about it — that it relieves one's grip and restores one's health — the plant you shall take in the month that men call August.

Pulver camb. XXVI.
[See the glossary on eronreann.]

Against liver-burning: take the dry sap of the plant which by another name is called chamæelea and by another name pulver camb; give it to drink in wine, and for intestinal pain it heals wondrously.

Against poison of a bee: take the same plant, pound it, let him drink it in wine; it will drive out all the poison.

Against repeated burning: take the same plant, and root of hnærner, and heont, and hemp, all of these plants alike; by weight pound them together into a fine powder; let him drink in wine for mouth-sores in men; with a full cup and a little for small children once; wondrously he will pass it out through the bowels.

2. If one be bruised,* take this wort, which we HART CLOVER.

(vessel); give to drink in wine; it also healeth for an

WOLFS COMB. XXVI. Dipsacus
silvestris. Bot.

1. For liver sickness, take juice of this wort, which
man nameth χαμαιλελαια,b and by another name wolfs
comb; give it to drink in wine, and to the feverish
with warm water; wonderfully it benefits.

2. For drink of poison, take this same wort; knock

departs.

3. For water sickness, take this same wort, and
ravens foot and heart clover and ground pine, of all
these worts equally much by weight; pound them to

men five spoonsfull, and to younger, and to the infirm,

APULEIUS. 123

2. If someone is bruised, take this plant, which we call Hart Clover, named chamaedrys; pound it in a wooden vessel; give it to drink in wine. It also heals incised wounds.

Figure of a snake. Manuscript V., folio 25 d.

3. For the bite of an adder, take this same plant and pound it very finely to dust; give it to drink in old wine; it will thoroughly drive off the poison.

4. For foot gout, take this same plant; give it to drink in warm wine, in the manner we described before. It wonderfully alleviates the soreness and brings about the cure. This plant you shall gather in the month called August.

WOLFS COMB. Chapter XXVI. Dipsacus silvestris. Bot.

1. For liver sickness, take the juice of this plant, which people call chamaelelaia, and by another name wolfs comb; give it to drink in wine, and to the feverish with warm water; it benefits them wonderfully.

2. For the drinking of poison, take this same plant; grind it to dust; give it to drink in wine; all the poison will depart.

3. For water sickness, take this same plant, along with ravens foot, heart clover, and ground pine, of all these plants equally by weight; pound them to fine dust; give them to swallow in wine. To young men, five full spoonfuls; to younger persons and to the infirm, and to women, three full spoons; to small children, one spoonful. It wonderfully draws off the water through urine.

*Latin: heals the convulsed and also those with ruptures.
b The English text has mistakenly used chamaeleon instead of chamaelelaia, and translated accordingly, as in article CLII, which is incorrect.

124                              HERBAL

Rather ground pine.

HEMP. XXVII.

For swellings, take the plant that men call ground-pine, and by another name hemp; pound it, and lay it on the swelling; mix the juice then with the wound, so that it be very warm; take a portion and press it on the wounds.

For internal soreness, take a drink of the same plant; let her drink it until she improves.

HAWTHORN root. XXVIII.

For loosening the bowels, take the plant that Greeks and English alike call hawthorn root; pound it fine; let one drink it warm in warm water; this will loosen the bowels.

RELIEF-PLANT (Lithwort). XXIX.

The plant that men call by the Greek name and by another name relief-plant, is found above the hills and on the slopes, wherever it grows beside rocks.

For all things that afflict men, to heal them quickly, of those that are engendered within: take the plant we called by the Greek name, and pound it; lay it on the affliction — all the things as we said before that are evilly engendered in a person's body — it heals them through and through.

APVLEIL. 125

HEMP. XXVII. Aiuga chamæ-
pitys. Bot.

1. For wounds, take this wort which is called
χαμαλπιτυς, and by another name hemp; knock (pound),

2. For sore of inwards, take the same wort, give

water; it will stir the inwards.


LITHEWORT. XXIX. Sambucus
ebulus, gl.

1. This wort, which is named hostriago, and by
another name lithewort, is produced about burial
places and on barrows, and on walls of houses, which
stand against downs.

2. For all things which are generated on a man by
way of disease, take this wort, which we called hos-
triago, and knock (pound) it; then lay it to the
sore. All the things, as we ere (before) said, which
are generated on mans body to loathe, it thoroughly
will heal.

translation:
APULEIUS. 125

HEMP. Chapter 27. [Ajuga chamaepitys. Botany.]

1. For wounds, take this plant which is called chamaepitys, and by another name hemp; pound it and apply it to the wound; if the wound is very deep, take the liquid that seeps out and squeeze it onto the wound.

2. For soreness of the internal organs, take the same plant and give it to drink; it will relieve the soreness.


RAVEN'S FOOT. Chapter 28.

1. To stimulate the internal organs, take the plant which the Greeks call chamaedaphne, and which the English call raven's foot; pound it to a fine powder; give it to drink in warm water; it will stimulate the internal organs.


LITHEWORT. Chapter 29. [Sambucus ebulus. Botany.]

1. This plant, which is named hostriago, and by another name lithewort, grows around burial places and on burial mounds, and on the walls of houses that face downhill.

2. For all conditions that arise on a person's body through disease, take this plant, which we call hostriago, and pound it; then apply it to the sore. Everything that, as we said before, grows on a person's body in a loathsome manner, it will thoroughly heal.


[Footnote a:] Raven's foot is Ranunculus ficaria. Botany. Chamaedaphne is Ruscus racemosus. A ranunculus, but not ficaria, is drawn in MS. V.; a Ruscus in MS. G.

translation:
If you wish to gather this plant, you must be clean, and before sunrise, going upward, you must take it; in the month that men call July.

Henbane. xxx.

For disease of the mouth: take the plants that the Britons and the English call henbane; pound them, and a pound of their juice give to drink, and hold likewise in the mouth; and even if a man should swallow some part of it, it will do no harm.

Again, for disease of the mouth: take the same plant called britannica; if you have not the fresh, take the dried; pound it with wine to the thickness of honey; use then the same remedy as we said before — it has the same properties.

For toothache, and if they are inflamed: take the same plant, whose juice from some has a wonderful virtue; whether you use it fresh or dried in winter — for it does not appear at every season — you must in summer preserve the dried; and keep it likewise. It will notably and wonderfully relieve the pain and heal with wine.

For hardening of the bowels within: take the juice of this same plant; give it to drink according to the strength that one may best endure without harm; it will wonderfully loosen the bowels.

BRIGHT-COLOURED HYDELE. XXX.

Cochlearia Anglica. Bot.

1. For sore of mouth, take this wort which the Greeks name βρεττανική, and the Engles dark hued hydele; knock (pound) it so green, and wring the ooze; give to sip, and let (the sufferer) hold it so in his mouth, and though a man swallow some dole (part) thereof, it will alike benefit.

3. For sore of teeth, and if they wag, take the same wort; it out of some wonderlike virtue will help; its ooze and its dust is to be preserved in winter, since it does not appear at every time; its ooze thou shalt hold in a rams horn; dry also the dust, and keep it. Verily, also, it sharply benefits towards the same use, swallowed with wine.

Cochlearia Anglica. Botany.

Against the rash that physicians call papulae: take the same plant, crush it, give the juice to drink in pure pressed wine; it will seem to him that she has wonderfully healed.

Wild lettuce. XXXI.

The plant that men call lactuca silvatica, by another name wild lettuce, grows in enclosed places and in sandy spots.

Against dimness of the eyes: it is said that if a man wishes to rise in the morning so that he may look toward the east, let him fill his eyes with the juice and bathe them, and he will pass through that into brightness of sight.

Also against dimness of sight: take the juice of this same plant of lactuca silvatica as described, mixed with old wine and with honey blended together, and let it be without smoke until it is reduced; then let a man take the juice of this plant as described, and wine and honey blended together, and place it in a single glass flask to use whenever he has need; from that you may bring about an excellent medical remedy.

WOOD OR WILD LETTUCE. XXXI.

Lactuca scariola. Botany.

1. This plant, which is named lactuca silvatica, and by another name wood lettuce, grows in cultivated places and in sandy ones.

Chapter XXXII: Agrimony

For pain of the eyes, take the plant that men call agrimony by one name and by another name agrimony; pound it, squeeze it through a cloth; if you do not then have it green, take it dried and steep it in warm water, so that you may break it up as easily as possible; then it will stop the discharge that goes from the eyes.

For pain of the bowels, take the root of the same plant that we called agrimony; give it to drink, and it will heal soundly.

For cancer and for internal sores, take the same plant, green; pound it and lay it on the sore, smoothly; it can heal the wound. If the plant is dried, steep it in warm water; it is said that it heals the same ailment similarly.

For the bite of a viper, take two handfuls of the same plant and two cups of wine; give it to drink, soundly; it will relieve the poison.

For warts, take the same plant, pound it in vinegar and lay it thereon; it will remove the warts.

For pain of the spleen, take the same plant; give it to drink in wine; it will remove the pain from the spleen.

APULEIUS. 131

AGRIMONY. Chapter 32. Agrimonia eupatoria. Botany.

1. For soreness of the eyes, take this plant, which is called agrimony, and by another name garclive; pound it fresh and green by itself; if you do not have it green, take it dried and soak it in warm water, so that you may most easily use it; then smear it on the eyes; it quickly drives away the infection and soreness from the eyes.

2. For internal soreness, take the roots of this same plant, which we called agrimony; give it as a drink; it benefits wonderfully.

3. Against cancer, and against wounds, take this same plant while still green; pound it; apply it to the sore as appropriate; it can cure the condition. If the plant is dry, soak it in warm water; it is believed to serve the same purpose.

Figure of a snake. MS. V., fol. 27 d.

5. For warts, take this same plant, pound it with vinegar; apply it to the warts; it takes the warts away.

6. For soreness of the spleen, take this same plant, give it to swallow in wine; it removes the soreness of the spleen.

Pubic sore. XXXIII.

For shin-sores, take the juice of the dry plant that men call by another name pubic-sore, mix it with oil of smooth-fenugreek, so that it will be healed thoroughly, and if it has swollen, pound it soft and well-macerated, lay it thereon.

For lame sinew, take the dry plant called by another name silverweed, let it soak in a vessel, press it so that it will be thoroughly dissolved.

Pubic boil. XXXIV.

If any hardness has come upon the body, take the plant that men call laparium, and by another name pubic-boil; take also old smooth-fat and the knuckle from the oven-baked meat, lay it crushed and mixed with the food that you think fit, lay it thereon, and it will heal the boil thoroughly.

Herb of gall, or centaury. XXXV.

Against liver disease: take the plant that some call greater centaury, and also what some people call herb of gall, and what some call by the same name; boil it in pure oil to drink. Wonderfully it purges; and it is better for the spleen to do the same.

Against swelling and against cancer: take the same plant, pound it, lay it on the wound. It does not matter that the wound has grown around with a rim.

This plant centaury is very good for fresh wounds and for healing them, so that the wounds close gently, and likewise it causes the flesh to close up, if a man applies it in the liquid in which it stands.

Lesser centaury. XXXVI.

This plant which men call centaurium minus, and by another name cupmelle — what the Greeks call it has been named, and some men call it febrifugam — it grows in cultivated lands and in open fields. Against adder bite: take the dust of this same plant dried, or pound it fresh, give it to drink in old wine; it heals them greatly.

APVLEIL 135

EARTH GALL, or Curmel. XXXV. Chlora perfoliata. Bot.

1. For liver disease, take the wort which the Greeks name centaurea maior, and the Engle churmell the greater, and which also some men call earth gall; seethe it in wine, give to drink; wonderfully it strengtheneth; and for sore of spleen do the same.

2. For wounds and for cancer, take this same wort, pound it, lay it to the sore; it alloweth not that the sore further wax.

3. This same wort centaurea is very efficacious to heal new and wide wounds, so that the wounds soon come together; and so also similarly it has effect so that flesh shall cleave together if it be soaked in the water in which the wort is.

FEVER FUGE, or the lesser Curmel. XXXVI. Erythræa centaureum. Bot.

1. This wort, which is named centaurea minor, and by another name the lesser churmel, and which also some men call feverfuge, is produced on solid lands and on strong ones. Also it is said that Chiron the centaur should find (found) these worts which we before named centaurea maior, and now centaurea minor; whence they also obtain the name centaureæ.

2. For bite of snake, take dust of this same wort, or itself pounded; administer this to the patient in old wine; it will produce much benefit.

APULEIUS 135

EARTH GALL, or Centaury. Chapter 35. Chlora perfoliata. Botany.

1. For liver disease, take the plant which the Greeks call centaurea maior, and which the English call the greater churmel, and which some men also call earth gall; boil it in wine and give it to drink; it strengthens wonderfully; and for soreness of the spleen do the same.

2. For wounds and for cancer, take this same plant, pound it, and lay it on the sore; it will not allow the sore to grow further.

3. This same plant centaurea is very effective at healing new and wide wounds, so that the wounds soon close together; and similarly it has the effect that flesh will knit together if it is soaked in the water in which the plant has been steeped.

1. This plant, which is named centaurea minor, and by another name the lesser churmel, and which some men also call feverfuge, grows on firm ground and on hard soils. [One] proclaims, as some say, for dim and painful eyes, so that the juice of the plant may be obtained.

138 HERBARIUM

Persolata, is Burdock = clate.

This plant, called boete, soothes swellings on bruises and heals all the nether parts.

For fever: take the leaves of this same plant, boil them, and apply them to the fever-patient; it relieves the fever.

For a canker on a wound: take the root of this same plant, boil it in water, bathe the wound with it; then take the plant, and garlic, and grease, pound them together with vinegar, place them on a cloth, and lay it on the wound.

For inner soreness: take the leaves of this same plant, strain them with a cloth, add honey, strain again, and give it to the patient to drink.

For a painful swelling: take the root of this same plant, pound it with salt and fresh water, and lay it on the swelling.

MS. V. is here much eaten out.

For a swelling that causes inner pain: take the roots of this same plant and the leaves of hawthorn, pound them together in equal measure, lay them on the wounds.

This plant, which some call by the other name Streapbeorgean, is found in shaded places, and in open ground, and also on hills.

For pain in the spleen: take the leaves of this same plant, boil them as described above, add honey, and give it to the patient to drink.

3. In the event that a cancer grows upon a wound, take this plant, boil it in water; bathe the wound with it; afterwards take the plant and soap and grease, pound them with vinegar, place them on a cloth, and lay them on the wound.

4. For internal soreness, take a draught of the juice of this same plant, and two draughts of honey; give this to the sick person to drink while fasting.

5. For the bite of a mad dog, take a root of this same plant, pound it with coarse salt, and lay that on the wound.

6. For new wounds that produce wet discharge or fluid, take root of this same plant and hawthorn leaves in equal quantities; pound them together; lay them on the wounds.

STRAWBERRY. XXXVIII.

1. This plant, which is named fraga (fragaria), and by another name strawberry, grows in shaded places and in open ones, and also on downs.

2. For soreness of the spleen, take juice of this same plant, which we call fragaria, and honey; give it to drink; it benefits wonderfully.

140 HERBARIUM

Pepper, it is called, greatly reduces swelling against eruptions and against internal sores.

Marsh Mallow. XXXIX.

This plant which one calls hibiscum and by another name marsh mallow is found in wet places and in fields.

For foot-sores, take the plant which people call hibiscum, pound it with old ale, lay it on the sore; by the third day it will have healed it. The juice of the plant settles many old sores in a wondrous manner.

For every gathering that forms on a person's body, take the same plant, boil it with ale, cress, and linseed and meal, lay it on the sore; it will dissolve all the hardnesses.

Horsetail. XL. Equisetum.

For when a man's stomach is upset, take the juice of this plant which the Italians call equisetum, mixed with spiced wine; let him drink two cups. One well may believe that it will heal the evil.

Along with pepper, it greatly benefits when drunk, for Strawberry — for oppression of the chest and soreness of the internal organs. Article 38.

HORSETAIL. Chapter 40.

1. If a man has become excessively bloated in the belly, take the juice of this plant, which the Greeks call Hippouris and the Italians call equisetum, in sweetened wine, and give it to drink in two draughts. It is confidently believed that this will cure that ailment.

142 HERBARIUM

If anyone suffers from a bleeding that irritates, let him take the juice of this same dry plant, boil it in strong wine without smoke, drink it, and then soon it will stop the blood.

Marshmallow. XLI.

This plant which men call maluæ hepaticæ, and by another name hocleaf, grows everywhere in cultivated places.

For bladder trouble, take quickly the dry plant that we called maluam hepaticam, one bundle of its roots boiled in water with vinegar to half, and when that liquid has stood long enough so that it cools within three days, filled as we said before to half the measure, let the fasting person drink it — it will heal him.

For running sores, take the same plant, pound it with old lard, and it will wondrously heal the running sore.

For itching sores, take the same plant, boil it in oil, and when you have them cooked together, pound the leaves together in a mortar, then lay it on a cloth and apply it so that you do not unbind it for two days — the sore will burst.

For fresh wounds, take the dry root of the same plant, burn it to dust, and apply it to the wounds.

HOCKLEAF. Chapter 41. Malva silvestris. Botany.
1. This plant, which is called malva erratica, and by another name hock leaf, grows everywhere in cultivated places.

2. For a sore of the bladder, take this plant which we called malva erratica, along with its root, weighing one pound; boil it thoroughly in water down to half the original amount, with the water measuring a sextarius (1½ pints) or more, and let it be boiled within three days, as we said before, down to a half; give it to the patient to drink while fasting; it will heal them.

3. For sore sinews, take this same plant, pound it with old lard; it wonderfully heals soreness of the sinews.

4. For a sore side, take this same plant, boil it, and after you have boiled it put it all together; then take the leaves and pound them in a mortar; then put them on a cloth and apply it to the sore, so that you do not unbind it for three days; you shall improve the sore.

5. For new wounds, take a root of this same plant, burn it to powder; apply it to the wounds.

Ox-tongue. XLII.

[See the glossary.]

The plant that the snails call in the Roman tongue lingua bubula, and also in English "ox-tongue," and by another name "hound's tongue" — it is found in cultivated places and in sandy lands.

If in any man the day-fever rages repeatedly, take from it one of those stalks, then take of it when it has three shoots; read over it this charm, and give the man to drink, and you will have cured him.

Also this same plant is good for those who suffer from the same condition as those who could not retain their food.

When another plant of this same kind likewise has some portion, take leaves of it; then when the stalk has been pressed in a vessel, it counteracts ague and worms.

For nausea, take this same plant and honey and a loaf that has been baked with grease, and bind it similarly to a poultice upon the limb, and it will break it apart.

For watery discharge, take the plant that is called bulbiscillitici, and by another name "squill," and —

HOUNDS TONGUE. XLII. Cynoglossum
officinale. Bot.

1. This wort, which the Greeks name βούγλωσσον, and the Romans lingua bubula, and also the Engle call glovewort, and by another name hounds tongue, is produced in cultivated places, and in sandy lands.

2. If any man have a tertian fever, or a quartan, take the root of this wort, when it has three shoots to seed; seethe the root in water; give (it) him to drink; thou shall cure him.

3. The wort also which has four seed stalks, benefits like that which we have before mentioned.

4. Besides, there is another wort like this, which hath in some degree a less leaf than the dock. A root of that wort swallowed in water, is an antidote against frogs and snakes.

5. Against oppression of the chest,ᵃ take this same wort and honey, and a loaf which has been baked with lard, in the manner in which thou wouldst make a poultice; wonderfully doth it disperse the disorder.

translation:
APULEIUS. 145

HOUND'S TONGUE. XLII. Cynoglossum officinale. Bot.

1. This plant, which the Greeks call βούγλωσσον, and the Romans lingua bubula, and which the English also call glovewort, and by another name hound's tongue, grows in cultivated places and in sandy lands.

2. If any man has a tertian fever or a quartan fever, take the root of this plant when it has three shoots going to seed; boil the root in water; give it to him to drink; you will cure him.

3. The plant that also has four seed stalks has similar benefits to the one we have mentioned above.

4. Besides, there is another plant like this one, which has somewhat smaller leaves than dock. A root of that plant swallowed in water is an antidote against frogs and snakes.

5. Against chest congestion, take this same plant and honey, and a loaf that has been baked with lard, and make a poultice in the usual way; it wonderfully disperses the disorder.

GLADDEN, incorrectly named. XLIII. Scilla maritima. Bot.

1. For water sickness (dropsy), take this plant, which is named βολβός σκιλλητικός, and by another

ᵃ Latin: Ad suppurationes in corpore. The old interpreter read suspirationes.
ᵇ The traditional figure may be Scilla nutans, Bot., or some other, but the leaves are drawn too broad for squills. In MS. Add. 17063, a flowerpot has been made out of the bulb. Βόλβος σκιλλητικός is in so many words the bulb of the squill, and should not have been confused with gladden, gladiolus. But this plant is used in place of others.

Rub it around the outside, take the inner membrane, boil it in a vessel, then let the warm juice flow with it together; also add to it honey and vinegar, a spoonful of rue, fill it full of brine, quickly the sickness shall be drawn out through the opening.

For pain of limbs: take the same plant's roots as are named cræban, the inner membrane, pound it in oil, a spoonful of it suffices, and soon it will ease them.

For the ailment that the Greeks name paronichial: take the juice of the same plant, pound the roots with vinegar and with white of egg, apply it to the swelling, it shall heal it.

For when a man cannot contain himself, that is, his bodily need: take leaves of the same plant, place them under the tongue, and soon it will restrain the need.

Chapter 44. Umbilicum.

This plant that the Greeks call cotyledon and the Romans name umbilicum is found in rocky places and in mountains.

Pound together, lay to the sores, let it [stay], it will heal them; where you find the plant, you must take it at Pentecost.

Attorlathe. XLV.

The plant that men call gall-wort and by another name call attorlathe is found in waste places and by roads.

For swelling of the joints, take this plant, pound it with hound's bane and lay it to the sore area where the swelling is; it will reduce the swelling. It also stops spitting of blood and heals pain in the hands, and cures all of that.

Horehound. XLVI.

For one who severely coughs and for the chest: take this plant which is called savory and manubium by the Romans, and in English is also called horehound; boil it in water, let the one who severely coughs drink it — it will heal him completely.

For soreness of the stomach, take the dry same plant, boil the juice in water, let him drink it; it will remove the soreness of the stomach and relieve the wind within him; let him drink the same plant well boiled in water — it will make him sneeze.

For pustules around the navel, take the same plant manubium, and pennyroyal, and elecampane, all equal portions by weight, boil in water, and with wine or vinegar lay to the navel — it will kill the pustules.

ATTORLOTHE. XLV. Panicum crus galli. Bot.

1. This wort, which is named galli crus, and by another name attorlothe, is produced in solid places, and against ways.
2. For bite of dog, take this wort, pound it with grease, and with a hearth baked loaf, lay to the wound, soon it will be healed; also this same is of benefit for a hard swelling, and removes it all.

HOREHOUND.a XLVI. Marrubium vulgare. Bot.

1. For colds in the head, and in case a man hreaks heavily (makes great efforts to clear his throat of phlegm), take this wort, which the Greeks name πράσιον, and the Romans marrubium, and also the English call it horehound, seethe it in water, give to drink to them that hreak heavily; it will heal them wonderfully.
2. For sore of maw (stomach), take juice of this same wort, give (the sufferer) to drink; it doth away the sore of the maw; and if fever vex him, give him this same wort in water to drink freely, it will raise him up.
3. For tape worms about the navel, take this same wort marrubium, and wormwood, and lupins, of all these worts alike much by weight, seethe in sweetened water and with wine, twice or thrice, lay to the navel; it killeth the worms.

a A mistake has occurred in MS. V. in the placing of the figure, which seems intended for Ceterach. Horehound is truly drawn as Prassion in MS. Bodley, 130: glossed horehounde in hand of xii. century. In MS. A., fol. 25 b, the figure has the flowers terminal, which ought to be axillary. The drawings in MSS. T. G. are monstrous.

translation:
APULEIUS. 149

[continuing from previous page] ...weight, pound together, apply to the swellings, it reduces them. This plant you shall gather at midwinter.

ATTORLOTHE [Grass of the Cock's Spur]. Chapter 45. Botanical name: Panicum crus galli.

1. This plant, which is called galli crus, and by another name attorlothe, grows in firm ground and along roadsides.
2. For a dog bite, take this plant, pound it with grease, and with a loaf baked on the hearth, apply it to the wound; it will soon be healed. It is also effective against hard swellings and removes them entirely.

HOREHOUND. Chapter 46. Botanical name: Marrubium vulgare.

1. For head colds, and when a person is coughing heavily and straining to clear phlegm from their throat, take this plant, which the Greeks call prassion and the Romans call marrubium, and which the English also call horehound. Boil it in water and give the drink to those who are coughing heavily; it will heal them remarkably well.
2. For a sore stomach, take the juice of this same plant and give it to the sufferer to drink; it will relieve the stomach pain. And if fever also afflicts him, give him this same plant steeped in water to drink freely; it will restore him.
3. For tapeworms around the navel, take this same plant marrubium, along with wormwood and lupins, equal amounts of all these plants by weight, boil them in sweetened water with wine, and apply to the navel two or three times; it kills the worms.

a A mistake has occurred in manuscript V in the placement of the illustration, which appears to have been intended for Ceterach. Horehound is correctly depicted as Prassion in MS Bodley 130, with the gloss "horehounde" written in a twelfth-century hand. In MS A, folio 25b, the illustration shows terminal flowers, when they should be axillary. The illustrations in manuscripts T and G are altogether wrong.

150                    HERBAL

For lip sores and for swelling, take the same plant, bathe toward the sores, apply it to those sores — it will heal them.

For a venomous bite, take the dry same plant, pound it in old wine, then it will draw out the poison.

For scab and for tetter, take the same plant, boil it in a vessel, wash the body with it, and bathe with it — it will drive out the scurf and the tetter.

For lung disease, take the same plant, boil it in honeyed ale, drink it — he will be wondrously healed.

For all stiffness of the body, take the same plant, pound it with leek, lay it on the sore — it will heal the wound wondrously.

Foxglove.   XLVII.

Iris xiphium.    For unknown eruptions that appear on the body, take the dry root of the plant that men call xirion and by another name foxglove, of equal parts of its inner portions mixed together, and equal portions of its inner parts together; pound them all together with pine; then dip a cloth in it, lay it on the sore — you will accomplish the cure.

For hardness and swelling, take the same plant bruised, press it and pound it, then take equal portions mixed together with leek; lay it on the sore — it will draw out the broken bones, and also whatever harmful thing is on the body it will drive away.

152 HERBARIUM

[It] is said that if someone with his foot steps on a snake-track, and a snake bites him, the nature of [this plant] is very harmful — take it against that.

Plant number XLVIII.

Take a handful of the roots together, take this plant which men call Callitricum, and by another name call Plant of the Path; pound it, apply it separately to the sore, and it heals it.
For a man's wound, take a quantity of the same plant, pound it on oil as Smyrna [prescribes], then the steam of it will quickly make it well.

Allium moly. XLIX.

This plant which men call by one name Temolum and by another name Ringwort — as Omenus says, its virtue is that Mencunius ordained it should be so — this plant's juice is very effective and its root system is very tough, and also broad like that of leek.
For pain from a bruise, take this plant, pound it and lay it on; it will ease the pain.

Holiotropion scorpiurus. This plant which the Greeks call Heliotropium and by the Latin name call Ventramnum — and also in English is called Sun-follower — grows in sunny places and in clean open ground and also in meadows.

(Page 154 — HERBARIUM)

[Introductory passage:]
...it straightens it up, it opens up, and it soothes it, and it heals it. For these remedies that we here prescribe against sores that have been applied.

Against all poisons: take the juice of the plant, pound it thoroughly, mix it finely with good wine, and drink it in pure wine — thus the poison dissolves.

For sleep: take the same plant's leaf, pound it, and lay it upon the limb where it is needed, so that it heals and closes up.

MÆÐENE. LI.

The plant that men call by the other name mæðene is called rýðmurt in Lucania. It has a white man's appearance, and it is adorned with rough stalks.

Against pain in the bones, and against fracture of bones: take the same plant, pound it, lay it upon the bone where the break is — it will quickly be well, like a poultice drawn together.

Also, the plant's juice heals every wound that afflicts the body — that is, if the man pounds the plant's root and lays it upon the wound, it heals all the injury.

HÝMELE. LII.

The plant that men call politnicum, and by another name hýmele, grows in old house-sites and also in upright places.

When the sun is setting they close themselves, and again when it rises they open and spread themselves; this is beneficial for the medical remedies which we have written after this.

2. For all poisons, take this same plant, pound it to very fine dust, or use its juice, and give it to drink in good wine; it wonderfully removes the poison.

MADDER. Chapter 51. Rubia tinctorum.
1. This plant, which is named grias, first grows in Lucania; it has the appearance of white marble, and it is adorned with four red stalks.

2. For leg ache and for leg injury, take this same plant, pound it, lay it on the leg; on the third day relief will come to him, as if a poultice had been laid there.

3. Also a root of this plant is beneficial for every sore that troubles the body; that is, when a man pounds the root and applies it to the sore, it heals the entire sore.

HOP TREFOIL. Chapter 52. Trifolium procumbens.
1. This plant, which is named polytrichon, and by another name hymele, grows in old house-sites and also in damp places.

translation:
For internal soreness, take the dry tender leaf of what we call politricum, which has spines on its surface; pound then the leaves and nine pepper corns and coriander, again nine corns, all together; give to drink in good wine, and when he goes to the bath — also those same plants cause both the veins and the arteries to grow hair.

Woodruff. LIII.

For a swelling in the womb, take the dry tender roots of the plant that grinds malochin, which is called azua and pomane aftula pegia; and also what is called angle, woodruff, that is named so; pound with pine, let him drink immediately, and he will soon feel relief from his internal soreness.

For inward leprosy, take the dry tender plant called pegia, mixed with strong vinegar; let him drink it — it will purge the bowels.

Poppy. LIV.

For soreness of the eyes, where it is that which they call tonnige, take the dry tender plant, the one that grinds moecopiar, which is called pomane papauer album, and also what is called white poppy; or the stalk, lay it with the juice upon the eyes.

For swellings and tumors, or those that are hardened, take the dry tender plant, pound with vinegar, lay it over the face — it will smooth out the sore.

2. For soreness of the internal organs, take leaves of this plant, Hop Trefoil, which we named πολύτριχον; its twigs are like swine bristles. Pound the leaves together with nine pepper corns and nine grains of coriander seed; give to drink in good wine, and let this be done when the patient goes to the bath. This plant is also effective at making either men's or women's hair grow.

Woodruff. LIII. Asphodelus ramosus. Botany.
1. If a man has an overgrown womb, take the roots of this plant, which the Greeks call μαλάχη ἀγρία, and the Romans call hastula regia, and which the English call woodruff; pound with wine and give to drink. You will soon see the benefit of this.

2. For looseness of the internal organs, take seed of this plant, which we called hastula regia, mixed with strong vinegar, and administer it to be drunk; it binds the internal organs.

Poppy. LIV. Papaver somniferum. Botany.
1. For sore eyes — that is, what we call blearedness — take the juice of this plant, which the Greeks call μήκωνα, and the Romans call papaver album, and the English call white poppy; apply the stalk with its fruit to the eyes.

2. For soreness of the temples or of the head, take juice of the same plant, pound it with vinegar, and lay it upon the forehead; it relieves the soreness.

ᵃ See article xxxiii. In the table of contents this is correctly translated from the Latin; but "poppexen" can only mean wrongly grown, not troubled with diarrhea. Similarly II.4, XL.1., LXIX.1.

If a person cannot stop vomiting, take the root of this plant, which men call by one name and name with another name, pound it fine, mix it with ale, strain it; let him drink it fully — it will help greatly.

[Opening fragment]
...to remove what is unpleasant, that it settles those further matters.


Kneeholly. LIX.

For the throat and for the stomach, take a full handful of the plant that people commonly call by one name cneopholen, also named wild plum shoots, mixed with honey; it will then heal the throat.


Galluc. LX.

This plant that one may identify by another name, galluc, is found on moors and in fields, and also in meadows.

For a chest inflammation, take the plant, grind it thoroughly, pound it into dust, give it to drink in wine, and so the inflammation will subside.

If a person has internal swelling, let him take the same plant, crumble and roast it on hot ashes, let him eat it while sitting with honey; it will heal him, and will also cleanse the stomach entirely.

For a stomach ailment, take the same plant and mix it with honey and with vinegar in a noticeably large quantity, so that it relieves the pain.

translation:
APULEIUS. 163

[Regarding] the man's swollen neck, who suffers the evil, it will give an experimental proof of that same virtue.

KNEE HOLLY, or Butcher's Broom. Chapter 59. [Botanical name: Ruscus aculeatus]

For wrist drop, and for stomach or belly complaints, take two cups full of the juice of this plant, which is called victoriola, and by another name knee holly; give it to the patient to drink on an empty stomach mixed with honey; it will soon reduce the wrist drop.

YALLUC, or Comfrey. Chapter 60. [Botanical name: Symphytum officinale]

1. This plant, which is called confirma (comfrey), and by another name yalluc, grows on moors and fields, and also on meadows.
2. For women's excessive bleeding, take this plant comfrey, grind it to a very fine powder, and give it in wine to drink; the bleeding will soon stop.
3. If someone has a rupture internally, let him take roots of this plant, roast them in hot ashes, then swallow them with honey on an empty stomach, and he will be healed; it also purges the whole stomach.
4. For soreness of the stomach, take this same plant, and mix it with honey and vinegar; you will find great benefit.

b The drawing in MS. V, fol. 34d, has comfrey leaves and no more. MS. A., fol. 30b, has leaves not quite so distinct, and the root has become bulbous. In MS. Bodley, 130, one of the mint tribe is drawn.

This plant, which one calls by another name [name given elsewhere], grows between streams and in rough places.

This plant shines at night like stars in the sky, and he who knows it says that it removes garlic-smell from people, and takes away their aches and pains, and such powers as one might wish to know of it.

Chapter 61.

1. This plant, which is named asterion, and by another name [name missing], grows between stones and in rough places.

2. This plant shines at night like a star in the sky, and whoever sees it, not knowing what it is, thinks he is seeing a ghost, and being frightened (as he naturally would be), he is laughed at by herdsmen and by those who know the properties of the plant.

translation:
[Page 170 — HERBARIUM]

At night it shines its light, and also its seeds are like those of darnel; and it is found by those who seek it along streams, gathered at night and prepared.

This plant is said to help a person who suffers from a monthly complaint; if a man thinks he is afflicted with that illness, it keeps him sound and raises him up, and if he carries it with him, the illness will not come near him.

For pain in the hip-bones, take smoke of the same plant, bind it with a linen cloth to the hip — it will heal it.

[Chapter LXVII — Verbena (Benbena)]

The plant that people call Peristereon, and by another name Benbenam, is well known among the doves from which it takes its Latin name Columbina.

Whoever carries this plant with him, as those who named Peristereon said, cannot be bitten by dogs.

For all hardened growths, take the dust of this same plant and have it drunk; it is said also that if its branches are rubbed upon children it benefits them.

White Bryony. LXVIII.

Bryonia dioica. For the spleen, take quickly the plant that one calls bryony by one name, and hymele by another; mix it among food, then it shall gently pass through the internal organs; it is very good that one should give it to drink mixed with a purging drink.

For when a man has worms in the bowel, take the seeds of the plant that one calls nymrete by another name; pound them with pine and give to drink.

If you give the plant to chew in cases of internal disorder, it will then cleanse the interior.

For those troubled with gout, take quickly the root of the plant that one calls cleavers by another name; mix it with him, and apply it to his joint; it will never fail to benefit him.

APULEIUS. 173

HYMELE. Chapter 68. (Humulus lupulus / Common Hop)

1. For soreness of the spleen, take this plant, which is named bryony in Greek, and by another name hymele; give it to the sick person to swallow with his food; then the disease shall gently pass out through the urine. This plant is so highly regarded that men mix it with their everyday drinks.

The Water Lily. Chapter 69.

1. In case a man has an overgrown belly, take seed of this plant, which is named water lily in Greek, and by another name [unnamed here], pound it with wine, and give it to drink.

2. Again for the same condition, give the root to the sick person to eat for ten days.

3. Again, if you give this plant in strong wine to be swallowed, it restrains the ill running (diarrhea) of the bowels.

CLOVER. Chapter 70. (Trifolium pratense / Meadow Clover)

For soreness of the jaws or back of the mouth, if a person carries with him a root of this plant, which is named in Greek klrsion, and by another name clover, and wears it about his neck, his throat will never trouble him.

translation:
LXXI.

This plant that the Greeks call by the Latin name "aluta" — and each people has its own name for it — is also called by the English "adder's wort" (against serpent's bite).

One needs, when treating a bite, to take the dry leaves of this plant that the Greeks call by that name, pound them in a vessel, lay them on the wound frequently, and wrap it around.

LXXII.

One needs, when treating a bite, to take the leaves of the plant that people call "scorpion-bean" by another name — let it be steeped in pure wine — pound then the plant and lay it on the wound frequently.

Take the juice of this same plant and pound it, and mix it with the oil that comes from a young unripe olive, so that it drives out the venom.

For the swelling that comes upon a person daily or every other day, take the same plant and bind it around the person's body: it will drive away the daily and every-other-day fever.

Felt-wort. LXXIII.

This plant that people call "verbascum" and by another name "felt-wort" is found growing in sandy places and in dunghills. The plant's juice is said to be as effective as mercury/quicksilver.

Woad. Chapter 71. Isatis tinctoria. Botany.

1. This plant the Greeks call isatis, the Romans call aluta, and the English also call it "for serpent's bite."

1. For a snake bite, take this plant, which is called scorodion, and by another name [blank], boil it in wine, and give it to the sick person to drink. Then pound the plant and lay it on the wound.

translation:
176
HERBARIUM

[Give] julixe to the old men, ryllan when he comes to church, and let him not thereafter suffer any evil injury to afflict him.

If a person finds himself feverish and dry, bind one tealzne [plant] upon him; he will not be troubled by any evil, nor will illness nor any evil come upon him.
Take the root of the same plant called uepbarcum, crushed together, lay it upon the wound within a short time; it heals the sore that the sheep suffer from, and it also makes them slender and fit; also our elders said and declared that this dried plant served well as a high remedy.

LXXIV.

He who wishes to travel a long way, let him have with him on the journey the plant that men call heraclean and by other names they call it; then he need not fear any enemy along the way, for it will protect him.

Celandine. LXXV.

For dimness of the eyes, and running of the eyes, and eyes growing together, take the juice of the plant that men call celidoniam and by other names call cylepenie; crush it with white pine resin and with honey and pepper, so that it is well blended; and smear it then within the eyes.

[Footnotes as transcribed above, being editorial variants from manuscripts H and B.]

(gave) this herb to Ulysses, the chieftain, when he came to Circe, and he after that feared none of her evil works. [FELT WORT. Article 73.]

2. If someone carries with him one twig of this herb, he will not be frightened by any terror, nor will a wild beast harm him, nor will any evil come near.

Article 74.

Whoever must travel a very long way, let him carry with him on the journey the herb called Heraclea, and by another name [blank], and then he will fear no robber, for the herb puts them all to flight.

CELANDINE. Article 75. [Chelidonium maius.]

1. For dimness of eyes and soreness and obstruction, take the juice of this herb, which is named chelidonia, and by another name like that celandine, pressed out of the roots; let it be well pounded together with old wine and honey and pepper, then apply it to the eyes internally.

Also for those who have swellings, that wise men from that milk of the plant take the same plant's juice and breathe it upon him so that it may be better for him.

Furthermore for dim eyes, take of the same plant's juice or the pale blossoms ground up and mixed together with honey mixed in, then gently with ashes apply to the sore eyes in warm water. This is a good remedy for darkness of the eyes.

For inflammation, take of the same plant, pound it, lay it upon the same inflammation so that it may seem to relieve the pain.

For toothache, give to eat of the same plant's roots.

180 HERBARIUM

MS. V. is here [imperfect] For blood within, take nine portions of this same plant, pour through a cloth and press the nasal passages with it; with that it sends out the blood.

Groundsel. LXXVII.

The plant that men call by the name groundsel in Latin — called Senecio — is born in fields and around villages.

For swellings, however old they may be, take the plant that is called Senecio, pound it with old lard, lay it on the swellings; it heals them quickly.

If a person has a limb dislocated, take the same plant, in the morning grind it, either then or at midday, pound it as those men previously said with old lard, lay it on; soon it opens the wound and clears it.

For rotten abscesses, take the same plant, pound it with lard, lay it on the rot; it softens it greatly and heals the sores within.

For pain in the loins, take the same plant, pound it with salt in the same manner as you would apply a cleavers poultice to the loins; likewise it heals and also relieves the sores within.

Fern. LXXVIII.

For wounds, take the dried root of the plant that men call by the Latin name Filix, which is called fern, pound it, lay it on the wound; and the noble plant's juice, with fern fronds, mix together and give to drink in wine.

GROUNDSEL. LXXVII. (Senecio vulgaris.)

1. This plant, which is called senecio, and by another name groundsel, grows on rooftops and around walls.

2. For wounds, even very old ones, take this plant, which we call senecio; pound it with old lard, apply it to the wounds; it heals them quickly.

3. If someone has been struck with iron, take this same plant early in the morning or at midday; pound it, as described above, with old lard; apply it to the wound; it will soon open and cleanse the wound.

4. For gout, take this same plant, pound it with lard, apply it to the feet; it relieves the condition; it also greatly benefits soreness of the sinews.

5. For soreness of the loins, take this same plant, pound it with salt as you would make a poultice; apply it to the loins in this way; it is also effective against soreness of the feet.

For when a young man has a swelling, take the same plant as when it grows on a beech tree, crush it with garlic and add a cloth soaked in it, and apply it to him for the while that the swelling persists; on the next day he will be healed.

Chapter LXXIX. Spice.

For pain of the spleen, take the leaves of this plant that men call by one name "spice" and by another name "quick," and boil them; then lay a cloth soaked in it upon the spleen; you will find relief from the fullness.

Chapter LXXX. Gladiolus (Iris).

For pain of the bladder and when a man cannot urinate, take the root of this plant whose outer part men call by one name gladiolum and by another name gladene; dry it, then crush it and mix it with treacle, fennel, and three peppercorns, and give it to drink.

For pain of the spleen, take the same plant gladiolum when it is young and dry; crush it very small into a fine powder, give it to be taken in warm wine; it is said that it heals the spleen wonderfully.

For pain of the inner organs and of the chest, take the plant called bengean, pounded, and into a preparation

Boðen. Chapter LXXXI.

The plant that people call by the Norman name boþen is found in fertile lands and in settled dwellings.

For toothache, take dry roots of the plant called boðen by the Normans, let him eat without swallowing; he takes the roots, holds that juice in his mouth, and it soon heals the teeth.

For one who is bedridden, take the roots of the plant, crush them with the juice of elder, and rub the bedridden person vigorously and you will heal him.

For itching, take the same plant, crush it and mix it with old wine, and for sores give to drink three days.

For roughness of the chest and pain of the inner parts, take dry roots of the same plant, one handful, put them in a pot and mix together, and also another handful of nettles, boil together in a vessel, give to drink, and he will be well.

For mouth wounds, take the same plant that is called by the Norman name, crush it, lay the pulp upon the wounds.

[lukewarm in goat's milk, or better still, in wine, administer this; the sore will cease.] GLADDEN. Art. 80.

BOTHEN. Chapter 81. Rosmarinus officinalis. Botany.

1. This plant, which is called rosemary, and by another name bothen, grows on sandy ground and in herb gardens.

2. For toothache, take a root of this plant, which we call rosemary, give it to the sufferer to eat; without delay it relieves the soreness of the teeth. Let him hold the liquid from it in his mouth; it will soon heal the teeth.

3. For the sick, take this plant rosemary, pound it with oil, and rub it on the sick person; it will heal him wonderfully.

4. Against itching, take this same plant, pound it, and mix its juice with old wine and with warm water; administer this for three days.

5. For liver sickness, and that of the internal organs, take one handful of this same plant, scrape it into water, and add to it two handfuls of nard and a stalk of rue; boil them together in water, give it to the patient to drink; he will be healed.

6. For fresh wounds, take this same plant, which we call rosemary, pound it with lard, and apply it to the wound.

Field carrot. LXXXII.

The plant that one calls wild parsnip, and by another name field carrot, grows on sandy slopes and in rough places.

For [purging] — men easily [use it]: take the root of this plant, the wild parsnip, boil it in water, then let the person bathe himself in it, and he will be healed.

For purging of the body: take the root of the same plant, the wild parsnip, boil it in water, and when it has boiled, mix it well, and let them drink it with wild celery; they will be purged.

Wound-herb. LXXXIII.

The plant that one calls perdicalis, and by another name wound-herb, is found among rocks and in walls and in rough places.

For rotting sores and for cancer: take the root of this plant, perdicalis, boil it in water, bathe then the feet and the knees; then pound the plant with a pestle and lay it on a cloth and apply it to the sores and to the knees — thus you will heal them well.

[A preparation] that relieves those who suffer from it, and clears the stomach of that person so that he digests it.

For eye pain and eyelid complaint, take dried and then pounded leaves, rubbed up in old wine, and apply to that same sore.

If the pain is in the ears, let the dried herb be soaked, and take the same pounded juice, drop it into the ear so that it runs through.

Polypody. LXXXV.

The plant that men call by the Latin name polypody and by other names, is called by those names because it is found growing on stony places and on old tree-stumps, and it has on each leaf two rows of little spots which shine like gold.

For headache, take the juice of the plant called polypody, clean and purified, boil it in vinegar with a little fat, and when the head is bathed with it, it relieves the pain.

Ground ivy. LXXXVI.

190                          HERBARIUM

For many days use a bath, do not come into cold water, nor eat heavily in an unwholesome way — so shall he find healing.

For toothache: take the juice of this dry silver plant, which we call nembun, boil it gently and hold it in the mouth.

For sore gums: take the juice of this same dry plant, with its root ground up, drink it in wine — it will relieve it.

If any evil man has harmed a person through any malicious intent, and bound him: take the dry silver plant, grind the root, give it to drink in ale, and sprinkle him with that water — he will be unbound.

                    Savine.  LXXXVII.

For the royal disease which men call in our tongue "jaundice" — take the plant that men call savin, and by another name call the same, give it to drink with honey; it will purge it so that the silver goes out with the wine, ground up.

For headache: take that same plant, savin, well ground up with vinegar and with oil mixed together, smear the head and the temples thoroughly — it will relieve it.

For deadly convulsions: take that plant, savin, ground up with honey, smear it on the wound.

Page 192

HERBARIUM

Chapter 88: For soreness of the eyes

This is for soreness of the eyes and swelling thereof: take the dry plant called hound's-tongue — which one may also call caput — and upon the cheekbone of the head it is called by that name; boil it in water, and then with that water bathe the eyes gently, until the soreness is eased.

Chapter 89: Bramble

This is for soreness of the eyelids: take the plant that men call bramble, also named by another name as meadowsweet; pound it, squeeze the juice upon the eye, until the eye is cleansed and healed in the same manner.

For soreness of the spleen: take the same plant, chopped, as meadowsweet, and let the roots be red; boil in water; give to drink fasting, with a little portion of dark liquid, each day, that drink will ease it.

For pain of the heart: take the same plant's leaves, pounded; lay them upon the chest where the pain is, until it breaks the soreness.

For fresh wounds: take the same plant, lay it upon the wounds without anything else; it will heal the wounds.

For soreness of the limbs: take some portion of the same plant, boiled in wine; and from that wine, let the limbs be bathed; it will ease all stiffness and discomfort of the limbs.

APVLEII. 193

HOUNDS HEAD. LXXXVIII. Antirrhinum
orontium. Bot.

For sore of eyes and swelling, take roots of this wort, which is called canis caput, and in our language hounds head; seethe them in water, and then bathe the eyes with the water; soon it (namely, the application) relieves the sore.

BRAMBLE.a LXXXIX. Rubus fruti-
cosus. Bot.

1. For sore of ears, take this wort, which is named eruscus, and by another name bramble, so tender, pound it; then take the wash made lukewarm, drip it in the ear; it diminishes the sore, and surely healeth.

2. For flux of wife (woman), take heads of this same wort, so tender, and of them let there be thrice seven; seethe in water to a third part; administer (this) to be drunk fasting for three days, so however, that thou every day renew the drink.

3. For heart ache,b take leaves of this same wort, pounded by themselves; lay them over the left teat; the sore passes off.

4. For new wounds, take blossoms of this same wort, lay them to the wounds; without any delay and mischief,c they will heal the wounds.

5. For sore of joints,d take some part of this same wort, seethe in wine to the third part, and with the wine let then the joints be bathed; (the application) relieves all the infirmity of the joints.

a The drawings in MS. V. and MS. Add. 17063 intend this.
b Ad cardiacos. Lat. In classical Latin hardly so much spoken of the heart as of the stomach.
c Aut flos aut mora (Lat. MS. Addit. 17063), blossom or berries. The interpreter blundered.
d Ad condylomata. Lat.
