APULEIUS. 193

HOUNDS HEAD. LXXXVIII. Antirrhinum orontium. Bot.

For sore eyes and swelling, take the roots of this plant, which is called canis caput, and in our language hounds head; boil them in water, and then bathe the eyes with that water; soon the application relieves the soreness.

BRAMBLE. LXXXIX. Rubus fruticosus. Bot.

1. For sore ears, take this plant, which is named eruscus, and by another name bramble, while still tender, and pound it; then take the resulting wash made lukewarm and drip it into the ear; it reduces the soreness and will surely heal it.

2. For a woman's excessive bleeding, take the heads of this same plant while tender, twenty-one of them; boil them in water down to a third; administer this to be drunk on an empty stomach for three days, making sure to renew the drink each day.

3. For heartache, take leaves of this same plant, pounded on their own; lay them over the left breast; the soreness passes off.

4. For fresh wounds, take blossoms of this same plant and lay them on the wounds; without any delay or harm they will heal the wounds.

5. For sore joints, take some part of this same plant, boil it in wine down to a third, and then bathe the joints with that wine; the application relieves all infirmity of the joints.

Against adder-bite: take of this same plant's leaves, crushed fresh, and lay them on the wound.

Milfoil. Chapter 90.

The plant that people call milfoil in our language is called by the alderman's name, Achilles, because its roots are said to heal those wounded by iron weapons, those cut and bruised by iron. And also some people call it by that name because Achilles healed someone with it, and that was the name of Telephon.

For toothache: take of this same plant's root, which milfoil is called, and eat it while fasting.

For wounds made by iron weapons: take the same plant crushed with nettles and lay it on the wounds; it will draw the wounds together and heal them.

For rupture: take the same plant, milfoil, crushed with butter, and lay it on the rupture.

So that a man may urinate more easily: take of this same plant, mix it with vinegar, and let him drink it daily; it will heal him.

If a man's wounds have grown cold: take milfoil and grind it very small and mix it with butter, lay it then on the wounds; they will quicken at once and become warm.

YARROW. Section 90. Botanical name: Achillea millefolium.

1. Concerning this plant, which is called millefolium, and in our language yarrow: it is said that Achilles the chieftain discovered it, and that with this same plant he healed those who had been struck and wounded with iron weapons. For this reason, some people also call it Achillea. With this plant, it is said that he likewise healed a man whose name was Telephos.

2. For toothache, take a root of this plant, which we call millefoil, and give it to the patient to eat on an empty stomach.

3. For wounds made by iron weapons, take this same plant, pounded with grease, and apply it to the wounds; it cleanses and heals them.

4. For a swelling, take this same plant millefoil, pound it into butter, and apply it to the swelling.

5. In the event that any man has difficulty urinating, take the juice of this same plant with vinegar and give it to him to drink; it heals him wonderfully.

6. If a wound on a man has become cold, take then the same plant millefoil, grind it very fine, and mix it with butter, then lay it on the wound; it will soon revive and warm it.

196 HERBARIUM

Apply thickly, take this same plant's root, bind it on the spine; then it will come as a remedy for him.

Again, for the same, take the same plant's root, boil it down into the wound, then it will soon be healing.

If any man's digestion is upset, or he cannot digest his food, take the juice of this same plant, mix it with water and honey and the juice altogether, let him drink it as a warm drink — then he will soon be better.

Again, for pains and aches of all kinds, and for every kind of inner disorder: take the same plant, grind it very small, boil it down, then take the liquid, fill it with good ale, give him that to drink; even if it seems as if nothing helps him from within.

If then a man has a rupture or some kind of internal swelling: take this same plant's root, pound it very well, boil it down in very good beer, let him drink it warm — I believe it will help him both against rupture and against all internal complaints.

For headache: take the same plant's root, make a poultice of it, lay it then on the head; then it will take away the pain soon.

For the kind of adder called the spalanius, take this same plant — three of its leaves — boil them in wine,

198 HERBARIUM

Grind it then finely and lay it on the wound, and after that take the plant and honey, mix them together, and smear the wound with that; then the wound will soon be healed.

For adder-bite, if any man is bitten by a viper, and he bathes himself in the water with it, he will be cooled of the venom of every kind of adder.
For a sting, take the same plant, and wheat grain; lay it on the wound, and it will soon heal.
Also for adder-bite, if the wound is swollen, take dry bark of the same plant, boil it in water, grind it then very small, lay it finely ground then on the wound; then if the sore is open, take the same plant unboiled, grind it very small, mix with honey, treat the wounds with that; then the wound will soon be whole.

Rue. XCI.

For bleeding from the nose, take the plant that men call rue by name, and one by another name below; apply it frequently to the nostrils, firmly, and it will stop the blood from the nostrils.
For toothache, take the same plant rue, give it to the patient in small mouthfuls to eat, or to drink in a drink.

For pain of the stomach: take seed of this same plant and add cress and vinegar; give to drink to one who is costive.

For soreness of the eyes and a swelling: take of the same plant, bruise it well, lay it on them; also take the roots, bruised likewise, mixed with honey smeared on; it will quickly heal well.

For what a man calls inflammation, when it rises up among the people, and is called a disease: take of the same plant, bruise it with vinegar prepared, pour it on then, and press it on likewise.

For dimness of eyes: take of the same plant's leaves, give to eat fasting, and let them drink on an empty stomach.

For headache: take of the same plant, rub it to drink on an empty stomach; pound also of the same plant and press it into vinegar; when the head steams with it, this plant is also named against death-spasms.

Horsemint. XCII.

For soreness of the ears: take of this plant, which man calls by the name of mentastrum and another name, called strongon; mix it, put it into the ear even if there be worms therein; through this they shall be killed.

2. For leprosy, take leaves of this same plant, HORSEMINT, Article 92, and give them to be eaten; the patient shall surely be healed.

WALL WORT, or ELDER WORT. Chapter 93. Sambucus ebulus. Botany.

1. In case that bladder stones develop, take this plant, which is called ebulum, and by another name elder wort, or dwarf elder, and which some men also call wall wort; pound it then until very soft, together with its leaves, and give it to drink in wine; it drives out the ailment.

2. For a snake bite, take this same plant, which we call ebulum, and before you cut it, hold it in your hand and say three times nine times, "Omnes malas bestias canto," that is, in our language, "I enchant and overcome all evil wild creatures"; then cut it with a very sharp knife into three parts; and while you are doing this, think of the person you intend to heal with it, and when you leave that place, do not look back; then take the plant and pound it, apply it to the wound; it will soon be whole.

3. For water sickness, that is, dropsy, take roots of this same plant pounded; wring them out so that you obtain four draughts of the juice, and add a whole grain of wheat, placing it together with the herb, and pray to the seven stars — that is, the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn — and place it under your pillow, and ask that they reveal to you in sleep under which star's protection you stand.

Footnote b: The drawing in MS. V., fol. 43c, is apparently meant for dwarf elder, as is MS. Add. 17063. In MS. Bodley, 130, there is also a rough likeness, with the glosses "walwort, danewort, wylde elder." Classical Latinity authorizes only ebulum, but ebulus is favored by the analogies.

Footnote c: Canto, Latin 1528, but the English text has the verbs in the imperative.

Rest every day, drink one, on those it causes great spitting. And it also draws out all the moisture inwardly from the chest.

Pennyroyal. XCIV.

This plant that one calls by the Latin name pollegium and by another name pennyroyal has many medical uses, though few people know them. This plant is of two kinds, that is to say two sorts. The one sort has white blossoms, and the other sort has red or brown blossoms; each is useful and wonderful, and they have within them the greatest colors when they bloom, and they nearly resemble each other and multiply.

For pain inside, take of this same plant pennyroyal and cumin, pound them together with water and lay them on the navel; soon he will be healed.

Again for pain in the stomach, take of the same plant pennyroyal, pound it and mix it with water, give it to drink in vinegar; it will greatly settle the upset stomach.

For itching of the skin, take of the same plant, boil it in boiling water, let it cool then until a man can drink it, and when he has drunk it, it will relieve the itching.

Again for internal pain, this same plant pennyroyal greatly helps, bind it to the navel so that it cannot fall from the navel; soon it will stop running.

When it comes about, take two portions of this same dried plant, press them in a cloth, in the time that the pepper rises within him, let whoever has a headache bind it around his head with this same plant, it will relieve the heaviness of the head.

If any internal organ be diseased, take three portions of this same plant, crush fresh pepper that smells strongly, pound it in oil and let him drink it.

If anyone suffers from chills and shaking, take of this same plant plantain and pennyroyal, pound them together with oil and with vinegar, and anoint him with it frequently.

If bladder stones have grown in it and upon it, take of this same plant plantain well pounded, and two cups of wine, mix together, let him drink it regularly, and it will in a short time relieve the discomfort, and within a few days it will heal the weakness, and will drive out the stones that grow on it.

If anyone suffers pain around the heart, or in the breast, let him eat of this same plant pennyroyal and drink it at once.

If sometimes men suffer from vomiting, take of this same plant and two cups of vinegar, let him drink it fasting.

For swelling of the stomach and internal organs, take of this same plant pennyroyal pounded, and in water or wine prepared, or through it alone, let him drink it, and soon the ailment will be released.

translation:
Chapter 101: Henbane

This remedy: take dry powdered juice of the plant that men call henbane by its common name, and oil; mix these together with salt and fat, ground fine; mix everything together, smear it, so that the rash will be healed.

Also for a rash and aching: take the same plant henbane, rubbed in vinegar and smeared; apply it to the swellings and the temples.

If anyone is burned: take the same plant henbane and one throat-wort, and one elecampane; prepare them, strain through a cloth, and add marrow and inner fat; prepare everything, then put it all together in one vessel; then add butter and half a pound of prepared fat of swine, and honeysuckle; boil all together until thick; then apply to the burn.

Chapter 102: Wormwood

This plant, which men call by its common name absinthium, that is wormwood, grows in tilled fields and on hills and on stony ground.

If a man has a swelling or other sore on his body: take the plant absinthium, boil it in water, then lay a cloth over the sore; when the body sweats, rub it in honey and apply it to the sore.

APULEIUS, page 217

OREGANO, Wild Marjoram. Chapter 101. (Botanical name: Origanum vulgare)

1. For a sore on the head, take the juice of this plant called serpyllum, also known by another name oregano, along with oil and burnt salt. Grind it all to a very fine powder, mix everything together, and smear it on the head; it shall heal.

2. Again, for headache, take this same plant serpyllum, boil it, pound it in vinegar, and smear it on the temples and the forehead.

3. If someone has been badly burnt, take this same plant serpyllum and ashthroat, or vervain, one bundle, together with one ounce by weight of silver filings or litharge, and roses weighing three ounces. Pound everything together in a mortar, then add wax and the fat of bear and of deer, half a pound by weight. Boil it all together, purify it, and apply it to the burn.

WORMWOOD. Chapter 102. (Botanical name: Artemisia absinthium)

1. This plant, which is called absinthium, and by another name ware-moth, or wormwood, grows in cultivated places, on open downs, and in stony places.

2. To remove welts and other sores from the body, take this plant absinthium, boil it in water, then place it on a cloth and lay it on the sore. If the body is too tender for this, boil it in honey instead, and lay it on the sore.

a The illustration in MS. V., folio 46c, shows root, stems and buds with swelling calyces, but no leaves, and looks quite unlike the actual herb. MS. A., folio 46b, matches MS. V.
b The distinguishing features of wormwood can be recognized in MS. T. and MS. A., folio 46b, though less clearly in MS. V., folio 45d.

220 HERBARIUM

When the remedy is prepared, strain it through a cloth inwardly, then filter it afterwards carefully.

CV.

Against a chest affliction, as this plant, which men call by the name ponclaca, is called by another name — by either of these two it is recognized — and also by another drink.

Chervil. CVI.

Against pain of the stomach, take the dry plant which men call ceperolium, and by another name chervil — bruise it, likewise green, and the small shoots, pound together in a mortar, and add a little cumin, strain with honey and green poppy, boil together, drink it — it soothes the stomach gently.

Brookmint. CVII.

Against the bladder, and for a man who cannot urinate, take the dry plant which men call by another name brookmint, seethe it for the sufferer in warm water, and let him sit over it — if he is able to endure it, and if he then cannot, let him drink it in wine; thus shall you heal him thoroughly.

Purslane. Article 105. Portulaca sativa. Botany.

For violent gonorrhea, this plant is of great benefit; it is called porcilaca, or purslane, and by another name [blank], to be taken either by itself or with other drinks.

CHERVIL. Article 106. Anthriscus cerefolium. Botany.

For soreness of the stomach, take three heads of this plant, which is called cerefolium, and by another name like it, chervil — green, and dwarf dwosle, or pennyroyal — pound them in a wooden mortar with a spoonful of fermented honey and a green poppy, and boil them together. Give this to be swallowed; it will then quickly strengthen the stomach.

BROOKMINT. Article 107. Mentha hirsuta. Botany.

For soreness of the bladder, and in the case that a man cannot urinate — that is, cannot pass water — take the juice of this plant, which is called sisymbrium, and by another name brookmint. Give it to the sufferer to swallow in warm water if he is feverish; if he is not feverish, give it to him to drink in wine. You will wonderfully cure him.

222                              HERBARIUM

                                    CVIII.

For the condition where a man cannot urinate: take the plant called olivetree [oliatum] and by another name called [gepylleban], pound it and press the juice; it powerfully relieves the bladder.


                              Lily.   CIX.

The plant one calls lily is also named lilium.

For inflammation of the eyes: take the plant that we call lily, and the bulb of the plant that is also called by another name halrwort; pound them together, every part, then take the bulb of the plant pounded and lay it on the inflammation — it will be healed.
For a swelling: take lily leaf pounded and lay it on the swelling; it heals it effectively and the swelling subsides.

                              Lactuca (Lettuce).   CX.

This plant that one calls tithymallos calatites and by another name is called lactuca grows in flat places and in fields.

APULEIUS. 223

Alexanders. Chapter 108. [Smyrnium olusatrum]
Again, for soreness of the bladder, and in case a man is unable to urinate, or pass water, take this plant, which is named olusatrum, and by another name horse parsley, pound it in boiled wine, and administer it as a drink; it will powerfully improve the flow of urine.

LILY. Chapter 109.

1. This plant is named λείριον in Greek, and by another name lily.

[Drawing of a snake.]

2. For the bite of an adder, take this plant, which we have named lily, and the plant bulbus, which is also called by another name hals wort, pound them together, and give to drink; then take the plant bulbus, lay it to the bite, and it will be healed. [See chapters 56, 128, 184.]

3. Against swelling, take pounded leaves of lily and lay them on the swelling; it heals sharply and effectively, and relieves the swelling.

LACTERIDA. Chapter 110. [Euphorbia lathyris]
1. This plant, which is named in Greek τιθύμαλλος γαλακτίτης(?), and by another name lacterida, is produced (according to Sprengel) in wet places and on shores.

224                          HERBARIUM

For pain of the bowels, take the juice of this dry plant mixed with tithymal, pound it in wine so that the bitter parts are strained through a strainer; then take of the plant's juice, strain it through a colander, squeeze it fully, and the one fasting shall be healed.

For warts, take of the same dry plant's milk and clotbur, apply it to the wart on the third day; rub it on the warts and they will be healed.

For inflammation of the throat, take of the dry silvery plant's seed-heads ground with a pestle, then mix with that.


Wild Thistle. Chapter CXI.

The plant that men call carduum sylvaticum, and by its common name wild thistle, is found in meadows and is good for gout.

For pain of the stomach, take of the same plant that is called carduum silvaticum, cut off the head, remove the prickly part, give it to eat in vinegar that has been spiced; it relieves the pains of the loins.

So that you need fear no evil encounters, take of the same plant carduum silvaticum in the morning when the sun first rises, and when the moon is in Capricorn, and keep it with you; as long as you carry it with you, no evil thing shall come against you.

226                    HERBARIUM

                           CXII.

The plant that one calls lupinum montanum and by another name randigum, grows on rough hillsides and in sandy places.

For pain around the navel, take the berries of this plant lupinum montanum, bruised, let the person drink them in a cup of vinegar without anything else; it will drive the pains out.

If one gives it to a child, take the same plant lupinum and pennyroyal, pound together, lay it on the navel.

This plant that one calls lactyrpidem and by another name giðcopn grows in sunny places and in sandy ground.

For pain of the inner bowels, take the dry plant, the root and the corn, well ground up, let the person drink it in warm water; soon it will move the bowels.

This plant that one calls lactuca lepoiana and by another name, similarly lactuca, grows in sunny places and in sandy ground. Concerning this plant it is said that when the hare in summer suffers from an intense fever, it heals itself with this plant. For that reason it is named lactuca lepoiana.

APULEIUS 227

Chapter 112. Yellow Lupine (Botany)

1. This plant, which is called mountain lupine, and by another name [blank], grows near hedges and in sandy places.

2. If tapeworms are causing trouble around the navel, take this plant, mountain lupine, pound it, and give it to drink in vinegar, one full draught; it will expel the worms.

3. If the same complaint troubles a child, take this same plant, lupine, and wormwood, pound them together, and apply them to the navel.

GITH CORN. Chapter 113. [The berries of Daphne laureola, which MS. V., fol. 49a, attempts to draw. See Flora Austriaca, pl. 183.]

1. This plant, which is called lacterida, and by another name gith corn, grows in cultivated places and in sandy ones.

2. For hardness of the bowels, take the seed of this plant, that is, the grains, well cleaned, and administer in warm water to drink; it will soon stimulate the bowels.

228 HERBARIUM

For, give him to take under his pillow, and he will be healed.

Chapter 115. Squirting cucumber.

Momordica elaterium, is probably meant by the drawing, MS. V., fol. 49 c.

This plant, which people call the wild cucumber, has also the name squirting cucumber; it grows near streams, by hot pools.

For swellings, take soap and a portion of drinkable wine; take the wild plant of the wild cucumber, boil it in oil to half a measure, and apply with it.

If a child has a swollen belly, take this same plant, dried and pulped, and wash the child with it; it will relieve what causes the child distress, so that the bloating passes from him, and he is no longer constipated when he eats.

Chapter 116. Hemp. Latin: Cannabis.

This plant, which people call Cannabis sativa, has also the name hemp; it grows in gravelly places and among hedges.

For swellings, take the root of the Cannabis sativa plant, pound it, and lay it on the chest; it will draw out what has swollen, and for a time it will ease the pain.

For bile complaints, take this same plant and nettles, pound them together with vinegar, and lay them on the sore place.

Place it for him, without his knowing it, under his pillow; he will be healed. [LETTUCE, Article 114]

WHERWHET, Article 115. Cucumber. [Latin: Cucumis]

1. This plant, which is named cucumis silvaticus, and by another name wherwhet, grows near the sea and in hot places.

2. For soreness of the sinews and for gout, take roots of this plant, which we call cucumis silvaticus, boil them down in oil to one third the original volume, and smear the affected area with it.

3. If a child is misborn — that is, a premature birth — take roots of this same plant, boiled down to one third, and wash the child with it. And if anyone eats the fruit of this plant while fasting, it will cause him harm; therefore everyone should take care not to eat it on an empty stomach.

HEMP, or CANNABIS, Article 116. [Possibly Cannabis sativa; Botanical note]

1. This plant, which is named cannabis silvatica, and by another name hemp, grows in rough places and along roadsides and hedgerows.

2. For soreness of the breasts, take this plant cannabis silvatica, pound it with grease, and apply it to the breasts; it reduces the swelling, and if any abscess is present, it draws it out.

3. For a burning chill — that is, a blistering or inflaming caused by cold — take the fruit of this same plant, pounded with nettle seed and soaked in vinegar, and apply it to the sore.

[Footnote a: A mistaken interpretation; the Latin reads "et inde se sublavet," meaning, of course, that the mother washes herself.]

Chapter 117. Rube [Rubia, Madder].

This plant, which one calls putam montanam and also by the name opium, resembling those, is called puban, and grows in villages and in uncultivated places.

For dimness of the eyes and for an evil sore: take of this plant's leaves, which we call putam montanam, dried, and boil them in old wine and pour into a glass vessel, and afterwards apply with it.

For soreness of the chest: take the same plant, putam rusticam, pound it in a mortar, then take as much as you can hold in three fingers together, put it into one cup of wine, and two cups of water; give to drink, strained, and let him rest for a while — soon he will be well.

For soreness of the liver: take one part of the same plant, and another half part of water, and as much honey as possible; boil together and give to drink — whatever his condition may be, you can heal him.

For one who cannot urinate: take nine stalks of the same plant, putam rusticam, and three cups of water; pound together with half a cup of vinegar; boil all together; give to drink nine times daily — he will be healed.

For pain of the kidneys, which one calls scorpion: take the seed of the same plant, putam rusticam; pound it in wine; give to drink — it will soothe it straightway.

APVLEII. 231

RUE.ª CXVII. Ruta montana.
Bot.

1. This wort, which is named ruta montana, and by another name like that, rue, is produced on downs and in uncultivated places.

2. For dimness of the eyes and for an evil cut, take leaves of this wort, which we named ruta montana, sodden in old wine, then put the extract into a glass vessel; afterwards anoint with the fluid.

3. For sore of the breasts, take the same wort ruta silvatica, pound it in a wooden vat; then take as much as thou may grip with three fingers, put it into a vessel, and thereto one draught of wine and two of water, administer to drink; let him rest himself then for some while; soon he will be whole.

4. For liver sore, take one grip of this same wort and one sextarius and a half of water, and just as much of honey, boil together, give to drink for three days, more if to him need be; thou mayest heal him.

5. In case that a man may not mie, or pass water, take nine stiels or stalks of this same wort ruta silvatica, and of water three draughts, pound together, and add a half sextarius of vinegar, boil all together, administer to drink constantly for nine days; he will be healed.

6. For wound by the venomous creature which is called a scorpion, take seed of this same wort ruta silvatica, pound it in wine, give it to drink; it relieves the sore.

APULEIUS 231

RUE, Chapter 117. Ruta montana.
Botany.

1. This plant, which is named ruta montana, and by another name similar to that, rue, grows on open downlands and in uncultivated places.

2. For dimness of the eyes and for an infected wound, take leaves of this plant, which we call ruta montana, boiled in old wine, then put the extract into a glass vessel; afterwards apply the liquid as an ointment.

3. For soreness of the breasts, take the same plant ruta silvatica, pound it in a wooden vat; then take as much as you can grip with three fingers, put it into a vessel with one measure of wine and two of water, and give it to drink; let the patient rest for a while; he will soon be well.

4. For liver soreness, take one handful of this same plant with one and a half sextarii of water and an equal amount of honey, boil together, give to drink for three days, or longer if needed; you will be able to heal him.

5. In case a man cannot urinate or pass water, take nine stalks of this same plant ruta silvatica, and three measures of water, pound together, and add half a sextarius of vinegar, boil all together, give to drink continuously for nine days; he will be healed.

6. For a wound from the venomous creature called a scorpion, take seed of this same plant ruta silvatica, pound it in wine, give it to drink; it relieves the pain.

ª I see no likeness between the herb and the drawings. See article 91.

232 HERBARIUM

Chapter Seven-and-Sixty. CXVIII.

This plant which one calls by the Greek name Heptaphyllon and by another name Septfoil, and which some men call Sevenleaf, grows on stony ground and on sandy lands.

For root-ache: take the plant called Septfoil, pound it finely, and mix with crocus and other ingredients; smear it on, then press the remedy there, and thus the soreness will be relieved.

Mistletoe. CXIX.

For headache: take the plant which one calls by the Greek name Ocimum and by another name Mistletoe, pound it with roses and rose-water or with vinegar, and lay it on the temples.

Also for eye soreness: pound that plant called Rylran and rub the eyes with it, and thus you will heal them.

For pain of the veins: take the juice of the pomegranate, which one calls by the Latin name Malum Granatum, and give it to drink.

Mint. CXX.

For eye soreness and for a swelling: take the plant which one calls by the Greek name Appium and by another name Mint, pound it well, and lay it on the eyes.

SEVENLEAF.a CXVIII. Setfoil. Tormentilla.

1. This wort, which is named ἑπτάφυλλον, and by another name septifolium, and which also some men call sevenleaf, is produced in cultivated places, and on sandy lands.

2. For gout, take this wort septifolium, pounded and mingled with saffron, smear then the feet with the ooze; by the third day it taketh away the sore.

MISTLE, now Basil.b CXIX. Clinopodium vulgare. Bot.

1. For head ache, take this wort, which is named ὤκιμον, and by another name mistle, pound it with ooze of rose or of myrtle, or with vinegar; lay it to the forehead.

2. Again for sore and swelling of eyes, pound this same wort in good wine, smear the eyes therewith; thou shalt heal them.

3. For sore of kidneys, do the same; give to drink with rind of the apple which is called malum granatum or pomegranate.

For sore and for swelling of eyes, take this wort, which is called apium, and by another name marche, well pounded with bread; lay this to the eyes.

3. For soreness of kidneys, do the same; give it to drink with the rind of the apple which is called malum granatum, or pomegranate.

translation:
Chapter 121 — Iris

This plant, which one calls hebenam and by the other name iris, is also called cnÿrocanter and ronðÿ, and it resembles gold in color.

For chest congestion, take thirty measures of the dried plant, grate it into one portion, mix it with wine, and let the person drink it three times before meals; it will drive out that which obstructs the belly.

Chapter 122 — Mint

For fever and pustular skin conditions, take the dried plant and also the plant which one calls by the other name mint; pound them together and work them into nine portions; it will reduce the swelling.

For old wounds or sores on the body, take the same plant, mint, pounded, and lay it on the wounds; it will heal them.

Chapter 123 — Dill

For itching and for soreness of the joints, take the plant which one calls by the other name dill; boil it down and take the herb and honey and mix them together; bathe the affected area with the liquid, and afterwards wash it.

[Preceding remedy continued:] Crush in pure wine nine times, taking a handful.

For a bladder ailment, take this same plant that we called fennel, a handful, and green leeks, and a measure of parsley roots and green leeks, both of them, and a small onion, and press out the juice, and boil down to reduce, and drink then nine cups of it fasting, or more, and he should bathe — but let him not drink cold liquid nor take cold drink, until the bladder ailment is healed.

Plant CXXVII.

This plant, which one calls "herion" and by another name "lib plant," is found growing in Gaul, that is in France, on the mountain that one calls Roscidus. It has leaves similar to leeks, and it has dark bluish-green blossoms like those of leeks, and it has seven roots and so many stems, and it spreads itself out in dry places, and not in wet ones. It blooms at every season, and it has red berries like beans.

For lung disease, take the juice of this plant, similar to what you use for a poultice — lay it on the wound and it will heal it. Then take the powder of this same plant and let the patient drink it fasting, for the strength of this plant is great.

240 HERBARIUM

Chapter 128. Half-pint.

For whooping cough, take the plant that men by its Latin name call album — also by another name called half-pint — dry it and pound it finely, sift it, and give it to drink in pine resin; it will cure the coughing.

Chapter 129. Parsley.

The plant that men call by its Latin name petroselinum, and also by another name some men similarly call parsley.

For adder-bite, take dry parsley herb, pound it very finely, strain it, lay it on the wound heated, and have the person drink it in pine resin.
For the same ailment, take the same plant pounded, lay it on the wound; it will heal it, and put the same herb on it.

Chapter 130. Caul (Wild Cabbage).

For all swellings, take the dry plant that men call by its Latin name brassica silvatica, and by another name caul; pound it with old ale, then as though you were making a poultice of cleavers, lay a thick, thin cloth upon the wound.
For a running sore, take the same plant brassica...

242 HERBARIUM

[Mix it] with the wild plant, adding to that mixture, as we mentioned above.

Take this drinkable preparation of the herb called pyrethrum on the same occasion as we spoke of before, so that the remedy of the plant may be both useful and health-giving.

Chapter CXXXI.

The plant called pyrethrum, which men call by another name "nadderwort," is born on rocky ground. There the plant of this same name grows; its kind springs up from one oak, and it has three leaves, one on each side, so that it shines all golden. Then there is another kind, which is stouter, and it is like one gilded with gold, somewhat thick. The third kind is blood-red, and it also looks golden on the surface. All these kinds of the plant pyrethrum have this property: whoever carries one of these plants with him, no kind of serpent will come near him while he carries it. That serpent called "cpireor" — whatever it breathes on, it dissolves and burns. Then the other kind, the stouter one called "hematiter" or "cnýroceralur" — whatever it breathes on or touches, it so destroys it that nothing remains but the bones. Then this plant

3. For gout, take this same herb brassica, in the same manner as we described before, and the older the remedy is, the more effective and healing it is.


ADDER WORT. Chapter 131.

1. This plant, which is named basiliske in Greek, and by another name adderwort, grows in the places where the adder lives, which is called by the same name basiliskos. Truly there is not just one kind of them, but they are of three kinds. One is holochrysos, that is, as we say in our language, that it shines entirely with gold. Then there is another sort called stellatus, that is in our tongue, spotted; it is as if it had a golden head. The third sort is sanguineus, that is, blood red; it also may be golden on the head. This herb basilisca possesses the powers of all these kinds. If, then, one carries this herb with him, none of these kinds of snakes may do him harm. The first snake, holochrysos, is named chryseos; it breathes upon and sets fire to whatever it sees. Next, the other, stellatus, is truly called chrysokephalos asterites; as for this one, whatever it sees shrinks up and perishes. Next, the third is named haimatites and chrysokephalos; whatever this one sees or touches flows away, so that nothing remains but the bones. This herb basilisca thus holds the full powers of all of them.

Basilica overcomes all serpents for one who carries it; and whatever person carries it with him, it protects against all snakes, and he will be safe.

This plant is like rue, and it has a milky sap like celandine, and it has a purple or reddish flower. And if one wishes to cleanse himself, let him wrap it in gold and in resin and in hart's horn and in ivory bone and in bear's grease and in pepper-corn and in honey compounded together, and place it around him accordingly.

APULEIUS 245

If any man carries this plant with him, he is protected against all kinds of snakes.

2. This plant resembles rue, and it has red sap like celandine, and it has purple blossoms. Whoever wishes to gather it should first cleanse himself, and then inscribe it with gold, silver, hart's horn, ivory, bear's tusk, and bull's horn, and lay around it fruits sweetened with honey.

MANDRAKE. CHAPTER CXXXII. [Atropa mandragora. Botany.]

1. This plant, which is named mandragoras in Greek, is remarkable and distinguished in appearance, and it is beneficial. You shall gather it in this manner: when you come to it, you will recognize it by the fact that it shines at night entirely like a lamp. When you first see its top, immediately mark it with iron, lest it flee from you; its power is so great and so well known that it will immediately flee from an unclean man when he approaches it. Therefore, as we said before, mark it with iron, and then dig around it so that you do not touch it with the iron, but earnestly dig the earth with an ivory staff. And when you see its hands and its feet, then tie it up. Then take the [root].

[Footnote: In the Latin text this is the last article. In the illustrations the root is shaped like a man; Manuscript V adds a dog: from the man's shoulders grow some leaves. In Manuscript G it is more clearly depicted — a dog pulling at the root, to which it is attached by a chain.]

You, take then the other end and tie it to a nearby post, and lead it so that the animal cannot cleanse itself unless it has the plants removed from it — that it may know how great a power the plant has over whatever things it draws out. Then it seems fitting to that same degree that it should be applied. Then when you see that it has drawn out, and you have the animal held, take it then in hand and also each of them, and squeeze out the juice from it into a glass vessel, and whenever it comes about that you must help some person with vapor, then help him with the same measure.

For headache and when a man cannot sleep: take the juice and smear on the temples with the same measure; the headache will be eased, and also you will quickly find how easily sleep will come to you.

For pain of the ears: take of the same plant the same portion, mix with oil, let it be of pure origin; pour it into the ear, and you will quickly find how readily he will be healed.

For foot disease, however severe it may be: take of the plant some twigs of the same plant, and of the plant some shoots of elder, a handful each, pound them to dust, wind them about the foot for seven days, and he will be healed, not only so that the swelling goes, but also

MANDRAKE. Article 132.

Tie the other end to a dog's neck, so that the hound is hungry; then cast meat before him, so that he cannot reach it unless he jerks up the plant with him. It is said of this plant that it has such great power that whatever pulls it up will soon be deceived in the same manner. Therefore, as soon as you see it jerked up and take possession of it, take it immediately in hand, twist it, and wring the juice out of its leaves into a glass vessel, or pitcher, and when the need arises for you to help any man with it, help him in this manner.

2. For headache, and in the case that a man cannot sleep, take the juice and smear the forehead; the plant also relieves headache in the same manner, and you will wonder how quickly sleep comes.

248                          HERBARIUM

Also these juices drawn out promote healing, and the sap of the bark cures completely.

For a skin eruption, that is, for a demonic fumigation: take from the body the same plant's dried root, the herb called money-wort, straighten it out, drink it in warm water — in that way he will most easily and quickly be healed.

Again, for the juices drawn out: take from the body the same plant's dried root, pound it to a fine powder, mix it with oil and fat; then those who suffer from the aforesaid breathlessness will be helped.

If anyone suffers from an evil itching on his neck, let him take from the plant's root at the middle, as much as he can hold, and he will expel all those ailments outward.


                    Physician's plant.  CXXXIII.

This plant, which men call in the healer's tongue and by another name "læcerynt," has long leaves and stems and tendrils, and its stalk is hollow within its nodes, and it is rough on its lower stalks, and its dried root is reddish on the pine-resin surface, and it is said to be good against all kinds of serpents, and powerfully against the stench of vermin — so powerfully that, as some men say, if one lays the plant's root against a serpent, it renders it feeble and without strength.

250 HERBARIUM

CXXXIV.

This plant, which one calls by the action name and by another name, is called harad; its leaves are like those of cinquefoil, and they are larger and rougher, and it has against the gnawing pain of the stomach long stems, and it has on the outer stalks a steely redness, similar to the acorn, but it is smoother and darker in color.

For a man who has blood and rheum mixed with coughing: take a dry portion of this plant, weigh out a pennyweight, crush it together with hazel nuts in the same manner as you would give an apple to a sick person to eat; it will heal him.

For pain of aching limbs: take the same plant, pound it and make a poultice, lay it on the sore place; it will ease it. In the same manner it heals old wounds.

Southernwood. CXXXV.

This plant, which one calls by the name abrotanum and by another name southernwood, is of two kinds. One kind creeps along the ground with boughs and has small smooth leaves, so that it looks more like stonecrop, and it has blossoms that are quite small; and it is of a bitter taste and larger and more bitter in the throat.

translation:
Against hiccups and against bone-ache and against a man's difficulty in urinating, take southernwood ground fine; it is good for that, pounded and soaked in water.

Against side-pain, take the same plant and betony, pound them together, and let him drink it.

Against poison and against adder-bites, take the same plant, southernwood, let him drink it in wine; it helps well. Anoint the body with oil and smearwort. Also against cold in the stomach it is well proven. Also that same dried plant strongly loosens, stimulates, or kindles.

Against the bites of the venomous spiders that men call wolf-spiders and scorpions, smear on the same plant; it is well proven.

Against soreness of the eyes, take the same plant, southernwood, and wormwood, and the plant that men call by one name melacidonia and by another name codonia, and with white pounded material apply it as a poultice; the soreness will be soothed.

These plants are, as those before us said, of two kinds, the one being like the other, and they have in all things alike power against the things that those before us said.

254 HERBARIUM

Chapter 136: Labep

This plant, which people call sion and by another name labep, grows on wet shores.

For stones: take the plant's roots growing on bladder, give it to eat either cooked or raw, and it will draw the stones through the midsection.

Also, this plant fylfse is good against diarrhea and against the closing of the bowels.

Chapter 137: Sigil hreonfsa (Heliotrope)

This plant which people call heliotropus and by another name sigil hreonsa grows on flat plains and by streams; it has leaves somewhat like mistletoe which are soft and broad, and it has round seeds, and those are of three kinds of colors.

For all kinds of flea-bites and scorpion stings, take the roots of this plant heliotrope, give it to drink in wine, and crush it and lay it on the wound; it will help greatly.

If worms breed around the navel in the belly, take the same plant and wild clover and watercress, pound them all together, give it to drink in water; it will drive out the worms.

LAVER. CXXXVI.

1. This wort, which is named σίον,a and by another name laver, is produced in wet places.

2. In case stones wax in the bladder, take this wort, give it to eat, either sodden or raw; it draweth out the calculi through the urine.

3. Also this same wort is of good benefit against diarrhoea and stirring of the inwards.

SOLHWERF.b CXXXVII. Scorpiurus or heliotropion. Heliotropion
Diosk. Europaeum.

1. This wort, which is named ἡλιότροπος, and by another name solhwerf, is produced on fat lands and on cultivated ones, and it hath leaves nigh such as mistel,c or basil; they be rough and broad, and it hath round seed, and that is of three kinds of colour.

2. For bites of all kinds of serpents, and of a scorpion, take roots of this wort heliotrope, administer it to drink in wine, and lay it, pounded, to the wound; it benefits much.

3. In case that worms vex about the navel in the inwards, take this same wort, and hyssop, and nitre, and cress, pound all together; administer to drink in water, it killeth the worms.

2. For bites of all kinds of serpents and of a scorpion, take the roots of this plant, heliotrope, give it to drink in wine, and apply it pounded to the wound; it helps greatly.

translation:
258 HERBARIUM

It grows from a single stem, with many branches, and the leaves are full of coverings on the outside —
V. is here eaten away. — long and sharp and thick and spreading, and the plant's stem is rough. It is useless.

For pain in the eyes and for swelling of the eyes and for rotting gums: take this plant, without the stem, pound it with fat; likewise, if you take clivers and pound it, lay it on sore swellings — it will soothe them.

For headache: take the same plant dry, pound it with rue and with steam-herb; the headache will be soothed.
For the swellings that a man calls swollen glands: take the same plant, pound it with pine nuts and swallow it; this will be beneficial.

For indigestion and for looseness of the bowels and for wind: if there is wind in the belly causing distress, the juice of this plant taken well will settle it.
Also this same plant is good for all swellings of the eyes; take the juice of it dry with pine resin, and then the eyes will be soothed remarkably well.

This plant that men call ellebonum album, and by another name tunrincz, and also some men call it peðebenze —

translation:
It is called, grows on hills, and has leaves like leek, dry and thin-rooted. A man should take around the middle of the root and also likewise all the shoots downward. It is very useful for medicines, that is, for soothing: when it is dry, that it has become somewhat smooth-rooted, and not so rough that it bends somewhat at the lower part, nor should it be brittle and tender when it has dried out, and when it is broken it smells entirely like smearing, and it is somewhat bitterly pungent. The large roots of the plant are long and hard and very bitter in taste, and they have such great power and are so full of virtue that they cause a man to sneeze. Then one should dry the plant's root as we said before, and cut the long ones into pieces the size of peas. It is a great medicine for all kinds of things, that one should then take ten pennyweights of the dried plant's root, measured rightly; yet a man cannot easily, because of its strength, let it be boiled on its own, but with some food mixed therewith, according to whichever the weakness may be, and as long as the weakness lasts, one should take it on beer or on black bread.

If then it is to be taken straight, one should take it in a pear sauce or with what is called smooth-ointment; all these should be softened and made smooth in the joints.

FROM DIOSKORIDES, ETC. 261

(This page is already in English, being Cockayne's translation of the Anglo-Saxon text. The content reads as follows in modern English:)

The plant called wood berry, or madberry, grows on open downland and has leaves resembling a leek. One should gather a root of this plant around midsummer, and likewise the whole plant, as it is very useful for medicinal purposes. A notable quality of this plant is that it has a small root, not entirely straight but somewhat bent in places; it is brittle and tender when dried, and when broken it gives off a smell as though emitting smoke, and it has a somewhat bitter taste. The larger roots, however, are long and hard, very bitter to the taste, and so powerfully and dangerously effective that they can suddenly choke a person. One should dry this root as described above, and cut it lengthwise into pea-sized pieces. It has many medicinal uses for various conditions, so that one should take ten pennies' weight of this root; however, one must never administer it on its own because of its potency, but always mixed with some food appropriate to the nature of the ailment. That is, if the condition is particularly stubborn, administer it in beer or in black broth.

2. If the patient is troubled with diarrhea, administer it in pea broth, or with the plant called oryza, that is rice, with fine flour; all of these, however, should first be boiled and softened in mild beer.

262 HERBARIUM

This plant thoroughly heals all old and festering sores, even though the patient has given up hope of recovery, through its loosening application.

CXLI.

This plant that men call by the name Buoptalmon, and by another name, is named after the hare and resembles a small leek, and it has a yellow flower, altogether like an eye — whence it takes that name. It is effective against the dry sores of the body; its leaves, bruised and applied as a poultice, heal every kind of swelling and tumor.

For the swelling of the body that comes from a flow of humors in the joints: take the dry plant, pound it in this measure, let him drink it; it will work upon him remarkably, and he will be as if he had come out of a hot bath.

Section CXLII.

Tribulus terrestris.

This plant that men call Tribulus, and by another name Gorrt, is of two kinds: one grows in cultivated ground, the other out in the open field.

For great heat of the body: take the leaves of the plant Tribulum, bruise them, and lay them on.

264 HERBARIUM

This drives away the swelling of the mouth and the gums, prepared together with abscess-growth and decay-growth: take of the dry plant a morsel, prepared; pound it with honey; it heals the mouth and the gums.

For a bladder stone: take of the same dry plant likewise, pound it well, and drink it warm; it clears away the stone.

For a nasal polyp: take of the same dry plant likewise, pound the seeds, mix them together, press them through; likewise let the man drink it; also take some of the same plant with its juice, prepared; lay it on the wound — it draws out the growth from the polyp-swelling.

Of the same plant likewise: applied to a pine-knot swelling, it is helpful against a venomous drink.

For the spleen: take of the same plant, with its juice, prepared; sprinkle into the area where it hurts; it kills the spleen-worm.

CXLIII.

Inula viscosa. This plant that men call conyza, and by another name is named: it is of two kinds, though one may be lesser than the other. The lesser has small leaves and is spreading, and has a very pungent smell; and the other has larger leaves and is upright, and has a heavy smell, and the roots of the plant grow downward uselessly. But of this plant well bound with leaves it relieves inflammation, and does not harm; and also when pounded and made into a poultice

Its vapor heals the nostrils' running, and it clears the ears, and similarly cures all swellings, and where there is a great internal soreness it relieves it, and it heals the natural disease, and as a poultice in vinegar it helps the sick.

This plant, boiled in a thick sauce with pepper, placed under the tongue, drives away the cough.

If a woman cannot give birth, take the flowers of this same plant and place them in the natural passage; then she will quickly deliver.

If the cold limbs are withered, take the juice of this same plant, boil it in oil, anoint the body with the oil; the withered limbs will be restored.

For headache, take the juice of these plants, make a poultice of the lower plant and apply it to the sore place; it will ease it.

Solanum insanum, or Sodomeum.

For a festering body, what is called in Greek errhinum — take the juice of this same plant that is called manicor and by another name, make a poultice and apply it to the sore place; it will be healed.

Against heartburn and against heat of the stomach and against soreness: take the same plant, crushed with oil; wash it and apply it as a poultice.

Against pain in the side: take the juice of this plant, boil it with water, bathe the sore place on the body.

CXLV.

Against the disease called glaucoma, and by another name called nyl on reaphmum: take the plant which men call glycynidham, and by another name call nyl; let the patient drink it warm — it is useful.

Also likewise: the juice of this plant, taken together with the breast, the liver, and the lungs and spleen crushed with geroðenan pine, heals; and it also restrains the swelling of the joints.

Against inflammation of the mouth: take the roots of the same plant, eaten or drunk in portions as directed; and it heals inflammation of the mouth. Also it heals wounds when applied as a poultice; and the roots when taken by mouth are not gentle but rather harsh.

CXLVI.

If a man cannot urinate: take the roots of this plant which men call by the name struttium and by another name; let him drink it — it opens the urinary passage.

translation:
272 HERBARIUM

[For ailments of] the body, it is beneficial for the body and for running of the nose, and for heat and for burning of the nostrils — all these things it heals.

For hard pain in the ear: take dry [herbs] of the same plant, mix with northern [herb], pour it over the hard ear; it will ease it and it will be well.

For the palate: take the same plant's dry [herbs] for the ailment which men call sore throat, let it be drunk on hot wine.

And if there is heaviness within and pain within, and pain in the limbs, cool it and drink it.

Ellen. CXLVIII. [Elecampane]

Otherwise Amaracus, or Origanum maioranoides (Kühn).

For smoky fumes [from the chest]: take the plant that men call elecampane, and by another name ellen, well pounded; it relieves the smoky fumes from the chest. Also likewise it relieves pain in the joints and internal pains and swellings.

For sprains and for bruising: take the dry [herb] of the same plant's leaves, pound elecampane and bruise it, and mix with fat, lay it on the place where it is to heal.

For foul-smelling sores: take the same plant and salt and vinegar, pound together and spread it; lay it on the foul sore and it will be healed.

[Footnotes as in original, recording variant manuscript readings]

This plant drives out all the evil humors wherever they collect, and it also causes the body to expel its impurities.

Omnimorphia. CLI.

This plant that people call Polios, and by the common name Omnimorphia, and some people call it by other names — it grows on hills, and from a single root it puts forth many branches, and it has a reddish, peppery smell, and a somewhat peppery taste.

For adder-bite: take the dried root of Polios, boiled in water, and let the patient drink it; it heals the bite.

For a cough of the lungs: put the same root in it and it will purge the bowels.

For disease of the spleen: take the same plant, Polios, boil it in vinegar, let the patient drink it; it is beneficial for the spleen; it heals it. Moreover, this same plant, whether applied fresh or burned to ash on an adder-bite, also quickly heals fresh wounds.

translation:
278 HERBARIUM

On the body for great swelling, on the same plant sow it and spread it and on the flesh rub it likewise, and it is grown in sunny places. That plant ground up and swallowed removes the pain in the bladder, and relieves the person of the single trouble, and helps the man's natural organ to recover.

For the fever that comes upon a man as a burning sweat, take the same plant ground up and let it be drunk on wine.

For pain in the shins and aching, take a dry measure of this same plant and drink it on wine, within seven days he will be healed.

CLIII.

Cnicus acarna, or Echinops lanuginosus, in the Vienna fig. (D.)

This plant that men call acanta leuce and by another name name it, is grown on stony ground and on hills, and its leaves are like a comb of the plant pulref, and they are white and whitish, and also thorny, and it has branches of a cubit's length long stems on round hollow stalks, otherwise a yellow flower on top.

For when a man has bleeding from the nose and for pain in the stomach, take the same plant acanta leuce, pound it thoroughly, let it be drunk on water with one cupful, it will stop the bleeding well.

For pain in the bladder, take this same plant, prepare it properly ground up, let it be drunk — it will cleanse the bladder.

translation:
280 HERBARIUM

For a sore throat, take the same plant, press it to a poultice, lay it on the throat — it removes the pain — squeeze the juice of the plant, mix it with honey, rub it well around the mouth and hold it there.

For a swelling, take the juice of the same plant, pound it well, cook it in a vessel — it helps both the drink itself and also against adder-bites when properly prepared.

Also this same plant, when hung up in a man's bedchamber, drives away adders.

[Burdock.] CLIV.

Onopordon acanthium, or Illyricum. Sibthorp and the fig. in the Vienna MS.

This plant, which men call acanthon and by another name burdock, grows in stony places, in valleys, and also in such places as fens.

For irritation of the bowels and for swelling of the bladder, take the juice of this same plant, its root pounded and mixed together, cook it in a vessel of warm water.

For lung-disease and for all such yellowing sicknesses as afflict the inner parts, this plant's juice is well prepared and benefits in the same way as was said above.

Cumin. CLV.

When the stomach is disordered, take the juice of this plant — which men call quimminon and by another name cumin —

3. For lung disease, and for the various ailments that trouble the bowels, this same plant is very beneficial, taken in the manner we described before.

translation:
282 HERBARIUM

Roasted in oil and mixed with ground rue, and gathered together and pounded, apply it as a poultice to that inner part.

Take the same plant quiminum and pepper, and mix with vinegar and run it through, and it clears the lungs; it is useful also in wine, it settles the breath and heals it well.

For internal swelling and heat, take the same plant pounded with bean-meal, apply it as a poultice; it heals the swelling.

Also likewise for nosebleed, it stanches it with mixed vinegar.

CLVI.

Carlina acaulis, or Acarna gummifera.

This plant which one calls camelleon alba by another name is called by some names; it has rough leaves somewhat spiny, and it has in the middle a broad round flat knob, and that knob is reddish-brown, and it has a rough seed and a rough root, and is very fragrant.

If the stomach aches around the navel area, take the juice of this same plant's root, or the dust, run it in wine or in water that has been heated, or press the expressed juice into the pounded wine; it takes away the stomach pain completely.

FROM DIOSKORIDES, ETC. 283

[Boiled] in oil and mixed with flour, and when so boiled together, work them into a plaster and apply it to the abdomen.

2. For tightness of the chest, take this same herb cummin, with water and vinegar, mix them together and give to drink; it will prove beneficial. Also swallowed in wine, it heals snake bite well.

3. For swelling and heat of the abdomen, take this same herb and wine berries, pounded with bean meal, work it into a poultice; it will heal the swelling.

4. It also, furthermore, stops a flow of blood from the nostrils, when mixed with vinegar.

WOLFS TEAZLE. CLVI. Dipsacus silvestris.

1. This herb, which is named chamaeleon leucos, and by another name wolfs teazle, has reversed and thorny leaves, and it has in its midst a round and thorny knob, which is brown-headed in the blossoms, and has white seed and a white and very fragrant root.

2. In case worms trouble a man in the abdomen around the navel, take juice or powder of the root of this same herb, give to drink in wine or in water in which marjoram or pennyroyal has previously been boiled; it cleanly drives out the worms.

a Dioskorides used the word didymon, a polite expression for orcheon, the Latin for which, testiculorum, has been translated as if it meant intestinorum.

b See article xxv. The figures differ. Dioskorides, iii. 10. Kühn and others now identify it as Acarna gummifera. MS. V. identifies it as Cnicus pratensis. The word "reversed" is not found in Dioskorides, but all the thistle tribe protect their leaves by thorns pointing backwards as well as forwards.

c Only oregano in Dioskorides.

translation:
...of the same plant the plant-name means "relief" — place it on the diseased spot, it relieves the same ailments; it has the property of relieving and curing the trouble of the bowels and easy afflictions.

CHAPTER CLVII.

This plant, which one calls by the name columbor and by another name, placed on the body, relieves and cures; it takes away the foul stench of the oxen and of all the body's limbs. Likewise this same plant draws out the stinking matter of the bowels, and also provides men with half-cooked food.

CHAPTER CLVIII.

This plant, which one calls by the name illyrica and by another name — it is gathered where illyrica grows, from its many appearances; its blossoms are thought to resemble in color the heavenly arch; its name in Latin means the same — and it grows most abundantly and most strongly in the land of Illyrica; it has leaves like those of the plant called gladden, and it has a small plant-name and a very strong scent. The man shall wrap it in a linen cloth and hang it in the shade until it is dry, as its nature is very hot and sleep-inducing. To soften [it], one takes as much of the plant's root as a fist-sized amount, crushes it with water, [adds] ten pennyweights of purified lily, drinks it on the joints, opens the pores, [does this] three days until he is healed.

Similarly, the dust of that same plant boiled on the joints eases sleep, and also relieves the swelling of the inner body.

Also similarly, the same plant relieves the blemishes of the face; as those who came before us said, the juice of the same plant taken inwardly against illness, mixed with vinegar and drunk, helps those who naturally suffer from it, and likewise relieves the inflammation called "gonophoeam." If it proves stubborn, the same method with wine mixed will open the passages of those suffering from monocular [conditions], even if they have long been neglected.

For swelling and all evil humors, take as much of the same plant's root as can be held in one hand, well dried, and then boiled; pound it and lay it as a poultice on the sore place — it will break it open.

Also in the same way it relieves the pain of the head-sore, mixed with vinegar and with northwort together.

288 HERBARIUM

[Chapter 159 conclusion] For worms, take the juice of cuckoo-flower, and the plant that is eaten in holes here, boil in wine mixed together, as a remedy against all poisons.

CHAPTER 160.

For the fever that comes upon a man on the third day: take the dry juice of the plant that men call by the name of helebore and mix it with pepper and blend it together, and give of it to the sick man to drink three days in a row on the first day, on the second day twice, on the third day three times. If you wish to apply this to healing a wound's swelling and soreness, he will be healed.

CHAPTER 161.

This plant that men call by another name: it is called water-dock, and it has long leaves and stems, and it sends out many shoots; it has thin leaves and somewhat curly at the tips; and it grows between the brown mud and between the muddy pools, as we said before — it resembles water-dock — and its root is astringent and causes sweating.
For snake bites: take the root of this same plant that we called water-dock, let [the patient] drink it in wine, both before the bite and after. The same drink also relieves pain in the loins.

290 HERBARIUM

And also grind it into flour of bran and smear it on. Truly, this plant has one power for the plant's stalk and another for its root.

CHAPTER CLXII.

The plant that one calls centimonibia and by other names is said to grow in groves and in marshy places and in valleys and in rugged places and in hollows. It has many great branches, and it causes relief of swelling in the joints, and it has the power to heal. If there is pain in the joints or swellings arise, take the plant's leaves, all dried and well crushed and ground, apply them to the wound; so you will heal whatever wound it may be, with this ointment.

CHAPTER CLXIII.

The plant that one calls scordium and by other names, its leaves smell like garlic, and it also grows where scordium is said to be found; this plant grows in marshes and its leaves are somewhat bitter to the taste, and it has sharp-edged stalks and yellow blossoms.

Against urinary urgency: take the plant called reonbior, pound it and place it in wine or mix it into a drink, let it be strained, have the person drink it, and it relieves the urinary urgency.

Also the same plant is said to be good against snake-bites and against all poisons, and against stomach pain as the physicians have said, for trouble with urination.

Against chest tightness: take the same plant, ten berries of it, mixed with honey, boiled and strained, let the person drink it once; it will clear the lungs of mucus.

Take the dry root of the plant for the body, pound it with honey, grind it, and it will drain away the pustules.

For discoloration of the skin and skin roughness around the body, take some of the same preparation and let the person drink it for the skin roughness — it will consume it.

Violet. Chapter 165.

Dioscorides considers that the plant which people call violet, and which by another name is called wall-flower, is of two kinds: one has rough leaves and a yellowish flower, and the other is yellow-flowered but rather more compact in its leaves, and is serviceable as a medicine.

For that inflammation of the throat and hoarseness, take the dried root of the same plant, ground up, and rub it under — it relieves the condition; likewise it also disperses tumors of the mouth.

For pains about the temples, those back-pains which they call "nardus" — which are particularly violent — and for flow of blood: take dried leaves of the same plant, ground up, and mix with clay, and it will heal all the ailments.

Dried root of the plant, ground with honey and mixed together, heals the canker-sores of the teeth, even if they have already fallen from the jaw.

For reducing tumors, take ten pennyweights of leaves of the same plant, ground in wine, and when drunk, or ground with honey, and

(The Vienna manuscript has a good figure of A. tinctoria (D.); MS. V. has a better one.)

This plant, which one calls by another name ancusa, grows in gardens and in level places. You shall gather this plant in the month that one calls Martius. There are two kinds of this plant: one is what the Africans call barbata; it is most useful for medicines and grows most abundantly in the land that one calls Persia. It has sharp leaves and thorny ones as well, apart from the stalk.

(V. is here fretted away.)

For a burning soreness, take of this plant, ancusa, seethed in oil and mixed with wax, as much as is needed for a plaster or poultice; lay it on the burning sore — it heals it remarkably well.

Coriander. Chapter 169.

(Plantago psyllium.)

This plant is called psyllion because it has red seeds, from which it is also called in Latin pulicapem, and some men also call it... and it has smooth leaves and a stem, and the stem is bushy and branching, and it is of a delicate nature and mild, and it grows in garden plots.

ᵃ CLXVIII. Anchusa tinctoria. Bot.

1. This wort, which is named ἄγχουσα, and by another name , is produced in cultivated places, and on smooth ones; and thou shalt take this wort in the month which is called March. There are two kinds of this wort, one is that which the Africans call barbatus, bearded; the other is much approved for leechdoms, and this is produced first in the land which one calleth Persia; and it is of sharp and thorny leaves, without a stele or stalk.

2. ᵇFor a bad burn, take a root of this wort anchusa, sodden in oil, and mingled with wax, in the manner in which thou wouldst work a plaster or a poultice, lay to the burn; wonderfully it healeth.

CORIANDER.ᶜ CLXIX. The fig. in MS. V. is neither Plantago psyllium nor Coriandrum sativum, but more like Pastinaca opopanax.

1. FROM DIOSKORIDES, ETC. 299

SECTION CLXVIII. Anchusa tinctoria. Botany.

1. This plant, which is named anchusa, and by another name [missing], grows in cultivated places and on smooth ground. You should gather this plant in the month of March. There are two kinds of this plant: one is what the Africans call barbatus, meaning bearded; the other is much more valued for medicinal remedies, and this one grows first in the land called Persia. It has sharp and thorny leaves, without a stem or stalk.

2. For a severe burn, take a root of this plant anchusa, boiled in oil and mixed with wax, in the manner you would make a plaster or poultice, and apply it to the burn; it heals wonderfully.

CORIANDER. SECTION CLXIX. The illustration in MS. V. resembles neither Plantago psyllium nor Coriandrum sativum, but is more like Pastinaca opopanax.

1. This plant is called psyllion, since its seeds resemble fleas (psylla being the Greek for flea), which is why in Latin it is also named pulicaria (from pulicem, meaning flea), and some people also call it fleawort. It has small, rough leaves, a stem that is bushy with branches, and it is by nature dry and tender, and it grows in cultivated places.

300 HERBARIUM

For a swelling and for all evil gatherings/tumors, take a dry pine-cone, rather well-crushed, and oil, enough to fill three bowls, mix together, boil, strain through a cloth; take then of that strained liquid the pine extract, lay it to the sore — it will be healed.

For a hard sore, put the liquid with a northern remedy and with plaster prepared.

CHAPTER 170.

(Rosa semper-virens and not R. canina is meant by Dioskorides — Daubeny.)

The plant that one calls by the name "cynosbatos" and names by another name — when one takes it from the wild, it is beneficial to the stomach and relieves digestive distress, and though it may somewhat disturb the bowels, and cause things such as loose movements or biting pains, yet it benefits the spleen well, as the flowering of the same plant, crushed together, heals a man so that he passes water freely, and it also clears the blood vessels.

For the spleen, take the same plant's roots, well prepared, lay them on the spleen — it will be effective and strengthening. And he who endures this medicine should lie quietly on his back, lest, being impatient, he perceive the harshness of the treatment too soon.

CHAPTER 171.

The plant that one calls "aglaoforis" and names by another name shines in the night like a flame, and it can help against many weaknesses/diseases.

3. For head sores, do the same, with juice of rose, and soaked in water.

Evergreen rose. CLXX. Rosa sempervirens.

1. This wort, which is named κυνὸς βάτος, and by another name evergreen rose, when a man taketh it from the stalk, is stiff to the palate, and unpleasant for meat when swallowed, but it notwithstanding purgeth the breast, and whatsoever things be harsh or bitter; though it vex the maw, yet for the milt it is of good benefit. A blossom of this ilk wort drunken, so leecheth the man, that it through the urine is led forth; and it also purifieth blood runnings.

2. Again, for sore of milt, take root of this ilk wort, well purified from the rind, lay to the milt, it is profitable and beneficial to it; and he who endureth this leechdom, shall lie upward, lest he impatiently understand the strength of this leeching.

b CLXXI.

1. This wort, which is named ἀγλαοφωτίς, and by another name pæony, shineth at night as a blaze, and it is powerful against many infirmities.

b It appears by the mediaeval marginal notes on Dioskorides, that the Ἀγλαοφωτίς is the same plant as the Pæonia, and the same phrase about "shining at night" is found in our text, at art. LXVI. 2. For swollen glands, and for all evil gatherings or abscesses, take an oil jar full of the seed of this plant, pounded, and two bowls full of water, mix together, and give to drink. Take of this same seed, make a poultice, apply it to the sore; it will be healed.

3. For sores on the head, do the same, using juice of rose, soaked in water.

Evergreen Rose. Article 170. Rosa sempervirens.

1. This plant, which is called dog-bramble in Greek, and by another name evergreen rose, when a man takes it from the stalk, is harsh to the palate and unpleasant to eat when swallowed, but it nonetheless purges the chest, and whatever things are harsh or bitter in it; though it irritates the stomach, yet for the spleen it is of good benefit. A blossom of this same plant, drunk, so acts upon the man that it causes fluid to be expelled through the urine; and it also purifies bloody discharges.

2. Again, for soreness of the spleen, take the root of this same plant, well cleaned of its bark, apply it to the spleen — it is profitable and beneficial to it; and he who undergoes this treatment shall lie on his back, lest he too hastily judge the strength of this remedy.

Article 171.

1. This plant, which is called aglaophotis in Greek, and by another name peony, shines at night like a flame, and it is powerful against many diseases.

Footnotes: a. See Dioskorides, book i, chapter 123, and note the variants "it is a shrub, of a tree-like nature" — it is almost a tree. b. It appears from the medieval marginal notes on Dioskorides that aglaophotis is the same plant as peony, and the same phrase about "shining at night" is found in our text at article 66. Pliny speaks of Aglaophotis as one of the fantastical tales of Demokritos, book xxiv, chapter 102. The illustration in manuscript V, folio 66a, is not peony, and appears monstrous.

Against the cough that comes upon a man from below, by which the throat is affected: take dry juice of the same plant, mix it with northern oil, and smear it on the chest; apply it gently so that he may recover.

If someone has a hoarseness in the throat, take of the same plant and boil it in broth; drink it and the hoarseness will be cured.

Against cramp and against bruising, take of the same plant; let him have it with him, and if anyone is afflicted with all kinds of swellings, it will relieve him of them.

translation:
The plant is slender of stem, and its leaves are long, its root rounded and its stalk narrow; and if it is of the rougher sort, its virtue is produced in dry places and in moist ground at their roots.

For constriction of the maw, take the same plant that we named above, crushed, and drink it in wine — not only because it opens the maw, but also because it relieves such flatulence of the bowels and loosens tightness of the belly; and also for roughness of the throat, and against the biting of adders, it serves well.

Likewise this plant is good against many liver ailments — the leaves of it keep the bowels well regulated when taken with the plant that men call olive-oil plant.

For sores of the chest, make a poultice: take the same plant to make a plaster and lay it upon the chest sore; it will draw out all the bad humors into the poultice and will ease the chest.

For the sting of scorpions, and against all kinds of adder-bites, and also for the bite of a mad dog, take the same plant, pound it to a plaster, lay it on the wound so that the wound is nevertheless first opened with an iron instrument, and afterwards place it so that the smoke and the stench do not escape. Likewise this same plant is good for inflammation, kept in the same manner proportioned, and it also relieves gout if a man applies it to the joint.

FROM DIOSKORIDES, ETC. 305

It produces sharp and thorny hairs, and it has a long root, with the outer part dark, and it has a good flavor. This plant grows in fields and in hard, stubborn ground.

2. For stimulating urination, take this same plant, which we called eryngium, pound it, and give it to drink in wine. Not only does it stimulate urination, but it similarly promotes menstruation, and it relieves bloating and inflammation of the internal organs. It is also effective against liver disease and against adder bites.

3. It also, furthermore, when taken with the seed of the plant called olusatrum, is of great benefit against many disorders of the internal organs.

4. For swelling of the breasts, take this same plant, make it into a poultice, and apply it to the breasts. It removes all harmful accumulations around the breasts.

5. For the sting of a scorpion, and for bites of all kinds of serpents, and also against the bite of a mad dog, take this same plant, work it into a plaster, and lay it on the wound, provided that the wound has first been opened with iron, and the application afterward so applied that the sick person cannot smell it. This same plant is also of good benefit against erysipelatous swellings, prepared in the same way. It also softens gout if applied at the onset.

a "Inflations."
b One of the carrots; olusatrum is alexanders, smyrnium olusatrum.
c This paragraph has but little from Dioskorides.

translation:
CLXXIV. [Burdock. MS. O.]

This plant, which one calls in our language PhilanthroPos — meaning, one that clings lovingly to people — it sticks to a man like a burr, and its root resembles a man's navel. One also calls it by another name, Clate. It puts forth many branches, and long and rough ones, and its stem is hollow in the middle, and it has stiff, smooth stalks, and white flowers, and a broad, round leaf, hollow in the middle, as we said before, resembling the shape of a man's navel.

For cuts and lacerations, and against the worms that one calls intestinal worms: take the juice of this plant, crushed in wine; let the patient drink it, and it will cure him.

For sore ears: take the juice of this same plant, drip it into the ear, and it will heal the soreness.

CLXXV.

This plant, which one calls Achillea, and by another name also, grows in sunny places and near water, and it has yellow flowers and white ones.

For fresh wounds: take knobs of this plant, crushed, and lay them on the wounds — it will take away the pain, and it will bind the wounds together, and will stop the bleeding.

FROM DIOSKORIDES, ETC. 307

Clote, clite, clivers. Chapter 174. [Galium aparine.]
1. This plant is named philanthropos, meaning in our language "man-loving," because it readily clings to a person, and it has a seed like a man's navel. Some also call it by another name, clote. From itself it sends out many branches, which are long and four-edged; its leaves are stiff, and it has a great stalk that is hollow in the middle, as we said before, in the manner of a man's navel.

2. For bites of adders and of the creatures called phalangia, or tarantulas, take a wash of this plant pounded in wine and give it to drink; it will be beneficial.

3. For soreness of the ears, take the juice of this same plant and drip it into the ear; it heals the soreness.

Sneezewort and yellow milfoil. Chapter 175. [Achillea magna, A. tanacetifolia, A. abrotanifolia, A. tomentosa.]
1. This plant, which is named achilleios, and by another name yellow milfoil, grows in cultivated places and near water, and it has yellow and white blossoms.

2. For fresh wounds, take the heads of this plant, pounded, and apply them to the wounds; this draws off the soreness, joins the wounds together, and stops the bleeding.
