310 HERBARIUM

[it] should be born, so that you shall take it clean when you gather this plant.

CHAPTER 177.

The plant that men call polloten, and by another name poppy, which some men also call by other names: it has stalks and branches and a stem, and roots, and then leaves, and its shoots and its passages, and its might and its virtue.

For a bite of a dog, take the dried leaves of this plant, mix with salt, lay it on the wounds — it heals the wounds truly.

Again, for wounds, take the dried leaves of the same plant, mix with honey, lay it on the wounds — each wound it heals.

CHAPTER 178. Nettle.

For a swollen wound, take the juice of this plant which men call urtica and by another name call nettle, mix with oil and with some burned salt, and then lay it on the wound — within a few days it will be healed.

For a rash, do likewise, and then lay the same remedy on the rash — it will be healed.

If any part of a person's body is broken, take the same plant urtica, mix it, lay it on the wound — it will be healed.

[Footnotes as printed, recording variant readings from manuscripts H, B, O, and V.]

Almighty God, who commanded you to be produced; you shall be clean when you pluck this herb. [THE CROTON OIL PLANT, Article 176.]

Black Horehound. Article 177. [Ballota nigra, Botany]

1. This plant, which is named ballote in Greek, and by another name black leek in Latin, and which is also called [name missing], has a thorny stalk, is dark and rough, with broader and darker leaves than a leek, a strong scent, and a sharp potency.

2. For a wound torn by a hound, take leaves of this plant, pounded with salt, and apply them to the wounds; this treatment, that is the process, heals wonderfully.

3. Again, for wounds, take leaves of this same plant, pounded with honey; apply to the wounds; it will heal every wound.

Nettle. Article 178. [Urtica]

1. For chilled wounds, take the juice of this plant, which is named urtica, and by another name nettle, mixed with the dregs of oil and a portion of salt added; apply to the wound; within three days the patient will be well.

2. For a swelling, do the same; that is, apply it to the swelling in the same manner; it will be healed.

3. If, further, any part of the body is injured, take the same plant urtica, pounded, and apply it to the wound; it will be healed.

[Footnote a: In translating Dioskorides (iii. 117), Pliny, the author of this error, read prasion as "leek" rather than "horehound." Poloten, crapan leac, Gl. Brux. The drawing in MS. V., fol. 64d, looks more like a leek than a horehound.]

translation:
[Page 312, HERBARIUM]

For pain of the sides, whatever cause it may come from — whether from cold or from some ailment — take the juice of this same plant and a good deal of elder, press them together until the liquid runs through; apply it within three days and you will be healed of it.

For pain of the back and of the kidneys, take the same plant, bruised, and mugwort pounded, and apply a good portion to the wound, keeping it within for three days; the person will be well.

For pain of sleep-disturbance, take the same plant, bruised on a mountain until it is quite soft; then increase the dose; take thereafter fresh water and likewise the plant prepared; then anoint with the medicine, and then lay him by the fire in a warm place, and it will cure the sleep-disturbance.

For the condition that you may not suffer from cold, take this same plant, mugwort, cooked in oil; then anoint the hands and the whole body; you will not feel the cold in any part of your body.

CLXXIX.

This plant that men call viper's bugloss, and by another name viper's herb, is good for many things. It is very effective against the bites of venomous serpents, and against wild beasts, and against poison, and against every kind of harm; and against envy and against fear; and if you carry this plant with you, you will be safe.

And readily gather them, then you shall take them thus and prepare them.

To the chief plant of many plants, useful in many ways, so that I may come to you, spreading joyfully, with my companions, so that it will be of many uses to me, and from its unpleasantness released — that is then upon this earth — I pray you, plant of many plants, to be of many uses, that you gladly come to me with your powers, flourishing, that I may be shielded and ever healthy and unharmed from poisons and from sudden illness. Then when you shall take them, you shall be clean from every uncleanness, and you shall take them when the moon is nine nights old and eleven nights and fifteen nights and thirty nights old and one night old.

316                              HERBARIUM

And also if they are scattered and broken up, and they are hollow inside, then that remedy is taken from inside them.

For a sore or ulcer growing in the bladder, and for a man who cannot urinate: take of dry plants of a well-known kind, crush them, let them be drunk in wine; that drives away the sore and cleanses the urinary passage.

CLXXXI.

This plant, which men call by the Greek name, and name in another tongue — it is called hare's ear, resembling somewhat the appearance of a hare's ear, and it grows in green pods in the manner of a large plant resembling rye; and its top is rough and sharp, yet pale within, and bitter in its flavor.

For the foul humor of the body, take of this dried plant's dried seeds, crushed, in smooth drink; give it to the person to drink, and it will purge the body thoroughly from within. And after the person has drunk the remedy, he must walk and sweat before he lies down; and when he begins to lie down he must frequently drink a mild drink of bees' products, lest the remedy cause the gums and uvula harm.

For scurf and for scab, take of this dried plant's dried leaves and crush them together, lay them on the sore — he will be healed.

This is for toothache and gum disease: take the dried juice of this same plant, soaked in vinegar, and hold it in the mouth; by means of that vinegar all the diseases of the mouth and of the gums will be healed.

CHAPTER CLXXXII.

This plant, which men call "zonzonion" and by another name, grows on rocky slopes and on pathways. Concerning this plant, it is said that its root resembles the appearance of a man, and the plant called "zonzon" also has branches there, and likewise eyes, and likewise nostrils, and likewise ears.

Also this same plant's root resembles every man, sometimes in the likeness of gold, sometimes in the appearance of silver; and when you wish to take this plant with its root, you must see to it that they do not run away, and so that its power may reach through the bright running — then with one stroke quickly pull it downward and bind it, so that it is all drawn up. It is said that a man may not look upon this plant's root uncovered. Whoever carries this plant with him, every evil that comes against him from a wicked man who curses him or bends him to his will — he turns it away.

Sea Holly, Article 182. Eryngium maritimum.

1. This plant, which is named Gorgonion, and by another name Sea Holly, grows in sheltered places and in wet ones. Of this plant, it is said that its root is compared to the head of the monster men call the Gorgon, and the root suckers have, as is also said, both eyes and nose, and the color of serpents.

2. The root will also cause any man to resemble itself, sometimes with a hue of gold, sometimes of silver. When you wish to dig up this plant with its roots, take care that no sun shines upon it, lest its color and its power be spoiled by the brightness of the sun. Cut it off with a crooked and very hard iron tool, and whoever cuts it should look away, for it is not permitted that a man may look upon its root unharmed. He who carries this plant with him avoids every evil footstep or track coming against him; indeed, for its sake the evil man turns himself away or gives way to him.

translation:
CLXXXIII.

The plant that one calls melilot, and by other names, grows on hedgerows and in meadows. When you wish to take it, do so during the new moon of the month called August. Take then the stem of the dried plant and bind it to a linen cloth, and hang it in your bedroom, so that the dimness of your eyes, or whatever ails them, will quickly be relieved and you will be well. This remedy is well known.

For inflammation of the sinews, take the same dried plant and make a poultice; when applied, the pains are soothed. It is also said of this plant that it blooms thrice in the year.

CLXXXIV.

The plant that one calls bulbur, and by other names, is also called trezea. When this plant acts on the stomach, it works quickly and effectively. When the other bitter part is prepared in the manner described, it is beneficial to the stomach in both respects and greatly strengthens digestion; and when they are consumed as food, they greatly strengthen the body.

FROM DIOSKORIDES, ETC. 321

CLXXXIII. Melilotus* officinalis?

1. This wort, which is named milotis, and by another name , is produced in cultivated and in wet places. This wort thou shalt take up in the waning of the moon, in the month which hight August; take then the root of this wort, and bind it to a yarn thread, and hang it to thy neck; that year thou shalt not feel dimness of thine eyes, or if it befall thee, it suddenly shall depart, and thou shalt be hale. This leechcraft is a proved one.

2. For tugging of the sinews, take ooze of this ilk wort, smear therewith; the spasm shall be alleviated. It is also said of this wort, that twice in the year it blossometh.

b CLXXXIV.

1. This wort, which is named βολβός, and by another name , is of two kinds; the one is red, and beneficial for sore of the maw; the other is bitterish to the taste; it is called σκιλλάδης; it is also more profitable for the maw; either of them hath strong main or virtue, and when partaken of for meat, they much strengthen the body.

FROM DIOSKORIDES, ETC. 321

CHAPTER 183. Melilotus officinalis?

1. This plant, which is called milotis, and by another name [unknown], grows in cultivated and in wet places. You should gather this plant during the waning of the moon, in the month called August. Then take the root of this plant, bind it to a yarn thread, and hang it around your neck. That year you will not suffer dimness of your eyes, or if it has already afflicted you, it will suddenly depart, and you will be well. This medical remedy is a proven one.

2. For cramping of the sinews, take the sap of this same plant and smear it on; the spasm will be relieved. It is also said of this plant that it blossoms twice in the year.

b CHAPTER 184.

1. This plant, which is named bolbos [bulb], and by another name [unknown], is of two kinds. One is red and good for soreness of the stomach; the other is bitter to the taste and is called skillades. It is also more beneficial for the stomach. Either of them has great power or virtue, and when eaten as food, they greatly strengthen the body.

* The gloss in H., "mellilotif corandreg," and the medicinal character of the herb, support this identification. The illustration in MS. V., fol. 65a, does not suggest it. Dioskorides, iii. 48, contains no such accounts.

b This article came originally from Dioskorides, ii. 200, on the edible bulb. The illustration in MS. V. is fantastic.

This is a remedy for apple and root disease, and for every blessed plant: take the roots of the plant, pound them and either steep them in honey mixed together, or lay them on the wound that a person then has a swelling from.

This same steaming water: take the same plant as the wise men spoke of, pounded, lay it on the inner parts; also pound it with honey and it heals wounds on the body, and likewise it relieves the sweating of the body; and also similarly mixed with pepper and pounded it heals the body's sweat; and also in the same way it eases the stomach.

For wounds that come from within themselves: take the roots of these plants, pounded with oil and with wheat meal and with rape, apply this food which you call cleavers, lay it on the wounds; also it opens up that which the Greeks call hostopytunas, which is what is known as scurf where the beard grows, and also what they call achonary, which is scab where the beard grows; soaked in vinegar or in honey, pounded, it clears the nostrils of the face.

Also similarly soaked in vinegar it heals the looseness and the flux of the inner parts.

Of this plant it is said that it should be born from a dragon's blood, on great mountains growing in thick clusters.

CLXXXV.

This plant that one calls colocynth, or cucurbita, or by what one also names frizullam — it resembles in all respects the other gourd-plants, with leaves like cucumber, and similarly it spreads and creeps; and its fruit is round and bitter, and if one is to take it at the time when it has finished ripening, it is then ready.

For disorders of the bowels, take the seeds, husked on the outside, without the kernel, ground together, and steeped in water, pounded fine — let one drink it; it purges the bowels.

text:
FROM DIOSKORIDES, ETC. 325

Colocynth.ª CLXXXV. Cucumis colocynthis.

1. This wort, which is named κολοκυνθὶς ἀγρία, that is, cucurbita agrestis, wild gourd, which is also named frigilla,b just as another gourd spreadeth abroad its stems upon the earth, and it hath leaves like the cucumber, and deeply cut (lobed and serrated), and it hath a spherical fruit and bitter, which is to be gathered at the time when it is turning its greenness to fallow.

2. For stirring of the inwards, take the inward neshness of this fruit, without the kernels, by weight of two pennies; give it, pounded in litho beer to be drunk; it stirreth the inwards.

ª Our text is originally from Dioskor., iv. 178. Not figured in MS. V.
b Frigilla, gl. Laud, 567, fol. 60 c, also.
source: Leechdoms, Wortcunning & Starcraft of Early England, Cockayne 1864

translation:
FROM DIOSKORIDES, ETC. 325

Colocynth. Chapter 185. Cucumis colocynthis.

1. This plant, which is called wild colocynth in Greek, that is, wild gourd in Latin, which is also known as frigilla, spreads its stems along the ground just like another type of gourd. It has leaves resembling those of the cucumber, deeply cut with lobes and serrations, and it produces a round, bitter fruit, which should be harvested when it is changing from green to a pale yellow color.

2. To stimulate the bowels, take the inner flesh of this fruit, without the seeds, weighing about two pennies' worth; give it pounded in light beer to be drunk; it will move the bowels.

a Our text is originally from Dioskorides, book iv, section 178. Not illustrated in Manuscript V.
b Frigilla appears as a gloss in the Laud manuscript, 567, folio 60c, as well.

translation:
326    THE MEDICINA DE QUADRUPEDIBUS

SALAD, which is called the king of plants, was known to Octavian the emperor for his healing of fevers, for his dry wounds and swellings. To many of the sick I am a remedy for your stomachs and for your weakness and helplessness, so that you need not seek great remedies from physicians, as I have described, those which we give to Aesculapius. I make known to you that it is fitting for you to gather the worthy plant at the right time, as it is well said.

Medicine for the Badger. I.

There is a certain animal that is called taxonem, which is called a badger in English, the dung of which, and of him then, from among creatures whose teeth have been drawn from it — those that it has the greater — and in the name of the Almighty God, I will protect you and keep your teeth from being knocked out, and when they ache, rub them on linens soaked in its fat, and smear it with gold or with a reel, so that it cannot touch your body; then neither hail shall harm you, nor thunderbolt, nor hail, nor evil man, nor anything of the perilous ones.

health to the Cæsar Octavianus, his friend, thus

to wit, that is, of leechcrafts of wild deer or wild
beasts;" as far as it is well said.

OF SEXTUS PLACITUS 327

PAPYRIENSIS.

1. They say that a king of the Egyptians, named Idpartus, sent a message of good health to his friend Caesar Octavianus, saying: "By many examples I am aware of your virtues and prudence, and yet I believe that you have never come to know remedies as great as those which I have learned from Aesculapius. I therefore make them known for your instruction, judging you worthy of this knowledge — namely, the medical arts concerning wild deer and wild beasts;" as far as it is well expressed.

Drawing of a badger. I.

2. There is a four-footed animal which we call taxonem, that is, brock in English — a badger. Catch that animal, and while it is still living and quick, remove its largest teeth, and say thus: In the name of [b] ... I slay you, and strike out your teeth; and then afterwards wrap the teeth in a linen cloth or garment, and set them in gold or silver so that they do not touch your body directly. Carry them with you, and neither lightning, nor hail, nor violent storm, nor evil man, nor

b There is no need to reproduce the irreverent invocation of the original text.

translation:
328 THE MEDICINA DE QUADRUPEDIBUS

[First paragraph:]
So that none of your cattle afflicts another, or whatever harm is done to the herd — as the abbot directed — take now the root of the plant called ruptwort, and this root's wort, and press out its juice; in the name of him who created everything, I take you for medicine. Then in whatever color or form as you have prepared it, and you have made it ready — if you have the root with you and its virtue — those hands that are afflicted with any disease, it will take away his sorrow quickly, and though the disease be great it will carry it away.

[Second paragraph:]
Take its blood, mix a little salt with the palms and mullen, and with each of the pressed juices of a beast that is failing or afflicted with any evil; put it in through the mouth, and after three nights they will be healed. This preparation cooks in three vessels, or in nine pots, until the liquid boils up so that it simmers; and keep it, if anyone needs to bathe a sore wound — bathing for three nights he will be healed. And likewise for wounds; and though a man be afflicted with any incurable and irremediable disease, it will heal and cure him. Take its juice and divide it, and bathe at the boundary-points of your lands and your boundaries and your homesteads and at your enclosures — cover them; then you and yours, being freed, shall be healthy in going and coming home.

OF SEXTUS PLACITUS. 329

...anything pestilential, nor shall the touch of any evil damage you, or if somewhat of evil comes to you, it shall quickly be torn asunder, as was the girdle of Obadiah the prophet. Then take the right forefoot with these words, and say thus: In the name of the.... I take you for a medicine; then in whatever conflict or fight you shall be in, you shall be victorious, and you shall do well in it, if you have the foot with you. With its fat, smear the horses which are in a fever, or in any ailment; it shall withdraw from them, and the span of their life shall be prolonged, and though it be a great ailment, it shall quickly depart.

3. Mix its blood with a little salt for horses and mules, and any four-footed animal which is struggling with pestilence or with any evil; administer it by means of a horn into the animal's mouth, and do so for about three nights; they will be healthy. Boil its brain in three measures of oil in a new pot, until a third part has boiled away; bottle it up and preserve it. If anyone is troubled with severe head pain after bathing, smear them with it for three nights; they will be healed. And likewise for the feet. And though a man be in any chronic and incurable disease, this remedy will heal and cure him. Take its liver, divide it, and bury it at the corners around your land boundaries, and at your borough wall foundations, and hide the heart at your borough...

translation:
330 THE MEDICINA DE QUADRUPEDIBUS

The species: all of its surface is beneficial throughout, and nothing of it is without value, and its little cry is small and quiet. It is well known that its skin, when applied to dogs and all draught animals and cattle, drives away vermin. Boil the hare's skin in water mixed with pennyroyal upon your wounds, and do not lose yourself in idle words about its juices. I wish that you would know, when it serves well to cleanse, that with its cleansing waters, if you move about the countryside around, its sap having been boiled, and you eat it, it is good for you and your intestines.

If it happens to a man that he cannot retain his urine, boil the kidneys in water with fennel, and then in milk with honey and thick broth, and soon he will be cured.

[Arts 5, 6, 7, 8, are thus placed in the MSS., but are not in the Latin, and do not belong to the badger.]

For a bloody flux: when the moon is fully nine nights old, after sunrise, as the moon rises, let the person who has a mulberry tree come to it, and with a slender twig of yours take an apple in your hand, and with three rings that are with your thumb, and with a ring press the apple so that it does not break, then lift it upward, and upward as he is applied to that upper portion of the body. Then hold it down, and apply it to the lower portion of the body, and then take the good apple.

gates; then you and yours shall be released in good health to go about and return home; all pestilence shall be driven away, and what was done before shall cause no harm, and there shall be little danger from fire. It is also known that his hide is useful for hounds and all four-footed livestock, to put upon them as a preservative against the danger of pestilence. Fasten pieces of the hide on your shoes; you shall never feel pain in your feet, most holy Caesar! I would have you believe that this wild deer is greatly beneficial, if on your cleansing days, as you travel through the world's circumference, you eat his flesh boiled and partake of it; it shall be good for you and your hosts.

4. If any evil has been done to someone, so that he may not enjoy his pleasures, then boil a testicle of the badger in running spring water and in honey, and let him partake of it, fasting for three days; soon he will be healed.

5. For flux of blood: when the moon is seventeen nights old in the sight of all men, after the setting of the sun and before the rising of the moon, come to the tree called morbeam, or mulberry tree, and from it take an apple, that is, a berry, with your left hand using two fingers — that is, with the thumb and the ring finger — a white berry which is not yet red; then lift it up, and raise yourself up; this is useful for the upper part of the body. Again put it down, and bow down over it; it is beneficial for the lower part.

translation:
It says then these words: apr · apr · apr · [certain foreign/Latin ritual words] tamer, restorer — then when you have spoken those words, take the apple and rub it on a woolen cloth steeped in water, and then boil it afterward with cress or with other herbs, and keep it so that the medicine does not run nor flow to the ground, then of the upper part of the body at any sore or at the ears, rub it on the face, then downward, rub it on the thigh.

For a louse-infestation, take the comb with which she alone combs her hair, and no man has ever combed with it before or after. Under the mulberry tree, comb it so that the hair falls on the comb; gather it together and blow upon it upward three times among the mulberry branches, and after a while gather it cleanly together again, and keep it so that the medicine will be there where the hair was combed.

Again, if she wishes that the bloody flux not come upon the comb, comb her hair under the mulberry tree, and gather the hair that falls on the comb, and put it in a twig that is bent downward and bound together, and again that will be her medicine.

If you wish that the pus be cleansed that could never become clean, press out the beginning of the matter from the sore, and rub it in three times, and put it on her body, and then it will be cleansed.

translation:
OF SEXTUS PLACITUS. 333

Before you take this apple or berry, say these words: "Away, away, away, as I lift you as a remedy against all hemorrhage of every blood and every drop of blood." When you have said these words, take the apple or fruit, and wind it up in a fine purple cloth, then bag it again in a piece of some other fine linen, and take care that this remedy touches neither water nor earth. When there is need, and the upper part of the body suffers from any sore or any difficulty, bind it upon the forehead; if it is on the lower part, bind it on the abdomen.

6. For a woman's flux. Take the comb with which she alone has combed her head, and with which no other person has combed nor shall comb. Under the mulberry tree, let her comb her hair there; let her gather what is left in the comb, and hang it on an upright twig of the mulberry tree, and again after a while, when clean, let her gather it from the twig and keep it. That shall be a remedy for her, for the one who combs her head there.

7. But if she wishes that her menstrual flow should come, let her comb her head again under the mulberry tree, and let her collect the hair that clings to the comb, and let her place it on a twig that is turned downwards, and let her collect it again; that is her remedy.

8. If you wish that a woman be purified, who could never be clean, make her a salve from the hair, and dry it somewhat, and put it on her body; then she shall be cleansed.

translation:
II. Medicine from the deer. [MS. O.]

This medicine: take deer's dung; it digests every food and drives away wind, when a man uses it as a drink in a decoction of eyebright.

This medicine: take deer's horn, burn it; mix together the ashes, five pennies' worth of pepper, six of black pepper, a little anise, take a spoonful of each, a spoonful of every kind of berry and seed, also a spoonful of drink; it heals the belly and bowels.

This medicine: for toothache, deer dung soaked and crushed strengthens the teeth, when a man drinks it properly.

This medicine: take the deer's lung, beat it till dry, and drink it in wine; then one will soon be well.

This medicine: to kill worms, take deer dung soaked in hot water; it kills the worms and drives them out.

Also to kill gnats: take the ashes of deer horn and burn them; when they smoke the gnats flee at once.

This medicine: for ear diseases of swine, where there is foul matter within; take a portion of fine deer butter, let the swine drink it mixed with their drink; then poured into the stomach with the drink, it is a good remedy.

This medicine: for the spleen, eat deer dung soaked, stewed in drink; it dissolves the spleen and drives it away.

Painting of a hart. II.

1. Against bite of snake;a a harts horn hath main or power to dry up every wet; hence it is used for an eye salve.

2. Against sore of head, drink by weight of five pennies b of ashes of harts horn; take one sextarius of wine, and two of water; take of this every day a cup full, and drink this drink. It also restraineth c sore of wamb.

3. Against wagging of teeth, harts horn burnt and pounded steadieth the teeth, if one wisely useth it.

4. Ad mulieris fluxum. Harts horn beaten to a dust, let her drink it in wine; soon she shall be well.

5. For worms, to kill them, drink burnt harts horn in hot water; it killeth and casteth out the worms.

6. Also to quell snakes, take ashes of the horn, and spread them where the snakes are; they soon flee away.

7. For the difficulties of women; this disorder d the Greeks hight ὑστερικὴ πνlξ, use the smallest dust of harts horn for three days in a drink of wine; if she be feverish, then let her drink it in warm water. That is a good leechcraft.

8. For sore of milt, take burnt harts horn in a sweetened drink; it shall dry up the milt, and put far away the sore.

translation:
OF SEXTUS PLACITUS. 335

Painting of a hart. II.

1. Against a snake bite: a hart's horn has the main power to dry up all moisture, and so it is used in an eye salve.

2. Against a sore head, drink five pennies' weight of ash from a hart's horn; take one measure of wine and two of water, and take a full cup of this mixture every day. It also relieves soreness of the womb.

3. Against loose teeth, hart's horn burnt and ground down steadies the teeth, if one uses it wisely.

4. For a woman's discharge: hart's horn beaten to a powder — let her drink it in wine, and she will soon be well.

5. To kill worms, drink burnt hart's horn in hot water; it kills and expels the worms.

6. Also to drive away snakes, take ashes of the horn and spread them where the snakes are; they will soon flee.

7. For women's disorders — the condition the Greeks call hysterical suffocation — use the finest powder of hart's horn for three days in a drink of wine. If she is feverish, let her drink it in warm water. This is an effective remedy.

8. For soreness of the spleen, take burnt hart's horn in a sweetened drink; it will dry up the spleen and take away the soreness.

a This title appears in MS. G. in Latin as "Ad omnes homines" ("For all people"); "humores" in the 1538 edition.
b "One drachm," in Latin.
c "It calms," in Latin.
d "Most wicked of the Greeks," in Latin and MS. G. But the 1538 edition reads "most wicked affliction."

Against ringworm, take the juice of a horehound, steeped, mixed with pennyroyal; against the same disease mixed with a little sneezing-herb, healing will come to him.

Again, against ringworm on the face, take the juice of horehound, against the same disease take pennyroyal, and when it has been steeped, take it again and put it in the sun to rise; apply the sneezing-herb to it and it will heal.

Again, against the same, take the juice of horehound, nine pennyweights, squeeze out the juice thereto, and of rosemary, take pennyroyal, mix and knead together, and rub it in to a poultice, and with pennyroyal mixed with it, it will well heal the scar.

Against kneecap ailment: if the joints trouble a man, and those previously afflicted in the joints go along the way limping.

To suppress them: take the juice of horehound, boil it, put the liquid into drink, and this will suppress them together.

Against the same: take horehound, put it in a kettle and pound it to a paste, put it into drink; it will heal likewise.

Against the bite of a snake, take horehound limbs, pound them, and add thereto three pennyweights of pennyroyal.

338          THE MEDICINA DE QUADRUPEDIBUS

Rub on once or twice on the place of the adder's bite, it helps the man with the snake-bite.

Against scab and dysentery, the interior fat is very good for smoking out worms.
Against the swelling from pepper, a bone is found around the heart, sometimes on the side, as if it were gathered there; if you hang that bone on the arm of the man, it will readily make her conceive.
Against internal pain and a binding in the belly, the liver of a hart, ground up, placed in warm water, quickly helps the man.
Against the bite of adders, the liver of a hart, burned until it smokes, or if you carry it with you, it drives away the adders.
Against loathsome sores and tumors, the interior fat of a hart, ground up and crushed together with crumbled materials and mixed together and made into a salve and smeared on, wonderfully heals them.

III. Medicine from the fox. [MS. O.]

[Margin note: Concerning the fox's testicles — the right one rubbed and given in drink is a love-potion; and the left one given to women. MS. H. margin.]

Against painful swellings in the joints that cause the fox's limbs to waste away internally, rub his fat with old oil and with turpentine and make it into a salve; apply it gently to the joints and it heals them.

Against a head wound, similar to what was described above, smear the salve on the head and it heals it wonderfully.

For pain of the ears: prepare it likewise as if you were going to burst it; take the same juice of raw elecampane and drip it into the ear; that will heal it wondrously.

For pain of the spleen: take lungwort, heat it on hot embers, and knead it, and add to it a penny's weight of the spleen; apply it wondrously, that will heal it; and then likewise.

For a wart: take a raw snail, grind it very fine, lay it on the wart; it will break it up and draw it away.

For a swelling: take lungwort, boil it in a vessel of water with pine, boil it; and old ale will heal it wondrously.

For roughness of skin: take a raw snail, grind it frequently; apply it, they will be whole.

For sore gums: take raw honey, mix it, grind it with the gum very fine; it will soon be well for him.

For headache: take the known herb, anoint the head on the outside with it; the head will be eased and relieved.

To bind wounds: take the uttermost portion of the branch, when you have hung it up to dry, put it on the wounds in a poultice.

For painful limbs: take a drug, take roots, so that the bones shall be rubbed smooth with it, frequently and repeatedly; that will wondrously heal it, and each one shall receive from it help likewise.

342 THE MEDICINA DE QUADRUPEDIBUS

[To prepare an ear remedy] — take some of it and put it to [the ear], then when he has rubbed it in with his dry [instrument] mix it with the thin broth.

For pain in the ears, take fox [grease], mix with salt, put with oil into the sore ear — it will heal it.
For dimness of the eyes, take fox [grease], mix with drone-honey, and put it on the eyes — it will heal them.
For pain in the ears, take fox [grease], melt it dissolved, put it in the sore ears — good healing will come to him.
For the smell of rotting, where the inner part is cut away where the skin has been gnawed, and if the condition is a putrefying decay, mix with oil where they have the failing of dim sight.

IV. Medicine for the hare. [MS. O.]

For an open sore, the hare's brain rubbed on the wound heals it wonderfully.
For pain in the ears, hare's lung pressed on and applied — when it is dry it will be healed.
For swellings and eruptions, hare's lung applied above and below, pressed on — the swellings will be healed.

For one who has lost the hare of his heart [i.e., is faint-hearted/fearful], add the juice pressed from the vine to dust, and give the middle portion of the juice of the vine to drink — six days on wine.

And for one who suffers from this thirty days, do so on wine and also on vinegar.

Every year he shall prepare this remedy for himself, and let him add oil to it when he sees fit; and let him use it in this way according to his need.

Remedies from the hare. IV.

1. For oversleeping, a hare's brain given as a drink in wine wonderfully improves the condition.

2. For sore eyes, a hare's lung placed and bound firmly on the affected area; the sore will be healed.

3. For foot swellings and injuries, a hare's lung bound above and below; the ability to walk is wonderfully restored.

4. For women whose child or fetus perishes through miscarriage, dry a hare's heart and grind it to powder, and add a third part of frankincense powder; administer it to be drunk for seven days in clear wine.

5. For those whom this often befalls, administer it for thirty days, either in wine or in a preparation of herbs.

translation:
When the pears that hang on wide branches have dried, take that same thing as a drink as a remedy for those suffering from rheumatic pains in the joints, and soon the health will be healed.

For dimness of the eyes: mix honey with hens' gall, and anoint the eyes therewith, and they will be brightened.
For men who have spinal disease and lung trouble: take lung of hare, and liver of hare, and mix them together, and take a portion of gall, and mix with honey, and boil all these things in good vinegar, and afterward strain with a cloth, and after drinking it, their health will soon be restored.
For disease of the bladder: take a raw hen, press it, and with salt rub it and with squeezed sheep's urine, apply it to the afflicted area, and it will wonderfully heal.
For the bite of a poisonous spider: give the person raw hen's intestines to eat; it is also good as a laxative if one gently swallows it; also it is good as a remedy for plasters.

For falling hair: boil hens' feathers, either fried or boiled in a pan in good oil until tender, then take the feathers and rub the scalp so that the hair will grow.
So that a woman may become pregnant: let her drink hens' brain, scraped and shredded, in drink, both together; if the woman alone drinks it, then she will conceive, and it will not be harmful to her in any way, neither for woman nor man.

10. For bite of spider, prepare a hares sinews,c and
give them the man to eat; it is also good if one
swallow them raw. Also they be good against nausea,
if sodden.

11. For falling hair, seethe or dress on a pan in good
oil a hares wamb; smear the hair and the head; then
the hair holdeth on, and the salve compels that it
shall grow.

12. In order that a woman may kindle a male child,
a hares belly dried, and cut into shives or slices, or
rubbed into a drink; let them both, man and wife,
drink it: if the wife alone drinketh it, then will she
kindle an ἀνδρογύνην; that is as naught, neither man
nor woman.

6. Next, for women who are ill at ease in some places after childbirth: reduce that same thing to a drink, to be taken fasting in warm water; the condition will soon be healed.

7. For dimness of eyes, a hare's gall mixed with honey and smeared on brightens the eyes.

8. For men who suffer from giddiness: a hare's lung and liver mixed together, with myrrh weighing four pennies, three of beaver-castor, and one of honey; this shall be boiled in good vinegar, then infused with sweetened wine, and after that let them drink it; it heals quickly.

9. For a sore bladder, shave into the man's drink a hare's kidneys, dried, roasted with salt, and fried; it heals wonderfully.

10. For a spider bite, prepare a hare's kidneys and give them to the man to eat; it is also good if one swallows them raw. They are also good against nausea if boiled.

11. For falling hair, boil or cook in a pan in good oil a hare's womb; smear it on the hair and head; the hair will then hold on, and the salve compels it to grow.

12. In order that a woman may conceive a male child, a hare's belly, dried and cut into slices, or rubbed into a drink — let both man and wife drink it. If the wife alone drinks it, she will conceive an androgyne; that is, as nothing, neither man nor woman.

For the same purpose, call a cock, wash its pipe after the manner described, and let it drink wine; then it will produce and give birth to a child.

A remedy to promote conception: take a cock's gall, of the pipe of the pipe, and of the pipe of the pipe, and then put their eggs together; and after they have copulated, if she conceives, for a time she should refrain from strong drink, and from the bath, to avoid being too hasty; thus she will conceive.

For a scorpion's sting and for a serpent's bite, cock's gall applied will bring about healing.

For children whose teeth are growing slowly, cook hens' gums and frequently use them to rub the teeth; they will become clean and without pain.

For pain in the buttocks, take the heel of a hen and press it on the spot with a cloth; it will heal.

For sore eyes, cook a hen's liver in wine, drink it, and use the broth to bathe the eyes.

For men whose tenth rib does not lie well, let them drink the same and smear their eyes with it, and press the liver against the side, and rub it with ointment.

For nosebleed, grind a hen's liver and spread it lightly on the spot; it will stop the bleeding.

translation:
v. [Medicine from the goat.]

For bleeding from the nose, if the inside of the mouth is wounded or a vein has burst, take the gall of a he-goat or she-goat, mix it with vinegar, and apply it to the wound; it will stop the bleeding from the nose.

For dimness of the eyes, take the gall of a he-goat, mix it with gall of a ox and with honey, and anoint the eyes with it; it will restore their brightness.

That same preparation may be used against soreness of the gums: mix the gall with honey together, and moisten the gums with it; it will heal them.

For all swellings that arise on the gums, mix the gall of a he-goat with ox-gall and bees' honey; one should also add in equal measure pepper and onion and garlic, and boil all together until it is fit to use as a remedy; then smear the gums with both sides of it until they are healed.

For dimness of the eyes, mix together a little pine resin with the gall of a she-goat, and smear with it; then they will be healed.

For bruises and contusions, mix the gall of a he-goat or she-goat with vinegar and anoint briskly; it will quickly heal the injury.

For pimples that grow on the bruised place, smear all the pimples with the gall of a she-goat; it will cleanse them from the bruised place and will reduce all the swelling.

1. For blood running from the nose, a mountain buck, that is, a wood buck or goat, a liver of this, broken up with vinegar, and thrust into the nostril, wonderfully rathely it stilleth the blood running.

2. For brightness of eyes, gall of a wild buck mingled with field bees a honey, and smeared on; the brightness cometh to them.

For all inconveniences that be produced in the fauces, a wood goats gall mingled with honey of field bees,b there shall be added, weighed to a like weight, myrrh, and pepper, and crocus, or saffron; seethe all in wine, till it be well wrought into a salve; then smear the sore chops therewith, each day, till that they heal.

5. For dimness of eyes, mingle together a wood goats gall and a little of wine; smear therewith thrice; then be they healed.

6. For a spotted face, a wood bucks gall, or a goats, mingled with water, and smeared on; quickly it cureth.

7. For granulations which wax upon the face, smear with goats gall; it will cleanse all the specks off the face, and diminish all the unsightlyness.

OF SEXTUS PLACITUS. 349

v. Remedies from a common male goat.

1. For a nosebleed: take a mountain buck — that is, a wild buck or goat — and use its liver, broken up with vinegar and inserted into the nostril; it stops the bleeding with remarkable swiftness.

2. For improving eyesight: mix the gall of a wild buck with honey from field bees and smear it on; brightness will come to the eyes.

3. That same mixture may also be used, as a stronger remedy, against a sore throat: mix the gall and honey together and apply it to the throat; it heals.

4. For all complaints that arise in the throat: mix a wood goat's gall with field-bee honey, then add equal weights of myrrh, pepper, and crocus or saffron; boil all of it in wine until it is worked into a salve; then smear the sore areas with it every day until they heal.

5. For dimness of eyes: mix together a wood goat's gall with a little wine; smear it on three times; then they will be healed.

6. For a blemished face: mix a wild buck's or goat's gall with water and smear it on; it cures quickly.

7. For pimples or granulations that grow on the face: smear with goat's gall; it will cleanse all the blemishes from the face and reduce all the unsightliness.

For pain of the eyes: take goat's gall mixed with oil or apple juice and new milk, apply it to the eye and it will heal.

For toothache: mix goat's gall with oil and rue, apply it frequently, and they will be healed.

For swelling of the hands: mix goat's gall with honey, apply it to the swelling and it will heal well.

For a pepper-stye: mix goat's gall with nettle-juice and rue; apply the poultice with a feather to the stye on the eyelid.

If a child is weakly and its body is loose, and it is sluggish: take goat's gall mixed with the juice of rue, draw it through a hollow reed, blow it into the child's mouth, and then its milk will sustain it and it will be healed.

VI. [Medicine from a goat.]

For swollen hands: take goat's dung, lay it in wine so that it becomes thin; then strain it through a cloth into a new vessel, pound it, then mix it with vinegar, apply it to the hands until they are healed.

To bring sleep: bind goat's dung under the head, and he will sleep soundly.

8. For soreness of the ears, and ringing in them, mix a wood goat's gall with fresh oil, or with apple juice, and warm it slightly; put it into the ears; it heals them.

9. For toothache, mix a wood goat's gall with oil; rub it on very frequently; then the teeth shall be sound.

translation:
For a skin condition of goats, rub the man gently with goat's hair; he will soon be well thereafter.

For bleeding from the nose, take goat's blood and mix it with burte; apply it to the nostrils — it will stop it.

For heat and itching of the eyes, take fresh goat's cheese opened and prepared with eye-salve; it will be a gentle remedy for him.

For earache, take fresh goat's cheese, pound it until soft, and it will heal.

For a swollen sore, take fresh goat's cheese and smear it on; it will draw out the matter.

For a snake bite, scrape the horn of a goat onto it in a drink; and also mix goat's milk with pine and blend it; drink it a few times — it will draw out the poison completely.

For intestinal leprosy, scrape goat's horn and mix it with honey, and grind it, and administer it to relieve the bowels of the intestinal leprosy.

For something swollen and for a ruptured internal vessel — take what flows out from within it, and what it sometimes discharges; mix the liquid with honey and salt and rub it on the affected area in the morning, and wash the body with it, and rub it in.

For intestinal complaints, whatever he eats, mix it; and give him the same drink for the bowel complaint so that the bound intestine may be loosened. As much as he drinks, so it will cleanse the interior.

For the liquid discharge, give him also a drink of goat's blood well mixed — it will heal him.

It removes toothache, and heals it, and so that it will not pain them any more.

For roughness: take goat's dung mixed with vinegar and the plant rmýne, mix with the juice, and it heals.

For swellings: take goat's dung mixed with honey and the plant rmýne, and on the swollen parts, also the swellings that are born inside the body, it removes them.

Take gall on pine resin, given to drink, and pour it on him and it heals him.

[VII.] Medicine for a ram. [MS. O.]

Take the seeds and the roots of the blue iris, boil in water, and after that in oil, and then let it cool on the stone, and carry it on the way, and rub it on — and if it is mixed with the dried wounds of the tormented sores, it will press them out.

The seeds and the roots that are on the body of a man, on the hands or on other limbs, or about the outer groin — smear them with the moisture that drips from the half-burned ram's lung — gently rub them away.

For swelling of the internal parts, and for flat sores, mix ram's lung-fat and bind it together, and it soon heals.

For scurf, mix ram's marrow and mix it with soot and salt and sand, and pull it along the way, and after that the plant rmýne — it will be very soothing.

[VIII.] Medicine from the boar. [MS. O.]

For every running sore, take the brain of a boar, prepared and boiled down to a drink; apply it on all the sores — it will heal them.

For a hen's bite, take the brains of a boar mixed with other ingredients, apply it bound on the wound — it will heal it.

For a dog bite, take the brain of a boar, boiled down and mixed together, apply it bound on the wound — it will heal it.

Also for swellings and bruised and broken limbs: take the boar's lungs, beaten very small and mixed together, and apply them warm — it will heal it.

For disease of the inner organs and the pleura, take the boar's spleen, press it to drink on an empty stomach; then give him a drink — he will soon be well.

Drench the patient thus: take the boar's spleen, and a sweet crab apple, grind them together in wine mixed together, and give the draught quickly while it is still warm to him.

If there are worms inside the ears, take the same preparation — it is very good for that purpose.

To cause a man to vomit, take the boar's gall and mix it with the gall, and then the man will have a great desire to purge.

For sick men with a full chest, take the boar's gall, press it to drink in wine or in a vessel — the drink will heal him.

VIII. Drawing of a boar.

1. For every sore, a boars brain sodden and wrought to a drink in wine alleviateth all the sore.

2. For sore of the coillons and of the yard,a mingle a boars brain with honey, and bind it on; wonderfully it healeth.

3. For bite of snake, a boars brain sodden and mingled with honey, wonderfully healeth.

5. For flux of inwards, work to a drink in wine a new liver of boar, and then let the man drink; it will soon be well with him.

6. To do away the seams of wounds,b take a boars liver, and some sweet apple-tree rind;c boil them together in wine, when mingled, and let the man drink; quickly they flee away from him.

OF SEXTUS PLACITUS. 359

VIII. Drawing of a boar.

1. For every sore, a boar's brain boiled and made into a drink in wine relieves all the sore.

2. For sore of the testicles and of the penis, mix a boar's brain with honey and bind it on; it heals wonderfully.

Drawing of a snake.

3. For a snake bite, a boar's brain boiled and mixed with honey heals wonderfully.

4. Again, for sore and wounded feet, a boar's lung beaten very fine and mixed with honey and reduced to a salve; this salve quickly heals the sore.

5. For internal flux, make a drink in wine from a fresh boar's liver, and then let the man drink it; he will soon be well.

6. To do away with the scarring of wounds, take a boar's liver and some sweet pomegranate rind; boil them together in wine when mixed, and let the man drink it; quickly they flee away from him.

7. If ears are sore within and there is matter there, apply the same salve; it is very good for that.

8. To bring a man to the fullness of pleasure, take a boar's gall and anoint the penis and testicles with it; he will have a great increase of desire.

9. For a man who has the falling sickness, make a drink from a boar's testicles in wine or in water; the drink will heal him.

10. Against vomiting and nausea, and drowsiness, take boar's suet and boil it in three half-pints of water.

[Against scabs:] burn it to ashes and roll it up, and put it into a drink, and give it to him so that he may drink it, and he will feel better, and his swelling will go down and he will be purged, and it will open the bowel-remedy that he drinks.

Against scab, and against bladder trouble: take equal parts of urine and bladder contents mixed with the same measured amount taken up, and let it remain until the liquid has run off, then boil and afterwards let it cool, and let the one who suffers from constipation eat of it, for it will heal him without fail.

For one who cannot urinate: take the bladder, spread it, and let the unhealthy one eat of it — it will heal them.

Against tumors: take cream and rub spearwort ground in wine, and give it to the person frequently — it will cure the tumor.


IX.  Medicine [for bite] of wolf.  [O.]

For wolf-smoke and for a fresh wound properly dressed with powder, well prepared, and boiled — let the one who suffers from ulcers eat of it; the skin sores that come upon him will not spread over him.

For sleep: lay the powder of the head under the pillow of the one who cannot sleep.

If you wish to prepare powder: put it on the fire, then burn it — it will not crackle as if you had singed it with the wolf's neck-hair and tail-hair, the outermost ones, in urine, except that you wind the side carefully so that the wolf sings around his side.

IX. Properties of a wolf.

1. For demonic sickness and for disturbed vision, give wolf's flesh, well seasoned and boiled, to eat to the one who needs it; the apparitions that previously appeared to him shall no longer trouble him.

2. For sleep problems, lay a wolf's head under the pillow; the unhealthy person shall sleep.

3. If you see a wolf's tracks before you see the wolf itself, it will not harm you, if you carry with you a wolf's ridge (back) hair and tail hair, the very tips of them, on your journey; you shall complete the journey without fear, and the wolf shall be troubled about his own journey.

For earache, take to remedy this: take the pulp of a ripe berry and the eye, and boil it, and rub it into that ear where it hurts, and wrap it so that warmth is maintained by it.

For pain of the spleen, take a remedy: give the patient pine resin to drink; take some whey with it. Some take inner fat and rub it on.

For scurf of the hair, take to remove it: take the juice of peppercorns, and mix with the sharp root so that the scurf that has fallen from the hair is washed off, so that the ointment does not hinder their growth.

If a man has a dead bean inside him, if he drinks a decoction of pine resin in milk with honey mixed in, like unto a morning drink, he will be healed.
If you frequently give a child bitch's milk with a remedy, mixed without delay, their teeth will grow.

For warts, take to remedy: take wool and rub it with bitch's urine on the warts and on the surrounding skin, and soon they will go away.
For men whose stomach is weak from above, take the juice of elder berries mixed with old oil, melted, and put it into the ear — it will benefit those bearing the affliction.
For fever, take the roots of plants that are under the elder tree's tongue, cut them away from the ground, hang them around outside, by the same method by which the fever is loosened, and he will soon be healed.

For a sore throat, take the lean shank of a roasted elder-cock and hang it on the arm — it will loosen the soreness in the throat.

4. To relieve eye pain, take a wolf's right eye, prick it to pieces, and bind it to the painful eye; it causes the sore to diminish if it is frequently applied.

5. For spleen pain, remove the spleen from a living dog, make it into a drink with wine, and administer it to be drunk; it heals. Some take a puppy's intestines and bind them on.

6. For unwanted hairs, to remove them, take wolf's marrow and smear it suddenly on the places from which the hairs have been pulled; the smearing prevents them from growing back.

7. A woman who may have a dead child within her, if she drinks wolf's milk mixed with wine and honey in equal quantities, will soon be healed.

8. If you frequently smear and touch children's gums with a female dog's milk, the teeth will come in without soreness.

9. To remove calluses and warts, take wool and wet it with a female dog's urine, bind it on the warts and calluses; they will quickly go away.

10. For men who can hear very little, melt together old oil, hound's fat, and juice of wormwood; drop it into the ear, and it will improve the hearing of the deaf.

11. For a bite from a mad dog, take the worms found under a mad dog's tongue, cut them away, lead them around a fig tree, and give them to the person who was bitten; he will soon be healed.

12. For a fever, take the right foot bone of a black dead dog, hang it on the arm; it will shake off the fever.

translation:
364 THE MEDICINA DE QUADRUPEDIBUS

If it happens that you cannot avoid it, when a dog has bitten someone, and his body is such that he cannot restrain himself when he comes to his water, wet him with it.

For men suffering from fits, take the pus of a white dog's sore, lay it on the bite as a poultice, and it will heal.

To drive out worms in children: take dog's dung, mix with a small amount of honey, and a little vinegar; this will drive out the worms. Also, take what the dog has gnawed on, pound it small on a grinding stone, and it will heal.

For able relief from pain: take the dung of a dark-colored dog, give it to drink, and it will heal the pain.

Knead the dung of a white dog, dried and ground fine, mixed with milk, and baked into a cake; give it to eat to the infirm person when the illness comes upon him, whether by day or by night, when he breathes heavily, so that it is loosened and he improves, and give it in drink.

For painful internal trouble: lay the dog's spinal matter on the inner parts, through the passage, and the painful swelling will flow out.

x. Medicine concerning the lion.

Those who suffer from dimness of sight, if they eat lion's flesh, they will not suffer from any such dimness again.

For soreness of the eyes: take lion's fat, melt it in a spoon, drip it in the eye, and he will soon be well.

1. Let those who suffer from apparitions eat lion flesh; after that they will not suffer any apparition.

For every tumor of the body that is to be drawn out, take elephant bone mixed with honey, pounded together and applied; it will powerfully draw out the tumors.

XIII. Medicine for a dog bite.

For all bites, if you encounter a rabid dog, take whichever puppy has not yet been weaned and you will notice no bite at all.

For a swelling caused by a dog's blood, it heals excellently.

For a dog's ear-membrane that is naturally diseased, pound the dog's brain and mix it, and let it be dissolved in brine; it heals.

For toothache, burn dog's tusks to ashes, heat strong wine, add that through it, and drink it, and do so frequently; the teeth will be healthy.

For a dog's tooth that has grown beyond the gum, burn the dog's tusk.

374 FLY LEAF

FLY LEAF LEECHDOMS.

In a different hand.

This is a remedy for eyes, against specks in the eye, and against mist, and against pain, and against worms, and against itching, and against diseased eyes, and against every known sore. Take rue, rosemary, and flower of rosemary, and flower of henbane, and flower of dwarf-elder, and flower of dwarf-elder stems, and two kinds of pellitory, and southernwood lily, and henbane, and lovage, and pellitory, and those plants together, and mix well together in honey of many kinds, or in his own urine, and mix oil to it, then put a good amount in the eyes, and smear the outside, and the swelling too, against all manner of swelling to eat, and to rub on, in whatever limb it may be.

This may serve for eye-salve: take a yellow stone and a salt stone and pepper, and weigh in a balance, and strain through a cloth, and put all of equal measure, and put all together, and strain again through a linen cloth. This is an abandoned leechcraft.

In a different hand.

For lung disease: Take wild horehound and hyssop and ground-ivy and bruised plant and brown plant and pennyroyal and ground psyllium, of each plant twenty pennyweights, and take one sester full of old ale, and boil the plants until the sester of ale is half boiled, and drink each day fasting a cup of warm ale, and in the evening of warm liquid, it is a healing remedy.

¹ A later hand has inserted e to make seal-salve. Read helpeth.

This is the best eyesalve for eye pain, and for mist, and for pin, and for worms, and for itchings, and for eyes running with teardrops, and for every known swelling: take feverfue blossoms, and dills blossoms, and thunder clovers a blossoms, and hammer worts b blossoms, and wormwood of two kinds, and pulegium, and the netherward part of a lily, and coloured dill,c and lovage, and pellitory, and pound the worts together, and boil them together in harts marrow or in his grease, and mingle oil besides; put them a good mickle into the eyes, and smear them outwardly, and warm at the fire; and this salve helpeth for any swelling, to swallow it and to smear with it, on whatever limb it may be.

2. This is efficacious for an eyesalve: take yellow stone (ochre), and salt stone (rock salt), and pepper, and weigh them in a balance, and drive them through a cloth, and put of all equally much, and put all together, and drive again through a linen cloth; this is a tried leechcraft.

LEECHDOMS. 375

1. This is the best eye salve for eye pain, and for clouded vision, and for eye infections, and for worms, and for itching, and for eyes running with tears, and for every known swelling: take feverfew blossoms, and dill blossoms, and clover blossoms, and pellitory blossoms, and two kinds of wormwood, and pennyroyal, and the lower part of a lily, and colored dill, and lovage, and pellitory, and grind the plants together, and boil them together in deer marrow or in deer fat, and also mix in oil; put a good amount of them into the eyes, and smear them on the outside, and warm at the fire. This salve also helps with any swelling — both swallowing it and smearing it on whatever limb is affected.

2. This is an effective eye salve: take yellow ochre, and rock salt, and pepper, and weigh them in a balance, and sift them through a cloth, and make all equal amounts, and combine them all together, and sift again through a linen cloth. This is a proven remedy.

3. For lung disease, take white horehound, and hyssop, and rue, and galluc, and brysewort, and brownwort, and wood marsh-herb, and groundsel — twenty pennyweights of each of these plants — and take a full measure of old ale, and boil the plants until half the ale has boiled away, and drink a cupful of it cold every day, and at evening a very little of it warm, as the last thing before bed. It is a healing remedy.

a Aiuga reptans (bugle).          b Parietaria officinalis (pellitory).
c Achillea tomentosa?
e Various herbs are known by this name.

376
FLY LEAF

In a different hand of the XII. century?

[Old English medical recipe, partially legible:] For swelling of the throat: take the plant called titulofa, and on the palate, and [take] garlic, take the juice of the herb, and three times [a portion], and take half a pennyweight, prepared, and [other ingredients including] fennel, cumin, and [other spices], each herb [measured to] a pennyweight, and six pepper corns, ground all together to dust, and put [it] in two egg-shells full — this is a good physician's remedy to give a man to drink, until he be well.

In a different hand.

FOR CORRUPTION OF THE BODY.

Pennyroyal, Dill, Lesser Centaury, Rue, Sage, Grains of peony — grind these equally and mix with old cervoise [barley drink] and give to drink fasting.

FOR STRENGTHENING THE VOICE.

Pellitory, Cinnamon, Mustard seed, Roasted cumin, Pepper — grind these equally and mix with skimmed honey, and use as occasion requires.

FOR FLUX OF BLOOD.

Take comfrey (for this is what confolida is), and make therefrom a drink, and give it to the patient suffering flux of blood to drink, and he shall be healed.

FOR BRINGING ON THE MENSES.

Juice of warantia [madder]¹ with wine, give her to drink; or of ash leaves. Alternatively: take savory and boil with milk, and give her to drink.

¹ glossed pner.

LEECHDOMS. 377

4. Against gout, and against wrist-drop: take the plant hermodactylus, by another name titulosa, that is, in our own language, the great crow leek (Allium ursinum); take the heads of this leek and dry them thoroughly, and take thereof by weight two and a half pennies' worth, and pyrethrum and cinnamon rinds, and cumin, and a fourth part of laurel berries (one fourth as much), and of the other plants, of each by weight of a half penny and six pepper corns, unweighed, and grind all to dust, and add wine enough to fill two egg shells; this is a true medical remedy. Give it to the man to drink until he is healed.

For inner giddiness.

FOR VERTIGO.

Take betony and mix it very much into your drink or into ale; and wash the head with the same liquid; and then wind it so that it wraps around the head and rub with a cloth; and let it be so all night.

Again for the same condition: take savine and betony and wormwood and mix them and boil in wine or in another drink very much; and take calstock and burn it to ashes; and take then the wrappings and pour the ashes among them and make so as to apply, and wash the head therewith; and take then the wrappings warm all around with savine; and bind to the head all night.

FOR PAIN IN THE CHEST.

Take hops of the kind that have grown on a branch, and press them very much, and make into dust, and sift through a cloth; and take honey and boil it very much; then after it has boiled add spices and pound them very much together and put in a box and note it down as needed. Again for the same: take groundsel and hyssop and steep them and put in a new earthen pot, one part of the groundsel and another of hyssop; and rub off the rough parts; and then the liquid and so the butter rises up so that the pot is full; and boil them very much together and wring then through a cloth; and use then as a plaster, fasting cold; and at night on hot, rubbed on or spread or eaten.

LEECHDOMS. 379

9. For giddiness.

Take betony, and boil thoroughly in wine or in old ale, and wash the head with the infusion, and then lay the wort, so warm, about the head, and wreathe with a cloth, and so let be all right.

10. Again, for the same: take savine, and betony, and wormwood, and marche, and seethe in wine or in other liquor thoroughly, and take cabbage stalks and burn them to ashes, and then take the infusion from the worts and pour over the ashes with it, and so make it into a ley and wash the head therewith; and afterwards take the worts warm, all except the savine, and bind to the head all night.

11. For pain in the chest.

Take elecampane roots and bark that has grown again, and dry thoroughly and make into a dust, and drive it through a cloth, and take honey and seethe it thoroughly; after that take the dust and mingle it therewith, and stir thoroughly together, and put into a box, and use when need be. Again, for the same, take redstalked horehound, and hyssop, and stamp, and put into a new pot, a layer of the horehound, and another of hyssop, and a third of fresh butter, and again the worts and butter, and so on till the pot be full, and seethe them thoroughly together, and afterwards wring through a cloth; and use when need be, fasting cold, and at night in hot ale, or broth, or water.

translation:
LEECHDOMS. 379

9. For dizziness.

Take betony, and boil it thoroughly in wine or old ale, and wash the head with the liquid, then place the plant, still warm, around the head, and wrap it with a cloth, and leave it like that, and it will be fine.

10. Again, for the same condition: take savine, betony, wormwood, and alexanders, and boil them thoroughly in wine or another liquid, and take cabbage stalks and burn them to ash, then take the liquid from the plants and pour it over the ashes, and so make it into a lye solution and wash the head with it; afterwards take the plants while warm, all except the savine, and bind them to the head all night.

11. For pain in the chest.

Take elecampane roots and bark that has regrown, and dry it thoroughly and grind it into a powder, and pass it through a cloth, and take honey and boil it thoroughly; after that take the powder and mix it into the honey, and stir them thoroughly together, and put into a container, and use when needed. Again, for the same condition, take red-stalked horehound and hyssop, and pound them, and put into a new pot in layers: one of horehound, one of hyssop, and a third of fresh butter, and again the plants and butter, and so on until the pot is full, and boil them all thoroughly together, then squeeze through a cloth; and use when needed, taken cold while fasting, and at night in hot ale, broth, or water.

For the blister, take nine eggs and remove their whites, and take the yolks and add pepper to them, and beat the yolks in a pan and wring it through a cloth, and take all of the membranes of the pine's eggs and all the membranes of the honey's interior, and of pine resin more, all the membranes of the pine, take them together and wring through a cloth, and smear that on the man, and it will soon be well for him.

For headache, take pennyroyal, pound it in English style, and pull it in oil, or else in clean butter, and smear the head with it.

Against blains, take nine eggs and boil them hard, and take the yolks and throw the white away, and grease the yolks in a pan, and wring out the liquor through a cloth; and take as many drops of wine as there are of the eggs, and as many drops of unhallowed oil, and as many drops of honey; and from a root of fennel as many drops: then take and put it all together, and wring it out through a cloth, and give to the man to eat, it will soon be well with him.

For head ache, boil in oil, or in clean butter, pulegium, that is in English, dwarf dwosle, and smear the head with it.

Of Beet.

For old and constant head ache, pound the wort which hight beet, and rub upon the temples and top of the head, thou shalt wonder at the leechdom. Again, for the same, pound celandine in vinegar and smear the head therewith, above the eyes: the man shall soon be better. For a paralysed body, work a bath. Take the netherward part of the mickle fern,¹ and elder rind, pound them together, and add thereto dregs of mede, and wrap² the man up warm. If sinews shrink, take beaten mugwort mixed with oil; when settled, smear therewith. Again, seethe the juice of mugwort in oil, smear therewith. leaf, and fennel, and ribwort, of all equal amounts, mix with milk, mix with water, and bathe with it. For swelling of the nerves: crush plantain leaves with a little salt and drink it fasting. Juice of black beet and its root, mixed with less than half honey, if poured into the nostrils so that it passes to the palate, all phlegms flow out, and it helps painful nostrils and teeth. Likewise, bundles individually of hyssop, savory dried, and oregano, macerate most thoroughly in soap for three days; by doing this every month, you will be healthy not only in the head, but also in the chest and stomach. For one whose head seems to split with pain: juice of ivy mixed with oil, and vinegar, anoint the nostrils, and it will immediately be calmed.

MS. Cott. Domit. A. 1, fol 55 b.

These pustules are to be treated with pennyroyal, elecampane, garlic, cepulle, radish, turnip, ground ivy, pot, honey and pepper; pound all these plants and press through cloth, and boil then in that honey.

MS. C.C.C. 41, p. 228, margin.

For eye-ache (altered to eye-ache).

Take the lower part of a henbane plant, pound through a heathen cloth, and press the juice, then put it in the eye.

translation:
LEECHDOMS. 383

For pain in the shanks and feet: take betony and mallow, and fennel and ribwort, in equal quantities, and mix with milk and with water; apply the mixture to the affected area.

These plants must serve for a salve against a wen: elecampane, garlic, chervil, radish, turnip, crow's foot, honey, and pepper. Pound all the plants, and strain through a cloth, and then boil them in the honey.

For pain in the eye:

Take the lower part of a bulrush, pound it, and strain it through a haircloth, and add salt; then squeeze the liquid into the eye.

384 CHARMS.

MS. C.C.C. 41., p. 226, in the margin.

Let nothing be stolen, let nothing be hidden, that which I own, that you had power over from above or below. I thought of the cross of Eadelen, and I thought of the knight hung on the cross, as I intend to find this property — not to lose it among others, not to pine for it, not to be vexed by it, not to be deprived of it. Gamund, God's thane, find that property, and keep that property and have that property, and bring home that property, so that he have no land by which he might take it away, nor ground, nor by any means that he take it away, nor that it heal itself away from him within three nights. I know its powers, its strength, and its might, and its protection — all that it enriches. As a river-plant grows, as a bullrush flourishes by a thistle, so may he who intends to take away this property, or who intends to harm it — amen.

MS. C.C.C. 41, p. 202, margin.

Against a swarm of bees.

Take earth, throw it with your right hand under your right foot, and say: I take it under foot, I find it on the ground; I have power against every creature and against each one, and against the great noise of their swarming; and when they swarm and speak, sit down, you victorious ones, sink to earth, never fly wild into the wood; be as mindful of my benefit as every man is of food and home.

text:
CHARMS. 385

To find lost cattle.

Neither stolen nor hidden be aught of what I own; any more than Herod could our Lord. I remembered Saint Helena and I remembered Christ on the rood hung; so I think to find these beeves, not to have them go far, and to know where they are, not to work them mischief, and to love them, not to lead them astray. Garmund, servant of God, find me those beeves, and fetch me those beeves, and have those beeves, and hold those beeves, and bring home those beeves, so that he, the misdoer, may never have any land, to lead them to, nor ground to bring them to, nor houses to keep them in. If one do this deed, let it avail him never. Within three nights I will try his powers, his might, his main, and his protecting crafts. Be he quite wary, as wood is ware of fire, as thigh of bramble or of thistle, he, who may be thinking to mislead these beeves or to mispossess this cattle. Amen.

For catching a swarm of bees.

Take some earth, throw it with thy right hand under thy right foot and say, "I take under foot, I am trying what earth avails for everything in the world and against spite and against malice, and against the mickle tongue of man, and against displeasure." Throw over them some gravel where they swarm, and say,—

"Sit ye, my ladies, sink,
"Sink ye to earth down;
"Never be so wild,
"As to the wood to fly.

"Be ye as mindful of my good as every man is of meat and estate."

translation:
CHARMS. 385

To find lost cattle.

Let nothing of what I own be stolen or hidden, any more than Herod could hide our Lord. I remembered Saint Helena and I remembered Christ hanging on the cross; so I intend to find these cattle, to keep them from going far, and to know where they are, to keep them from harm, and to love them, not to lead them astray. Garmund, servant of God, find me those cattle, and fetch me those cattle, and take possession of those cattle, and hold those cattle, and bring home those cattle, so that the wrongdoer may never have any land to lead them to, nor ground to bring them to, nor houses to keep them in. If anyone does this deed, let it never benefit him. Within three nights I will test his powers, his strength, his force, and his protective skills. Let him be quite wary, as wood is wary of fire, as the thigh is of bramble or thistle — he who may be thinking to mislead these cattle or to wrongfully take possession of them. Amen.

For catching a swarm of bees.

Take some earth, throw it with your right hand under your right foot and say: "I take the earth underfoot; I am testing what earth can do against everything in the world, and against spite and against malice, and against the great tongue of man, and against displeasure." Then throw some gravel over them where they swarm, and say:

"Sit down, my ladies, sink,
Sink down to earth;
Never be so wild
As to fly to the wood.

Be as mindful of my welfare as every man is of his food and his property."

MS. Cotton Vitellius E. xviii., folio 13 b.

This is a remedy for a thorn in your body.

[Sing] around your thorn each evening to help him · AGIOS · AGIOS · AGIOS · [take two] . . . lante thorns with bristles · then strike on each side of the thorn [with] whichever edge: one goes northward · until the end · then let that thorn be pressed against the slope · and the other one . . . . . . . . . over that other thorn.


MS. C.C.C. 41, p. 292, margin.

Against all old pains and cramps.

The right hand of the Lord has done valiantly, the right hand of the Lord has exalted me, I shall not die but live and declare the works of the Lord. The right hand glorified is in virtue; your right hand has broken the enemies, and by the greatness of your majesty you have overthrown your adversaries, you sent forth your wrath which consumed them like stubble. So by these words, thus shall you be cast out, most unclean spirit — let the fire of hell take the tears of the eyes from you — depart from the head, from the hair, from the lips, from the tongue, from the neck, from the chest, from all the joints and limbs of this person, so that the devil shall have no power over the person N. from the head, from the hair — neither to harm, nor to touch, nor to cause sleep, nor to touch, nor to oppress, nor at midday, nor in waking, nor in laughter, nor in lightning, without end. But in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit is one eternal God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever.

CHARMS. 387

This is to cure thy cattle.

[Sing] over thy cattle every evening to be a help to them, the Tersanctus. [Take two] four edged sticks and write on either stick, on each edge, the Pater Noster to the end; and let fall the inscribed stick on the floor, and the other . . . .

MS. C.C.C. 41, p. 346, margin.

For diseased eyes.

O holy Lord, eternal Father, almighty God, who healed the eyes of the sons of Tobias and of many blind men, the hands of the lame, the feet of the crippled, who art the resurrection of the sick, the happiness of martyrs and of all saints, I pray thee, Lord, that thou mayest raise up and illuminate the eyes of thy servant N., in whatever condition of ill health, and deign to heal him with heavenly remedies; grant to thy servant N. that, armed with justice, he may resist the devil and obtain the eternal kingdom. Through [Christ our Lord].

For diseased ears.

O King of glory, Christ, send forth the angel Raphael; exclude Fandorohel from the ears of thy servant — let him soon depart from tormenting the ears — but through the angel Raphael let health of hearing be restored to him. Through [Christ our Lord].

For a great sickness.

We adjure thee, O God our Savior, send forth the angel Laniel; exclude the evil one who causes pain and suffering of the stomach; but through the sleeping angel, thy holy one, grant health to thy servant, and in thy holy name grant him healing. Through [Christ our Lord].

MS. Cotton Vitellius E. xviii.

[If lungs be afflicted with cough:]

...to the hill, and pray to ashes in the midst, the fumitory mass [bag or so] thereto holy water, and pour into their mouth in the midst [fumitory mixed] together, and sing that thy psalms then after [Have mercy upon us] our [Lord] and Expel the Lord and Whosoever will.

Ibid.

If sheep be afflicted with fennel on.¹

[Take] a little amount of ale and pour it into each of the sheep's mouths, and do so that [they nod/bow their heads] and that it may come to their healing.

MS. C.C.C. 41, p. 400; margin.

Partly alliterative. I enclose myself in this journey and in God's protection — I bind myself with the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit — let no evil thing of land, no demon of the air, afflict me, and let nothing weary me; let no man nor woman forget me, nor bewitch me, nor take away my strength, nor have power to keep me back; but heal me, Almighty God, and thy Son our Lord, guard all thy servants; Lord, as I trust in thee, our Creator, protect and save me; and likewise men: Moses and Jacob and David and Joseph and John and Anna and Elizabeth and Mary, and also the holy Mother of God, and each of the holy angels defend me.

¹ Of uncertain signification.
