CHARMS. 389

If cattle have disease of the lungs.

. . . . and burn to ashes on midsummers day : add holy water, and pour it into their mouth on midsummers morrow ; and sing these three psalms over them : Psalm li.st, Psalm lxviii.th, and the Athanasian creed.

If sheep be ailing.

Take a little new ale, and pour it into the mouth of each of the sheep ; and manage to make them swallow it quickish ; that will prove of benefit to them.

A charm or prayer.

I fortify myself in this rod,¹ and deliver myself into See Wanley, Gods allegiance, against the sore sigh, against the p. 119. sore blow, against the grim horror, against the mickle terror, which is to everyone loathly, and against all the loathly mischief which into the land may come: a triumphant charm I chant, a triumphant rod I bear, word victory and work victory : let this² avail me, let no night mare mar me, nor my belly swink me, nor fear come on me ever for my life : but may the Almighty heal me and his Son and the Paraclete Spirit, Lord worthy of all glory, as I have heard, heavens creator. CHARMS. 389

If cattle have disease of the lungs.

[Text begins mid-sentence] ...and burn to ashes on midsummer's day: add holy water, and pour it into their mouth on midsummer's morning; and sing these three psalms over them: Psalm 51, Psalm 68, and the Athanasian Creed.

If sheep are ailing.

Take a little fresh ale, and pour it into the mouth of each of the sheep; and manage to make them swallow it quickly; that will prove beneficial to them.

A charm or prayer.

I fortify myself with this rod [probably a holy cross], and place myself under God's protection, against the painful sigh, against the painful blow, against the grim horror, against the great terror that is loathsome to everyone, and against all the loathsome harm that may come into the land: a triumphant charm I chant, a triumphant rod I bear, I speak victory and work victory: let this avail me, let no nightmare trouble me, nor my stomach afflict me, nor fear come upon me ever in my life: but may the Almighty heal me, and his Son, and the Holy Spirit, Lord worthy of all glory, as I have heard, creator of the heavens. Abraham and Isaac and such men, Moses and Jacob, and David, and Joseph, and Eve, and Hannah and Elizabeth, Sarah and also Mary, mother of Christ, and also a thousand of the angels I call upon to be a guard

translation:
390                          CHARMS.

I protect myself against all enemies; they have afflicted me and tormented me and injured my throat; may God heal me, men heal me, may the attendants stop it; if the glory of heaven's hand be over the holy ones, over the joints, the throat, the entrails, the angels' prayers, all the blessings, may that be a hand over the heart; Matthew's helm, Mark's protection, John's bright light, Luke's guard; my sword and shield are John's glory; the prayers of Zephaniah, the prophets' lord; I now encounter all the angels' joy; hateful bidding, I now encounter — may God's mercy, God's grace, and gentle light bind up the afflictions; the assembly gathers, the simple hymn heals against all enemies; I encounter that against which, in the Almighty's service, in his strength, I may dwell enclosed from the hateful, which assails me among the angels; may the glory be established, and my whole hand, the horn's cup of glory, for as long as I may dwell in life. Amen.

MS. C.C.C. 41, p. 216.

This man must say when his enemy, whosoever it may be, troubles him. C[h]rist said — he or any other said a word: Bethlehem was the name; through him who was born in the church — if he is afflicted over all the middle-earth, as a thief lies in bed troubling mankind. By the cross of Christ and prayer, may he who goes to the East lead back by Christ's cross, and said: the cross of Christ from the west

text:
CHARMS. 391

to me against all fiends. May they bear me up and keep me in peace and protect my life, uphold me altogether, ruling my conduct; may there be to me a hope of glory, hand over head,¹ the hall of the hallows, the regions of the glorious and triumphant, of the truthful angels. With all blithe mood I pray, that for me, hand over head,¹ Matthew be helmet, Mark brynie,² a light lifes bulwark, Luke my sword, sharp and sheeredged, John my shield, embellished with glory. Ye Seraphim, guardians of the ways! Forth I shall depart, friends I shall meet, all the glory of angels, through the lore of the blessed one. Now pray I to the victor for Gods mercy, for a good departure,³ for a good, mild, and light wind upon those shores; the winds I know, the encircling water, ever preserved against all enemies. Friends I shall meet, that I may dwell on the Almightys, yea, in his peace, protected against the loathsome one, who hunts me for my life, established in the glory of angels, and in the holy hand of the mighty one of heaven, while I may live upon earth. Amen.

A charm to recover cattle.

A man must sing this when one hath stolen any one of his cattle. Say before thou speak any other word. Bethlehem was hight the borough, wherein Christ was born: it is far famed over all earth. So may this deed be in sight of men notorious, per crucem Christi. to me against all fiends. May they bear me up and keep me in peace and protect my life, sustain me entirely, governing my conduct; may there be for me a hope of glory, with victory assured, the hall of the saints, the realms of the glorious and triumphant, of the faithful angels. With completely glad heart I pray, that for me, with victory assured, Matthew be my helmet, Mark my coat of mail, a bulwark for a life in the light, Luke my sword, sharp and keen-edged, John my shield, adorned with glory. You Seraphim, guardians of the ways! Forth I shall go, friends I shall meet, all the glory of angels, through the teaching of the blessed one. Now I pray to the victor for God's mercy, for a good journey, for a good, gentle, and light wind upon those shores; the winds I know, the encircling water, ever preserved against all enemies. Friends I shall meet, so that I may dwell with the Almighty, yes, in his peace, protected against the loathsome one who hunts me for my life, established in the glory of angels, and in the holy hand of the mighty one of heaven, while I may live upon earth. Amen.

May it reduce — I in sup — I said the pipe — the cross of Christ from the south may reduce, and in the north I said the cross of Christ is hidden, and the discovery is that the Jews crucified him; those baths the physicians healed — so that they could not prophesy — nor ever after was a bath concealed, nor the pipe, through the cross of Christ.

If a horse be taken lame, if it be in his foreleg or in his bridle, if it be in the other leg, sing this on his fetlock and kindle three candles of wax — no man may conceal it. If it be on one of the other sides, then sing thou it on three of its sides, and sing first upward, and Peter, Paul, Patrick, Philip, Mary, Brigit, Felix — in the name of God — and Christ — who seeks finds.

MS. Bibl. Bodl. Junius, 85.

Against difficulty in childbirth.

Mary the Virgin bore Christ, Elizabeth the barren bore John the Baptist. I adjure you, infant, whether you are male or female, by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, that you come forth, and depart, and harm her no further, nor cause her any foolishness — amen. The Lord, seeing the weeping sisters of Lazarus at the tomb, wept before the Jews and cried: Lazarus, come forth — and he came out, bound hand and foot, who had been dead four days. Write this on wax that has never been applied to any work, and bind it under her right foot.

CHARMS. 399

A charm for bewitched land.

Here is the remedy, how thou mayst amend thine acres, if they will not wax well, or if therein any-thing improper have been done, by sorcery or witchcraft.

Take then at night, ere it dawn, four turfs on the four quarters of the land, and mark how they formerly stood. Then take oil and honey and barm and milk of every cattle which is on the land, and part of every kind of tree which is grown on the land except hard beams, and part of every wort known by name Acer pseudo except the buckbean(?) only, and add to them holy platanus. water, and then drop of it thrice upon the place of the turfs, and then say these words: Crescite, that is wax; et multiplicamini, that is and multiply; et replete, that is and fill; terram, that is this earth, etc. And say the Paternoster as often as the other formula, and after that bear the turfs to church and let a mass priest sing four masses over the turfs, and let the green surface be turned towards the altar, and then let the turfs be brought to the places where they were before ere the setting of the sun. And let the man have wrought for him four crosses of quickbeam, and let him write upon each end, "Matthew, etc." Let him lay the cross of Christ upon the lower part of the pit, and then say, etc. Then take the turfs and set them down therein, and say nine times these words: Crescite, as before, and the Paternoster as often, and then turn eastward, and lout down nine times humbly, and then say these words:

I stand towards the east
For grace I entreat
I pray the Lord glorious
I pray the Lord good and great

translation:
CHARMS. 399

A charm for bewitched land.

Here is the remedy for how you may restore your acres if they will not grow well, or if something improper has been done to them through sorcery or witchcraft.

At night, before dawn, take four pieces of turf from the four corners of the land, and note which way they originally lay. Then take oil and honey and yeast and milk from every animal on the land, and a piece of every kind of tree growing on the land except hardwood beams, and a piece of every known herb except the buckbean only, and add to these holy water, then sprinkle it three times on the place of the turfs, and say these words: Crescite, that is, grow; et multiplicamini, that is, and multiply; et replete, that is, and fill; terram, that is, this earth, etc. Say the Paternoster as often as the other formula, and after that carry the turfs to church and have a priest sing four masses over them, and let the green side be turned towards the altar, and then have the turfs brought back to the places where they were before the sun sets. Have a man make four crosses of quickbeam for you, and write "Matthew, etc." on each end. Lay the cross of Christ upon the lower part of the pit, and then say, etc. Then take the turfs and set them down in the pit, and say nine times these words: Crescite, as before, and the Paternoster as often, then turn eastward and bow down humbly nine times, and then say these words:

I stand towards the east
For grace I entreat
I pray the Lord glorious
I pray the Lord good and great

400 CHARMS.

Invoke the great Lord, pray to that stomach — Lord, I pray.
I pray to the holy guardian of the heavenly kingdom, I pray to the earth and up to heaven, and to the holy stomach, and to the power of heaven, and to the high necessity, that I may open this with the Lord's teeth, through humble thought, to speak that which is beneficial for us to fill the earth's surface with profit, through the rightful teaching of the stomach, so that he who soothes bitterness may speak thus: that it was harsh on earth in the kingdom. In the Lord's glorious name give praise, and then say the litany, and speak then: Holy, Holy, Holy — to the end. Then ring the bell, and sing the Benedicite, and the Magnificat, and the Paternoster, three times, and commend it to Christ and to Saint Mary, and to that holy company to guide and to the peoples, and to the one who owns the land, and to all those who are subject to him. When all this is done, let a man take unknown advice from almsmen and tell him two such, just as a man takes nine from him, and gather all his sweepings together, and then upon that...

I pray to the holy ruler of the heavens, I pray to the earth and to heaven above, and to the truth, to saintly Mary, and to the might of the heavens and the halls on high, that by the grace of the Lord I may through firmness of thought speak forth this incantation, and wake up the lacking crops for our worldly benefit, fill up the fields of earth with firm belief, and adorn these grassy plains — as the prophet said, that he who on earth dutifully deals out his alms to those in need shall have honor, doing his Lord's will.

Then turn yourself three times in the direction of the sun's course, and then lie stretched out along the ground and there recite the litanies, counting every saint's name as one. Then say the Tersanctus to the end; then sing the Benedicite with arms extended in the position of the crucified Jesus, and the Magnificat, and the Paternoster, three times, and commend it to Christ and to St. Mary and to the Holy Cross, for love, and for reverence, and for grace for him who owns the land, and all those who are subject to him. When all that is done, let one take unfamiliar seed from almsmen, and give them twice as much as was taken from them, and gather all his plough equipment together; then let him bore a hole in the plough beam

From a tree: fennel, and hallowed turnips, and hallowed salt. Take then the red herb, set it upon those rules of the body, speak then: "ence, ence, ence," against the mother of the womb. Grant to him, eternal almighty ruler, remedies, growing ones and thriving ones, and breeding ones and multiplying ones, and provisions — recipe for swellings: and for those swellings of the navel, a remedy; and for those white swellings, a remedy; and for all bodily swellings, a remedy. Grant him eternal glory, and his holy ones in the heavens, so that his body may be freed from all harmful ones, and he may be delivered from all evil, from all sorcery of the land. Now I bid this suffering man, that he who perceives this poison shall not be able in any way to turn it about, nor shall any man who is too cunning be able to open it, so that no venom may spread through him.

and put therein styrax and fennel and hallowed soap and hallowed salt, then take the seed as above, and put it on the body of the plough, then say,

Mother Earth ¹

God Almighty
And his hallows
In heaven who are,
That his farm be fortified
Gainst all fiends, gainst each one,

Gainst baleful blastings every one,
Which sorceries may
Through a land sow.
Now I pray the wielder of all,
Him, who made this world of yore
That there be none so cunning wife ²
That there be none so crafty man
Who shall render weak and null

translation:
And put into it styrax and fennel and consecrated soap and consecrated salt, then take the seed as described above, and place it on the body of the plough, then say:

Erce! Erce! Erce!
Mother Earth!
May the Almighty grant you,
The eternal Lord,
Fields growing
With shoots spreading freely,
Fertile, vigorous growths,
The crops of the land,
And the broad
Crops of barley
And the white
Crops of wheat
And all the
Crops of the earth.
May God Almighty
And his holy ones
Who are in heaven
Grant the owner
That his farm be fortified
Against all fiends, against each one,
And may it be defended all around
Against every harmful blight
That sorcery may
Sow across the land.
Now I pray to the ruler of all,
To him who made this world long ago,
That there be no woman so clever with words
And no man so cunning
Who could weaken and make void
Words so skillfully and neatly spoken.

Footnotes: ¹ "eopþan" is in the vocative case. ² A talkative woman.

translation:
When a man has a wound inflamed and the wound-channel festered, say then: "Be whole, you noble wine-berry; be you spread open in God's embrace, nobly filled with usefulness."

Take then meal of every kind and bake a man an unleavened loaf of bread, and knead it with milk and with holy water, and lay it under the festered wound-channel; say then: "Full of healing, noblest of wine-kin, bright blooming, you are blessed by the name of the holy one who created the heavens and the earth on which we lie; may God who laid the foundations grant us that every grain of our corn come to use." Say then three times: "Crescite. In nomine patris. Et benedici. Amen." And the Lord's Prayer likewise.

CHARMS. 405

Then let one drive forward the plough ¹ and cut the first furrow ; then say,

Hail to thee, mother earth
Mortals maintaining ;
Be growing and fertile
By the goodness of God,
Filled with fodder
Our folk to feed.

Then take meal of every kind and let one bake a broad loaf, as big as will lie within his two hands, and knead it with milk and with holy water, and lay it under the first furrow. Then say,

Land filled with fodder
Mankind to feed
Brightly blooming
Blessed become thou
For the holy name
Of him who heaven created,
And this earth
On which we live,
May the God who made these grounds
Grant to us his growing grace,
That to us of corn each kind
May come to good.

Then say thrice, "Crescite, etc." and the Paternoster thrice.

CHARMS. 405

Then let one drive forward the plough ¹ and cut the first furrow; then say,

Hail to thee, mother earth,
Sustainer of mortals;
Be growing and fertile
By the goodness of God,
Filled with fodder
To feed our people.

Then take meal of every kind and let one bake a broad loaf, as big as will fit within his two hands, and knead it with milk and with holy water, and lay it under the first furrow. Then say,

Land filled with fodder
To feed mankind,
Brightly blooming,
Be thou blessed
For the holy name
Of him who created heaven,
And this earth
On which we live.
May the God who made these grounds
Grant to us his growing grace,
So that to us every kind of grain
May come to good.

Then say thrice, "Crescite, etc." and the Lord's Prayer thrice.

¹ Sulh is feminine, Æthelstan's Dooms, xvi. p. 88; Edgar's Laws, i. p. 111.
